These norms serve as equivalent characterizations for the spectral Barron space. However, deep RL often struggles with sample inefficiency, which severely limits its applicability in real-world scenarios where data is scarce. World models have been proposed as a solution by training a generative process that simulates data from the actual environment, thereby enabling RL training without access to the true dynamics. This study examines the integration of generative models with reinforcement learning agents to more effectively solve decision problems in environments where the data distribution is unknown. Results show that the optimized agents, trained exclusively on this synthetic data, achieve sample efficiency comparable to models trained directly on real vehicles with limited data. This research expands upon our prior work, which applied the same technique to complex video games. Among these characteristics, radio emission varies significantly, defining sources as either radio-quiet (RQ) or radio-loud (RL). Recent observations reveal that some RQ galaxies exhibit jet activity detectable via either X-ray coronal emission or mid-infrared (MIR) dust radiation, a phenomenon known as "hidden" jet power. This study investigates the intrinsic links between optical line properties, low-frequency radio jets, and MIR dust radiation by analyzing a sample of 33 RQs displaying X-ray and MIR signs of hidden jets, compared against 135 RQs without such jet indicators. Our findings demonstrate that RQ jets show little dependence on black hole mass, accretion rate, or spectral shape, yet they strongly correlate with optical line luminosity, specifically the [NII] 6.5 \mu m to H$\beta$ ratio, MIR continuum, and the [OIII] 6300/5007 \AA line ratio. Additionally, utilizing a standard jet power metric, we observe a sequential increase: hidden jet power rises from samples with no jet signs to those with MIR jet signs, followed by a increase in samples with X-ray jet signs, despite overlapping uncertainties, confirming that RQ hidden jets predominantly drive dust sublimation. We propose that these outcomes are explained by standard jet properties modulated by black hole mass, accretion rate, and orientation, along with standard host galaxy properties governing AGN radiation processing via star formation and light scattering by dust. Consequently, this study establishes that standard weak jets in RQs, whether ionizing dust to produce MIR radiation, magnetized to generate sublimation zones, or confined to create X-ray coronas, are intrinsically tied to strong optical line diagnostic ratios, thus validating their hidden power. Finally, we outline future research directions for investigating these relationships. Such insights are vital for a holistic understanding of how standard weak jets externally energize and reshape their immediate surroundings, potentially influencing broader cosmic structures, for over a billion years, despite their minor contribution to total cosmic energy output. By connecting standard weak jets to highly energetic cosmic phenomena like weak BL Lacertae and microquasars, this framework offers a novel framework for examining the fundamental questions of cosmic origin and development.

MASAD was developed to support urban planners and policymakers in locating and characterizing various anomalies within metropolitan regions through spatial data. The system's efficacy was validated through three use-case studies conducted on metropolitan datasets from Delhi (India), Marseille (France), and Madrid (Spain). Additional evaluations reveal that the system can reduce the time required to pin-point anomalies in large metropolitan regions by up to 55%. Additionally, the computational efficiency of MASAD was demonstrated to be up to 45 times greater than the nearest neighbor algorithm in pin-pointing anomalies. Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by (Friedman 2007) and further explored by (Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008), this approach enables the inference of conditional independence structures within multivariate datasets. While originally formulated for fully observed data, this framework has since been extended to handle cases involving missing values (Lace 2019) and multivariate networks, as detailed in (Ghahramani 2020). GGLasso implements these latest developments, supporting both sparse and regular graph structures across datasets with missing values across multiple networks. While primarily an optimization toolkit, it includes utility functions for analyzing the resulting graphs and investigating data characteristics. For network analysis, we offer tools to calculate and examine network centrality and community detection. To validate the library's implementation, we provide a comprehensive suite of tests utilizing synthetic data, public datasets, and genetic data. All example code and resources can be accessed at https://github.com/MoGiRa/MGGLasso. Additionally, we include instructions for performing community detection and assessing network properties. This resource serves as a convenient platform for inferring interactions from multi-omics data and interpreting network outcomes through metrics such as degree distributions, clustering coefficients, and Loops. Finally, we outline how to interpret and analyze the output network using various metrics, including average link density, the Golub-Rand index, and the normalized mutual information (NMI) index.

In speech recognition systems designed for noisy environments, acoustic models trained on clean data often struggle to operate effectively when significant background noise is present. Although numerous techniques have been developed to mitigate this issue, our approach leverages pitch analysis and voicing detection to enhance speech recognition performance under noisy conditions. First, we utilize fundamental frequency analysis and voicing detection to construct likelihoods between observed noisy features and acoustic states. Second, we apply these likelihoods within an HMM-based recognition framework. Our methodology demonstrates superior performance compared to standard Gaussian-Gaussian models when significant background noise is present. Keywords: Voicing Detection, Pitch Analysis, HMM Speech Recognition, Noisy Environment.

Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) augmented by six singlet leptonic superfields. Non-zero neutrino masses arise via the inverse seesaw mechanism, facilitated by mixing among the three doublet leptonic superfields. Although R-parity remains conserved, lepton number is explicitly broken in this framework. We assess the influence of NMSSM and inverse seesaw parameters on the $B_s \to (3 \ell) + {\rm ass.}$ process, identifying eight dominant diagrams that include two-loop contributions. These effects are exponential; consequently, the diagrammatic contribution to the $(3 \ell)$ final state is significant only if the diagrammatic coupling of the NMSSM is also non-negligible. Furthermore, we examine the NMSSM contribution to the $(3 \ell)$ final state under the assumption of mass-degenerate neutrinos with a hierarchy driven entirely by the inverse seesaw mechanism, alongside linear growth of neutrino masses. Our findings indicate that the NMSSM contribution to the cross-section is several orders of magnitude smaller than the standard model value, a result consistent with the NMSSM impact on other $B_s $ decay channels. Finally, we analyze the NMSSM effect on the resonance region, observing that the neutrino mass hierarchy predominantly determines the behavior of the $(3 \ell)$ final state. Specifically, when the NMSSM contribution to the $(3 \ell)$ final state exceeds the standard model contribution, the resonance region contributes more significantly to the $(3 \ell)$ final state for a 5 deg/hierarchy than for a 25 deg/hierarchy. This is because the two-jet + $(3 \ell)$ channel includes the two-jet + $(3 \ell)_{res}$ component, which is more probable for the 5 deg/hierarchy scenario.

has emerged as a vital instrument in the deep learning field. However, despite notable recent achievements, current methods largely fail to address the high computational costs associated with training architectures on large-scale datasets. This work examines recent efforts to enhance NAS efficiency by providing a comprehensive analysis of their methodologies, outcomes, and fundamental strategies. NAS for cost reduction is generally divided into two categories: fine-tuning existing models or searching for new ones. In fine-tuning, researchers typically adjust hyperparameters related to model size, though recent proposals may also modify hyperparameters linked to training duration. When searching for new models, recent research often employs different loss functions or hyperparameters to guide the discovery of efficient architectures. This paper provides an in-depth examination of these approaches, covering methods, findings, and potential avenues for future research. Ultimately, the study aims to structure recent contributions and highlight critical future directions within this rapidly evolving area. The discussion spans various scenarios, including constant or reduced data sizes and scenarios without datasets. Overall, recent research demonstrates the feasibility of training NAS models within hours while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art models trained in weeks. Additionally, the paper explores potential reductions in computational costs through the strategic selection of evaluation metrics. Finally, significant opportunities remain for enhancing both efficiency and performance; in particular, integrating human feedback during the search process to yield models that best align with specific utilization contexts represents a promising avenue. Ultimately, the goal of this survey is to establish a framework for evaluating architectural proposals and to direct future efforts toward achieving efficient, human-centric Neural Architecture Search. For readers interested in reduced computational costs, an open-source repository containing recent proposals can be accessed at: https://github.com/b091129/NAS-Reducing-Computing-Costs.

of Federated Learning (FL). Recently, Federated Distillation (FD) has emerged as a novel FL paradigm characterized by distinct communication characteristics. FD utilizes ensemble distillation, facilitating the exchange of model outputs—expressed as soft labels—for training the client local models, while aggregating the global model through server distillation from these fed soft labels. Despite its potential, current FD frameworks suffer from inefficient communication due to unoptimized data exchange and excessive transmission volumes. To address this, we introduce a new efficient communication strategy for FD. On the client side, we propose compressed distillation data, achieving sparse representation through entropy-based truncation. We further incorporate quantization as an optional refinement to further reduce transmission costs. On the server side, we developed a novel federated distillation aggregation method that integrates ensemble soft labeling into the aggregation process. This approach leverages the diverse estimation perspectives offered by distinct client models to enhance the quality of the global model. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly improves communication efficiency without compromising learning performance. Specifically, we observe communication reduction rates exceeding 90% on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 datasets, with minor impacts on learning performance. Furthermore, comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of individual components within our proposed framework. Comprehensive cross-domain tests confirm the method's efficacy in this novel FL scenario. Furthermore, our approach exhibits robustness against backdoor attacks. Overall, this research represents a novel contribution to the emerging field of Federated Distillation. Code: https://github.com/jianli1999/FL_Code.

This study addresses dynamic orchestration in NDN-based networks where nodes possess both application-layer (APL) and network-layer (NL) applications, along with varying QoS needs for data propagation during transmission. We introduce a distributed name-based routing strategy that optimizes routing paths for multiple flows regarding end-to-end (E2E) latency while accounting for memory constraints at each node. The model is dynamic, adapting to changes in node dynamics and demand arrival patterns. End-to-End simulation results utilize Python for scripting and Ono for simulation execution. The findings demonstrate that the proposed name-based routing design achieves optimal results in most scenarios. Specifically, across multiple demand arrival instances, the design reduces E2E latency by approximately 17%, saves computational memory by over 13% compared to Cooperative Proxy Indication (CPI), and reduces latency by 10%, reducing CPU usage by roughly 11%. Finally, simulation studies assess the sensitivity of the design to parameters such as caching, routing, and E2E delay. These attributes indicate that the proposed design effectively optimizes both E2E latency and memory usage in multiple dynamic scenarios. Furthermore, the research highlights that a modest reduction in CPU usage enables an order-of-magnitude increase in throughput for a given latency target, as faster delivery allows nodes to cache and forward additional demands without exceeding their delay budgets. Overall, the proposed design successfully enhances resource utilization in dynamic scenarios. Finally, we illustrate the implementation of an ontology service using Piglet, Knack, and PyKnowledgeGraph, followed by a discussion on integrating security features into the proposed routing design.

Piglet is a Python-based framework that enables secure, scalable, and fault-tolerant processing of biological data through an mapreduce programming model. It provides fault tolerance, scalability, and a flexible programming model for handling biological data. However, its performance degrades under high demand loads, creating a need for alternative designs to handle such scenarios. This paper outlines the development and analysis of a custom routing design for NDN that incorporates dynamic caching and routing to address this issue. Our design demonstrates an ability to manage a 100,000 demand increase across multiple nodes within a short timeframe, maintaining low latency throughout the process—a capability that standard NDN protocols or PyPlinkt-based designs cannot achieve.

a stretched Euler–Bernoulli beam defined on a star-shaped metric graph with three identical edges. The edges are hinged at their outer vertices, while the central vertex allows for both translation and rotation; the rotational motion is influenced by a combination of elastic and frictional forces. We provide comprehensive findings regarding the asymptotic distribution and structure of the spectrum for the linear operator linked to the abstract spectral problem within a Hilbert space. Within this framework, we demonstrate that the eigenvectors constitute an unconditional or Riesz basis, enabling the direct derivation of exponential stability for the associated $C_0$-semigroup. Additionally, we show that the specific connectivity conditions guarantee exponential stability even in the absence of elastic effects on the edge slopes. Finally, we compare the exponential decay rates of the semigroup and its adjoint to those of a reference family of unitary operators, thereby establishing that the system's dynamics are similar to uniform contraction. Some of these outcomes extend previously established results concerning the asymptotic distribution of the spectrum for differential operators of order $2k$ on finite graphs to the specific case of a star-shaped Euler–Bernoulli beam. Similarly, other findings complement analogous findings regarding the dynamics of a star-shaped beam governed by fourth-order differential equations. Our methodology relies on several mathematical areas: the spectral theory of unbounded symmetric operators, exponential stability of $C_0$-semigroups, and the dynamics of distributed parameter systems. These areas are essential for analyzing the long-term behavior of the stretched beam model. Similarly, the specific geometry of the beam influences the results. We examine the asymptotic distribution of the spectrum for both the differential operator and its Frechet adjoint, considering the role of beam elasticity. Our primary finding is that the differential operator possesses a complete set of eigenvectors forming a Riesz basis in $L^2(\Gamma)$, a property that is not guaranteed for more general star-shaped beams or beams with concentrated parameters. Furthermore, unlike in differential operators, the differential and integral forms of the eigenvalue problem are equivalent in the context of Euler–Bernoulli beams. We also highlight that the specific geometry of the beam is not solely responsible for the exponential stability of the associated $C_0$-semigroup. Similarly, the combined effect of frictional and elastic forces on the slope does not prevent the exponential stability of the system's adjoint. These findings are supported by similar results achieved for other star-shaped fourth-order differential operators. Our approach is significantly aided by the asymptotic distribution of the spectrum

This paper demonstrates how to extend these techniques into a more comprehensive framework capable of attacking both on-policy and off-policy RL agents across diverse algorithms, environments, and task types. Specifically within gaming contexts, we illustrate how this framework can be utilized to create targeted cheats for online RL players. We compare two distinct attack strategies: direct environment manipulation versus the injection of counterfeit oracle information—including estimated state-values, return estimates, and preferred action signals—for off-policy RL agents. Our results reveal that environment manipulation is generally feasible only when the attacker possesses full access to game parameters, whereas counterfeit oracle injection is significantly easier to execute though largely limited to off-policy RL players. We anticipate that understanding the unity and diversity of adversarial RL attacks will facilitate both defensive preparations and further research in this field. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this adversarial RL cheating framework to offline RL and evolutionary strategy RL.

The primary challenges involve both the evolving dynamics and the numerical optimization required for the risk measure. To address the non-stationarity, the algorithm tracks a moving average of the risk gradient to derive the non-stationary policy gradient (NPG) update rule, establishing convergence rates for the expected return that match those of stationary RL. For the risk measure aspect, the algorithm estimates the $\mathbb{Q}$-function at each step of an episode to approximate the reward gain, followed by an average of these estimates across episodes to estimate the return gain for the policy gradient. The core algorithmic innovation enabling this convergence rate lies in utilizing the Lipschitz continuity of the entropic risk measure to bound the return gain by the product of the entropic parameter's magnitude and the average of the $\mathbb{Q}$-function values under the visiting state distribution of the policy. Consequently, the proposed method is termed Gain-Gated Q-learning (GQ-learning). Under non-stationary settings, the method achieves a regret bound of $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3}K^{1/3}+\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ represents the total steps, $K$ the number of episodes, alongside other standard parameters. Compared to existing non-stationary risk-sensitive RL approaches, GQ-learning demonstrates either a regret bound improvement or reduces dependency on the entropic parameter's magnitude—the hyperparameter controlling risk aversion. Experimental evaluations on grid worlds and a game show that GQ-learning achieves higher rewards than competing risk-sensitive algorithms across both non-stationary and stationary environments, with performance closely aligning with theoretical predictions. The volume of issues generated over time creates a detailed record of an organization's operational workflow. This record can be mined to derive insights into how projects are initiated and executed, making it valuable for both current manual monitoring and future temporal analytical studies. This paper presents an exploratory study that employs a deep learning-based title classifier to initiate basic automated manual processes, specifically tracking the open status of issues. We present empirical results on a real-world ITS containing over 3,000 issues and discuss the implications for automating both the initiation and monitoring phases. While our current method relies on title classification, it serves as a foundation for more sophisticated issue monitoring systems that may utilize additional features or methodologies in the future. However, standard DML systems relying on weighted arithmetic mean aggregation often suffer from high model loss, poor robustness to Byzantine attacks, and sluggish convergence on non-IID data. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces a novel DML framework utilizing the weighted harmonic mean. The primary objective of this paper is to introduce a Bayesian method for estimating a subset of $p$ parameters when the dimension $p$ exceeds the sample size $n$, assuming known error variance. The methodology utilizes a novel class of evidence-weighted, precision-matrix-based approximate posteriors derived from the conditional conjugate model. This framework yields explicit formulas for both approximate mean and mode estimators, which are proven to be consistent, selection consistent, and nearly optimal regarding L-risk. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates computational efficiency, is straightforward to implement, and accommodates irregular penalty matrices. We establish rigorous theoretical guarantees, including bound estimations, selection consistency, selection bias analysis, minimax lower and upper bounds for L-risk, and prove that the approximate posterior contracts to the true value at an optimal rate. The methodology is validated through simulations and applied to a genomics dataset with $n=128$ and $p$ ranging from 100 to 1,000. These experiments confirm that the method effectively identifies the true signal subset, and we further illustrate how the procedure can be adapted to handle group sparsity. These theoretical findings can be extended to other Bayesian linear models with known variance that feature analytical approximate posteriors derived from conditional conjugate pairs. high-efficiency manufacturing, this study analyzes the energy consumption optimization of a four-axis machining center utilizing the Pareto-optimal solution of a multi-objective optimization model. The planning and control of four-axis machines is crucial due to its impact on operational efficiency, quality, and energy usage. However, excessive, unnecessary, and suboptimal energy consumption occurs when the current axis control optimizer fails to account for the distinct physical characteristics of individual spindles and axes. To mitigate interspersed, superfluous, and planned energy waste, an individual axis control optimizer was tailored to the specific physical attributes of each spindle and axis of the four-axis machining center. A simulation-based energy consumption performance analysis was then conducted to evaluate the effects of these optimization strategies on the machinery's overall energy usage. Results demonstrate that the proposed individual axis control optimizer reduces the four-axis machining center's energy consumption by an average of 12.86% compared to the conventional controller. Furthermore, considering the differing power consumption rates of spindles at varying speeds, the model achieves an average further reduction in energy usage of 7.36%. These significant savings contribute to numerous low-carbon emission opportunities, offering substantial potential for widespread adoption and promotion within green manufacturing.

While both models share identical symplectic groups, their T-duality-invariant formulations result in different physical dimensions for their spectra members and yield distinct massive state contributions to the amplitudes. In these closed string models, four-point functions are governed by Moerchen's four partition functions rather than the string basis functions used in open-string involving models. Our analysis reveals that tree loop amplitudes derived from Moerchen's functions are numerically stable across the entire kinematic range. Conversely, one loop amplitudes, which are nominally closed string corrections, exhibit poor numerical stability despite being calculated using unitary worldsheet theory constraints, a stark contrast to the stable one loop amplitudes seen in semi-closed string models with the same symplectic group. We conclude by proposing an explanation for the varying numerical stability of numerically computable string amplitudes based on their winding number content. This insight is essential for determining whether the strings found in realistic string vacuum candidates, which typically possess both massless winding states and winding number zero states in their closed string spectra, yield computationally stable four-point amplitudes. Based on our analysis, the answer is not straightforward. Furthermore, we observe that in both semi-closed and closed string models, four-point amplitudes can be expressed as linear combinations of only three partition functions at both tree and loop levels. ulators, such as quantum gas microscopes, has seen significant advancement through automated correlation detection at fixed time points. However, the intrinsic dynamic nature of quantum evolution demands the explicit extraction of time-dependent characteristics. This work introduces an efficient method for automatically identifying gate control-specific unitary dynamics in multi-particle systems, utilizing lattice occupation data from experimental images or stochastic simulations. By employing a variant of the complete decoupled dictionary learning approach, this technique enables the decomposition of evolution paths into a set of fundamental dynamical trajectories. In contrast to model-dependent fitting procedures, this dictionary of motions relies on the system's physics without requiring parameter tuning for specific initial conditions. Notably, the decomposition recovers dynamics even in highly overcomplete basis sets, where traditional fitting methods fail, and in scenarios involving random many-body dynamics, thereby returning the evolution path to its generative form. This approach is expected to uncover essential information regarding controlled quantum dynamics, bridging the gap between laboratory observations and theoretical models, while also offering tools for characterizing unknown quantum states. Its efficiency relies on discarding precise timing details in favor of coarse-grained time points, highlighting its utility for coarse-grained experimental data from quantum microscopes and a broader range of interacting quantum systems. We demonstrate this decomposition using simulated microscropic images of a random circuit, showing that it successfully recovers the circuit's structure, thereby establishing the principle of correlation learning for the automatic reconstruction of quantum evolution paths from interacting many-particle systems. This work is based on R. Glaser, R. van Louwe, C. K. Thomas, C. K. Jensen, C. G. Granstrom, C. G. Granstrom, and T. B. B. B. "Dictionary Learning of Quantum Dynamics from Microscopic Images," submitted to PRL, 2022. The dataset is available at https://github.com/RicoGlaser/qm_dict. The dictionary is provided in the form of fundamental dynamical motions, which are shown to decompose the quantum circuit into its building blocks, as depicted in Figure 1 of the paper.

Utilizing a Monte Carlo approach, we incorporate uncertainties related to nitrogen production routes, stellar population synthesis inputs, and galactic evolution model parameters, thereby generating robust statistical predictions of nitrogen evolution. We further evaluate various core-collapse supernova scenarios, including the impact of nitrogen produced via the rapid neutron capture process in explosions of low-mass massive stars. When applied to a representative sample of nearby galaxies, our model successfully replicates observed radial profiles of nitrogen/oxygen ratios, and existing constraints from globular clusters and the interstellar medium support the plausible involvement of SNe Ia in nitrogen production. Our findings indicate that in most nearby galaxies, thermonuclear supernovae contribute significantly to the total core-collapse supernova nitrogen yield at various evolutionary stages, potentially accounting for up to 50% of these yields in certain systems. The inclusion of weakly convective explosions from low-mass massive stars as an additional nitrogen source helps our models align even more closely with observational data. Consequently, we propose that thermonuclear supernovae are a primary source of astrophysical nitrogen across the local universe. This conclusion supports the hypothesis that astrophysical nitrogen was a primary constituent consumed during early planetary formation in some protoplanetary disks, and it offers potential implications for interpreting stellar measurements of asymptotic giant branch stars and white dwarfs regarding primordial nucleosynthesis. Finally, we suggest that future high-precision measurements of nitrogen isotopic abundances in ancient stellar populations could serve as a robust probe of the core-collapse supernova wind yield. Specifically, neurological and mental health networks characterize inter-regional brain connectivity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), a non-invasive technique measuring blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. Edges in these networks represent functional connections, quantified as temporal correlations or coherence between raw fMRI time series. Consequently, analyzing edge alterations becomes pivotal for diagnosing neurological and psychiatric conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, autism, depression, and schizophrenia. This thesis introduces the Edge Z-score, a novel z-score metric designed to normalize edge features within network-based subgroup comparisons. The method enhances the detection of pathological changes in fMRI-derived networks by reducing comparison bias, thereby improving the accuracy of diagnosis through edge-oriented edge-centric (NOEC) machine learning classifiers utilizing the edge feature-enumerator approach for network subgroups. Using intra-individual between-subject (IBS) normalization, the NOEC classifier achieves approximately a 40% increase in classification accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art methods across two tasks: detecting Alzheimer's disease with 80% average accuracy, and classifying autism-schizophrenia comorbidity with at least 70% accuracy. Furthermore, the IBS approach facilitates between-subject functional connectivity transfer learning, leveraging a source network comparison-baseline to improve classification performance in target networks. Finally, the work outlines several open research challenges regarding the future standardization of network-based subgroup comparison analysis. The source code for the between-subgroup NOEC classifier is freely accessible and fully implemented. Should they adhere to the same physical principles as larger flares, they would generate hard X-rays (HXRs), albeit at a significantly lower intensity. A sustained and abundant occurrence of these events could supply the vast energy required to maintain the corona's high temperatures. Despite this theoretical potential, direct observations of such continuous HXR emission from the quiescent Sun have remained elusive to date. In 2010, Hudson and Diamond applied novel statistical techniques to archival solar and microlensing data to indirectly detect them. This study conducts a fresh statistical investigation into the implicit detection of solar nanoflares using the methodology previously outlined by Hudson and Diamond. We utilize updated, higher-quality data from RHESSO covering 2001–2007, alongside HXR data from RESSO for the period 2006–2007. Additionally, we compare our findings against the (non-detection) of nuclear-flare events during the same timeframe. Using this re-examined data, we establish an upper limit of approximately $10^{24}$ ergs$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ for the average emission measure of nanoflares in the quiescent corona, a代表 increase of three orders of magnitude from their earlier estimate. While various assumptions can influence this result, the ultimate conclusion remains unchanged: directly detecting nanoflares is unlikely. However, the new data allows us to refine statistical methodologies for future applications. Ultimately, the newly derived upper limit points toward an exceptionally bright population of nanoflares, implying that direct detection may become feasible with upcoming solar X-ray missions. Alternatively, an upper bound of 1 nW m$^{-2}$ for the nanosolar flare flux is derived, which exceeds the upper bound previously determined by Schrijver et al. (2009) based on HXR data. This represents the first statistically determined, observable upper limit for quiescent nanosolar flare flux. Keywords: Sun: activity -- Sun: coronal heating -- Sun: flares

The concept of quantum complexity stands as a primary driver for understanding the interior of black holes and the nature of holographic duals to anti-de Sitter spacetime. However, formulating a comprehensive definition for quantum complexity in general quantum many-body systems has proven difficult, largely because of the vast Hilbert space associated with high particle numbers. An intuitive proposal by Susskind characterizes complexity as optimizing over unitary circuits, balancing unitary depth against the number of elementary gates. Subsequent efforts to generalize this concept have yielded intriguing insights, yet definitions remain contested due to the lack of uniqueness in an optimization problem. In this paper, we propose a definition of state complexity tailored for quantum many-body systems where entropy is known or computable. We demonstrate that, for both black hole scenarios and generic quantum many-body systems, this definition shares essential features with existing proposals while ensuring a unique formulation that is amenable to calculation in many contexts. The analysis utilizes a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ recorded at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV using the CMS detector at the LHC. Event selection criteria mandate exactly two same-charge leptons (electrons or muons), moderate missing transverse momentum, and two jets characterized by large rapidity separation and a high dijet mass. The signal significance was observed at 5.5 standard deviations, compared to an expected 5.7 standard deviations under the standard model. The measured-to-expected event yield ratio at leading order is 0.90 $\pm$ 0.22, and a cross-section of 34 fb has been established for this process at next-to-leading order within a specific phase-space region. This result provides the first direct observation of electroweak same-charge pair production and serves as a valuable dataset for testing standard model predictions regarding electroweak phenomena among the least corrected. Furthermore, the data places the most stringent current constraints on several beyond-the-standard-model theories, including those predicting additional contributions to electroweak same-charge pair production. These alternative effects are significantly suppressed in the neutral current Higgs boson production process, making the two measurements complementary. Additional insights are offered regarding models featuring large couplings to third-generation fermions. Finally, this finding represents a pivotal benchmark for the interpretation of future measurements at high-energy proton-proton colliders.

Consequently, maintaining these shared files is crucial; however, numerous open-source projects suffer from duplicated maintenance efforts across multiple repositories. This duplication wastes valuable developer time. To address this, we introduce Libsyn, a system designed to facilitate the shared maintenance of library code. Libsyn allows any repository to specify its reliance on another repository's updates. Our GitHub data analysis confirms the existence of thousands of project pairs that could save approximately 2,000 hours annually if they utilized Libsyn. This capability supports use cases observed in GitHub, where libraries are depended upon by various applications without further divergence.

This study examines local moment dynamics specifically within disordered insulators, driven by short-range repulsive electron-electron interactions. We investigate paradigmatic models of interacting insulators—namely, one-dimensional Hubbard chains with quenched randomness—using density matrix renormalization group and strong-disorder renormalization group techniques. Our analysis of chains featuring random fermion hoppings or random chemical potentials, across both half-filling and away-from-half-filling regimes, reveals exponential decay in charge and fermion two-point correlations, alongside power-law decay in spin correlations characteristic of the random singlet phase. These numerical findings can be qualitatively explained by considering the large-interaction limit of the Hubbard chain, where a nearly integrable model emerges consisting of free nearly-chiral fermions that interact via a four-fermion Thomas-Fermi contact term proportional to the local charge density. This contact interaction induces the formation of local magnetic moments, resulting in a final Hamiltonian composed of nearly-chiral fermions coupled to localized spin-$1/2$ impurities. Our derived analytical spectrum for this nearly integrable system exhibits fermion and spin separations, with scaling functions for correlations that show good semi-quantitative agreement with our simulations. Notably, the spin-scaling velocity is determined by the backscattering of nearly-chiral fermions off local magnetic impurities. At both half-filling and away-from-half-filling, the spin-scaling velocity follows a $1/\sqrt{Z}$ proportionality relative to the charge-scaling velocity, where $Z$ represents the backscattering strength. Additionally, we investigate local magnetic moments near the insulator-to-metal quantum phase transition. While local moments persist at the transition, spin and fermion scalings decouple near the critical point, giving rise to a Luttinger liquid ground state. This theoretical framework supports the emergence of local moments in Mott insulators with fermion scalings but without charge gaps, such as the half-filled attractive Bose-Hubbard model, certain band insulators like La$_2$CuO$_4$, and bulk antiferromagnetic superconductors. These systems are significant because the $U(1)$ current fails to be conserved due to explicit symmetry-breaking terms in the action. We demonstrate the existence of kink solitons by analyzing a system of first-order ordinary differential equations. Despite the non-conservation of the $U(1)$ current, our methodology remains applicable for deriving topological charges and theoretically supporting the stability of these solitons. Furthermore, we find that the Montonen-Sarker-Trullinger-Bishop model supports both single-component kinks (which vanish under one component but not the other) and double kink configurations (which feature an internal excitation). We provide a topological interpretation of these solutions and present their profiles, along with profiles of associated currents and topological charges, as functions of coupling parameters. The internal excitation of the double kinks is non-oscillatory, governed by a single real frequency determined by the action's parameters. This contrasts with conservative systems possessing both single- and double-kink states, where the internal excitation is generally complex. We offer a geometric analysis of the internal excitation and discuss the stability conditions for these solitons. Our findings expand the current understanding of non-conservative soliton solutions and have potential applications in various interacting physical systems. Finally, we consider possible extensions of this study to harmonic lattice systems. Throughout the paper, natural units with $\hbar=c=1$ are employed, and $\phi$ and $\psi$ denote the two scalar fields.

While deep RL has proven effective for high-dimensional continuous control tasks, it often fails on problems characterized by sparse rewards or sensitive dynamics. Our proposed method addresses this by decomposing the task into two phases: motion planning and motion imitation. In the planning phase, a feasible trajectory is computed by directly sampling the state space using approximated dynamics, avoiding the inefficiency of exploring random control signals. Subsequently, the imitation phase trains a control policy to replicate this planned motion within the actual dynamical system. This strategy was successfully applied to derive near-optimal strategies for a pendulum swing-up task and a highly sensitive robot navigation task, completing learning in just a few hours. Although we use a simple neural network controller, integrating this algorithm with advanced motor control techniques is expected to further enhance performance. We examine two primary growth mechanisms expected to act synergistically in high-redshift, star-forming progenitors of local massive galaxies. The first involves gaseous dynamical friction, which drives stellar-mass BHs—formed in intense nuclear starbursts—toward the center, accumulating a central reservoir. The second involves binary BH mergers near the galactic center, which reduce the total BH mass as energy is radiated away during each merger. Our results indicate that in typical star-forming galaxies, the BH Eddington ratio serves as the sole regulator for the BH-to-halo mass relation, regardless of whether it is measured as the total BH mass, the mass of non-merged stellar-mass BHs, or the mass of stellar-mass BHs in double BH binaries across all cosmic epochs. Consequently, we derive two distinct scaling relations: $f_{\ast} =0.0034(0.98)[0.97+(0.06)B](M_{\ast}/M_{\odot})^{-2.28}$ for the total BH mass function and $f_{\ast} =0.0034(0.98)[0.97+(0.06)B](M_{\ast}/M_{\odot})^{-2.25}$ for the pre-merger stellar-mass BH mass function, where $M_{\ast}$ is the characteristic stellar mass, and $B$ represents the BH bulk accretion efficiency, here set to $0.25$. When integrated over the halo mass function, these relations predict the standard BH Eddington ratio $0.1(0.13)(0.15)$ for stellar-mass BHs given an $\Lambda$CDM model with a stellar BH characteristic mass of $7M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, the spread in Eddington ratios is shown to be governed by the variance in BH Eddington ratios within individual dark halos, as well as variations in stellar mass and cosmic expansion history. The fractional fluctuations in the BH mass function are primarily driven by the clumpiness of the ISM in galactic centers, the clumpiness of gas in large halos, and the variance in the star-formation rate

Nevertheless, mechanically characterizing HEAs presents substantial difficulties due to their inherent difficulty in processing and fabrication. To address this, we present a molecular dynamics (MD) framework based on the machine-learning-assisted reactive potential (ML-AEP) that enables the simulation of both canonical (compact) and porous compression tests for an arbitrary cubic HEA. By applying this model, we investigated two specific alloys, focusing on their mechanical responses to compression to evaluate the validity of the potential. Furthermore, we explored how porosity and the arrangement of pre-strain dislocations influence the compressive behavior of HEAs. Our findings indicate that porosity significantly alters the stress-strain response; specifically, at low porosity levels, the mean stress decreases while the elastic modulus remains unaffected compared to non-porous samples. Additionally, the placement of pre-strain dislocations plays a pivotal role in the mechanical behavior of both porous and canonical HEAs under compression. These results provide deep insights into the compressive behavior of HEAs when pre-strain dislocations and porosity are present, validating the highly efficient ML-AEP machine learning potential through comparison with experimental data and the reactive neural network (ReaxFF) under various physical conditions. The study also highlights the profound dislocation activity observed in HEAs during porous compression, marking it as a critical feature distinguishing HEAs from traditional alloys. Ultimately, this work paves the way for developing new testing methodologies using porous HEAs to assess their load-bearing capabilities within high-disorder systems. Furthermore, the molecular models presented here extend beyond the specific materials studied, offering a generalized methodology for predicting the mechanical response of compact and porous metallic alloys to compression. This capability enhances our understanding of macroscopic compression testing techniques, opening avenues for extensive applications where mechanical probing of metallic materials is required. Finally, the high accuracy achieved by the ML-AEP potential across a broad range of mechanical behaviors demonstrates its exceptional capacity to model chemical reactivity and mechanical phenomena in metals, positioning it as a powerful tool for investigating various phenomena central to mechanical physics. Combined with the efficiency inherent to machine learning potentials, this chemistry-focused molecular modeling approach provides extraordinary insight into the mechanical behavior of these advanced alloys, making it ideal for exploring unexplored, tunable material properties using advanced metallic HEAs. Overall, this research establishes a foundation for establishing structure-property relationships among advanced high-disorder metal systems, which is essential for their effective application across multiple fields and industries. In recent years, the scoring attack against cryptosystems has garnered substantial attention from the AI community,driven partly by the inherent challenges in creating black-box adversarial examples. Recently, Li et al. introduced the concept of inter-domain transferability in scoring attacks against lattice-based cryptosystems, demonstrating that scoring attack success is independent of specific lattice-based schemes while offering theoretical bounds for scoring attack success rates. This paper advances research in scoring attacks against lattice-based cryptosystems by leveraging bound analysis to accelerate inference during scoring attacks. Furthermore, we propose a novel inter-domain scoring attack designed for the HE-RNS scheme, which utilizes external adversarial examples to manipulate the oracle's output. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed attack achieves an attack success rate of 100% while reducing the average attack time by 4.5 times compared to the baseline approach.

While it is widely believed that quantization serves as an implicit regularizer enhancing generalization, this concept has lacked formalization. This paper models binary weights in a perceptron as a random variable within a specific probability distribution. By extending this framework, we derive a novel random feature model known as the Gaussian Shrinkage Feature (GSF), which includes the Möbius feature as a specific case. Leveraging the analysis of the perceptron error bound, we prove that increasing the analysis point of the GSF reduces generalization error, a finding supported by experimental data. The holographic R\'enyi entropy inequality, which corresponds to the convexity of the associated polytope, stands as a single, non-trivial constraint among all such inequalities. It serves as a foundational element in defining the hologamixoid, the first non-trivial entropy monoid extending beyond standard quantum mechanics. This study examines the connection between polyhedral geometry and various mathematical structures designed to encode entropy monoids, with a specific focus on: (i) entropy exclusion principles; (ii) the entropy exchange principle; (iii) the weak strong subadditivity exclusion principle; (iv) the strong strong subadditivity exclusion principle; and (v) a general class of entropy exclusion principles derived from the weak strong complementarity principle. These concepts are illustrated using the specific context of the hologamixoid. Additionally, the work generalizes the construction of entropy monoids via polyhedral methods to encompass a broader range of dual quantum systems. Finally, it establishes a lower bound for the rank of any proposed quantum entropy monoid that satisfies the convexity of the corresponding entropy polytopes, leveraging the concept of the gamma invariant. This lower bound is demonstrated to be achievable within specific subclasses of the hologamixoid, thereby linking the gamma invariant directly to the rank of the algebra. These findings may offer valuable insights into the structure of a potential gravity dual for quantum field theory. Additionally, the principles regarding exclusion and entopy exchange are generalized to dual quantum systems. Any comments or suggestions are welcome. Furthermore, the author requests that the title "Dual Quantum Systems, Holography, and Entropy Monoids" be retained, as the terms "dual quantum systems" and the "hologamixoid" were coined by the author to represent a specific class of quantum systems that share the same dual geometric polytopes.

In this work, we construct GFF-valued processes on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ driven by an SLE$(\kappa)$ and its extensions, where $\kappa \geq 8$. We demonstrate that these processes generate a GFF-valued process on the imaginary surface corresponding to the SLE. While imaginary surfaces for SLE with $\kappa \in [4,8)$ were previously handled by Miloshenko and Sheffer, who noted that defining them via GFFs on domains bounded by SLE paths requires substantial modification and remains an open problem, we adopt a different approach by defining them directly through domains and GFFs. Using both methodologies, we subsequently derive conformal invariance results for both the SLE and the GFF. Moreover, conceptually, our findings suggest that the SLE can be viewed as a "gradient flow" for the GFF valued on the imaginary surface. Finally, many concepts from quantum gravity find natural home on imaginary surfaces rather than on the original domain traced by SLE. For instance, the imaginary surface supports a canonical canonical quantum quantum surface (CQUS) measure, defined as the law of a GFF conditioned to have no winding between $0$ and $\infty$, which serves as a quantum analogue to the Radon–Nikodym density of the CQUS measure relative to harmonic measure. This contrasts with the original domain, where no canonical quantum surface measure exists without additional assumptions. We further prove that both the imaginary surface and the CQUS measure are invariant under conformal maps generated by chordal SLE. These concepts are fundamental to both original and extended SLEs with SLE-decorated GFFs, where the GFF interacts with the path according to specific rules. Notably, in the original domain of chordal SLE with SLE-decorated GFF, we establish for the first time a canonical quantum surface measure and explore its relationship with the imaginary surface. These developments represent the foundational step toward quantum reversal theory, as outlined in Quantum Reversal Theory – I and – II. Keywords: Imaginary surface; Gaussian free field; SLE; Quantum surface;

This work represents a specific instance of a broader paper by H-O Kreiss and J. Lorenz, which extends their primary findings to higher dimensions. While the established estimates demonstrate continuity with respect to the initial data, the associated constant grows factorially at higher orders. Consequently, if the initial data possesses high-order regularity, the corresponding constant remains bounded. Our approach draws inspiration from F.-J. Schüfftan's methodology for the 2D case, which he detailed in an unpublished manuscript from 1977. An essential instrument in this work is a generalized version of the Bernoulli inequality, previously utilized by the author in previous research. That tool demonstrates that the maximum norm of any intermediate-time derivative is controlled by the maximum norm of the initial data multiplied by a constant that depends solely on the spatial dimension and the derivative order. Furthermore, we examine how these estimates evolve when the initial data is perturbed, highlighting the impact of the initial constant on the large norm behavior of the solutions. Finally, an overview of related literature is provided. These findings are dedicated to Prof. Michael J. Strauss. (One page)

demonstrating to a computationally limited client that the output of a circuit $C$ is correct. This area sits at the intersection of quantum computing and complexity theory. Currently, the leading protocol relies on interactive proof systems utilizing quantum cross-probing, which depends on the existence of fully homomorphic encryption. These proofs are extremely intricate and offer only modest improvements over the best known linear quantum error-correcting codes. Consequently, there is a growing need for simpler verification methods.

We introduce a verification scheme based on the Hadamard test rather than cross-probing by assuming a set of quantum one-time pads. In this framework, the client prepares these pads and the circuit $C$ by applying random Hadamard gates to basis states. Verification proceeds in two phases: first, the client checks that the server's output matches the applied random Hadamard gates; second, the client performs a Hadamard test to confirm that the resulting states are identical. We demonstrate that this protocol is both simple and secure, requiring just two rounds of interaction and placing the security burden on classically held secrets instead of quantum ones. Furthermore, when the circuit $C$ corresponds to a specific type of random unitary error-correcting code, the protocol is secure if the Schur-Weyl duality binding key is information-theoretically secure. Most significantly, this enables the efficient verification of post-selected quantum computation with simple encryption keys. Since post-selected quantum computation is believed to be classically simulatable, our approach represents the inaugural verification method that is not contingent upon fully homomorphic encryption. Finally, we extend this scheme to create a straightforward scheme for verifying quantum polynomial time computation.

Most quantum computing applications are unlikely to benefit from the complexity of cross-probing proofs. Our approach is particularly well-suited for scenarios involving repeated quantum computations, such as quantum machine learning where circuit $C$ may be queried thousands of times. By employing quantum one-time pads and applying quantum encryption directly to computed states rather than performing multiple quantum computations under encryption, our method reduces the number of interactions to two. We also discuss how to generalize this scheme to handle arbitrary circuits. Additionally, we examine two rounds of interaction where measurements are performed by both the server and the client, highlighting its relevance to quantum machine learning. Specifically, we show that computational limits can be lowered from computationally secure to statistically secure by making fewer assumptions about quantum one-time pads—shifting from learning-with-error to orthogonal design learning to preprocessing key generation. However, recent developments in reinforcement learning suggest a distinct and potentially superior model for understanding the biological mechanisms of spatial perception and navigation. This study examines reinforcement learning within homogeneous environments using circular (polar) and 2D Cartesian coordinate systems. We demonstrate, through agent simulations, that these representational systems are more efficient than their 3D counterparts. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the information geometry inherent in circular coordinates eases certain mathematical challenges in reinforcement learning, likely contributing to their evolutionary stability in animals. These aspects offer a potential explanation for why primate spatial neural systems adopt a 2D circular geometry embedded within 3D Euclidean space. Additionally, our results reveal that the advantages of circular coordinates in reinforcement learning may be more widespread than previously thought, as they could significantly benefit agents operating in complex, non-homogeneous, or hostile environments. Finally, we investigate mixed coordinate systems that evolve based on task context, providing an explanation for the emergence of such systems in certain animal species. We emphasize a key benefit of circular geometry in spatial cognition: its natural alignment with temporal evolution under uniform sampling, a property that may be vital for both biological and artificial spatial systems. Ultimately, this research aims to advance current computational and mathematical approaches to the learning and processing of spatial information in animals by incorporating emerging representations in these domains. Furthermore, our proposed methodologies hold potential applications in novel, efficient artificial coordinate systems for future robotics and navigation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/HeshmatyLab/spatial-geometry-reinforcement-learning. Recently, neural networks have become the dominant approach for SELD, with convolutional, recurrent, and attention mechanisms being widely utilized to address various SELD scenarios and efficiently model temporal and spectral dimensions. These networks generate short-term features that are converted into a long-term representation via global average pooling before final classification and direction estimation; however, this global averaging can lead to performance degradation. To mitigate this issue, this paper introduces an Inverted Residual Attention Module (IRAM) designed to capture local patterns and enhance performance. Additionally, we propose an Attention Map Refinement Module (AMRM) to improve the accuracy of the attention mechanisms within IRAM. The proposed model was evaluated on two datasets: ESC-50 and SoundScene. Results demonstrate that our method surpasses baseline models in SELD tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance regarding detection and classification on the ESC-50 dataset and attaining zero failure to detect and zero false alarm on the SoundScene dataset. Furthermore, the model exhibits high performance in direction estimation across both datasets. To support future research, the implementation code has been made available at https://github.com/aryan-akhtar/Inverted-Residual-Attention-Module. This repository allows users to access sound files from the SoundScene dataset and test the model to visualize the attention map activation regions. Additionally, the SoundScene dataset utilized in this study can be obtained from https://data.vicwitalski.com/soundscenecomplete/ at a compression ratio of 0.127. Replicating the results requires a GPU with a minimum of 8GB VRAM. Consequently, direct attribution of these sound files is not feasible without violating privacy principles. However, the SoundScene package includes annotations indicating whether sounds were recorded indoors, outdoors, or in mixed environments, enabling the model's evaluation and comparison on this dataset. Conversely, recent wireless applications have explored the benefits of allowing simultaneous transmission by intentionally managing and even leveraging signal interference. Prominent techniques such as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), joint source-channel coding, and compute-and-forward rely on advanced encoding and decoding strategies, demanding significant computational effort from receivers. Unlike most research focusing on interference mitigation, decoding efficiency, and performance analysis, this work addresses the practical challenge of minimizing execution costs—specifically CPU cycles and consumed electricity—when using these methods. We assess the feasibility of performing computations alongside NOAMA decoding on resource-constrained edge devices within an Internet of Things (IoT) context using realistic hardware profiles. Our comprehensive computational analysis reveals that while NOMA enhances spectral efficiency, it can paradoxically increase computational complexity under certain conditions. Central to this finding is the significant impact of gate activation delays on the processing times of resource-limited edge devices. Leveraging these profile data, we propose practical algorithms for simultaneously designing NOMA superpositions and the computational architectures of their receiving devices. Simulation results validate that these methods can significantly lower processing costs—at the expense of moderate increases in communication latency—without compromising overall wireless system performance. Furthermore, we extend this research to compute-optimal designs for IoT edge devices capable of absorbing a specific quantity of inter-device interference. Experimental evaluations confirm that simultaneous transmission combined with the proposed device architecture can accelerate diverse computational workloads by rapid, energy-efficient processing on simultaneous receiving devices. This approach marks a substantial step toward utilizing wireless channels for decentralized, simultaneous computation among edge devices within an IoT framework. Finally, we illustrate a scenario involving two smart meters simultaneously transmitting video data from surveillance cameras to a central server, where utilizing NOMA and the proposed device architecture results in substantial reductions in CPU consumption and electrical usage. We anticipate that this study will inspire further investigations into simultaneous computation architectures within IoT environments. Supplementary materials, including additional figure details and source codes for replicating our experimental results, are available at https://i2pm.kaist.ac.kr/Publications/. However, the stochastic structure of GAF zero sets is complex, hindering direct theoretical analysis. This study investigates spectrogram analysis by examining the stochastic geometric properties of their level sets. We derive rigorous theorems validating the use of level sets for signal detection and estimation within hidden Markov models (HMMs). Although computing exact level sets is generally intractable, we propose a simple and efficient approximation method. These theorems establish that level set geometry possesses rigorous statistical properties suitable for signal analysis. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that both maxima and level sets achieve accurate time-frequency localization. Furthermore, the proposed HMM-based signal estimation leverages rich stochastic geometric properties of level sets to generate precise estimates even in high-noise conditions where maxima fail. Finally, although HMMs are not always necessary for analysis, we demonstrate their critical role in signal estimation. By observing the random evolution of level sets over time, we construct next-state transition probability functions for HMMs, revealing how the latent state's dynamics depend on observable features. This approach proves effective for detecting periodic signals embedded in random noise by utilizing both maximum likelihood estimation and level set geometry. Both simulations and real-world experiments confirm the efficacy of the level set approach. Key findings include the derivation of the first rigorous theorems on level set statistics and the application of these theorems to signal analysis and estimation. distinct flavors of El Niño—the East Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP)/Modoki types—affect global climate variability. While many prior studies relied on linear multivariate statistics or composite analysis, the former often assumes a consistent linear statistical dependency across all phases of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), an assumption that may not hold given the inherent nonlinear characteristics of these events. This study statistically assesses the EP and CP patterns within the composite time series of selected sea level pressure (SLP) and tropical precipitation anomalies. Using 20 overlapping 11-year High Pass Filters to isolate intra-decadal variability, we analyze 23 years of Topex/Poseidon satellite altimetry-derived global mean SSTs, correlated against 23 years of satellite microwave radiometer-measured global landfalling rainfall. An Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) of the satellite SST record isolates the decadal component, enabling a correlation analysis with global sea surface temperature variations derived from Atlantic, Pacific, and Antarctic ocean heat content. Our findings indicate that composite SLP anomalies contain two flavor structures: an EP flavor dominant in the first half of the record and a CP flavor emerging in the second half, supported by statistically significant time-dependent cross-spectral coherence between filtered SLP and intra-decimal SSTs. Furthermore, a declining power spectral density in filtered SLP anomalies toward the latter part of the dataset reveals a concurrent shift in the EP to CP flavor. Finally, we correlate the intra-decimal SST component from EMD with filtered SST variations in the Pacific, Southern, and Atlantic oceans, examining their respective contributions to the decadal climate shift. Specifically, the component from the Southern Ocean is found to be the primary driver of the EP flavor, while the Atlantic plays a greater role in the CP flavor. This decay is attributed to an EP-to-CP flavor shift occurring during strong La Niña cold events in the Southern Hemisphere. Furthermore, a component of deep internal variability, rather than stochastic noise, drives the decadal climate shift, consistent with earlier observations. These results may assist in predicting future EP-to-CP transitions in ENSO impacts on global climate. Furthermore, as both EP and CP flavors are now recognized as distinct within the ENSO regime, these flavors should be considered when evaluating future EP/CP impacts, such as those on stratospheric ozone.

We present a potentially significant observational indicator of MBH formation within dwarf galaxies: a continuous mass spectrum of MBHs in these systems would imply a primary formation mechanism dependent on the gas mass of the host galaxy's dark matter halo. Additionally, a simultaneous campaign to measure gas kinematics in these systems would help mitigate current challenges regarding assumed inclination and outer boundary conditions. This approach would enable a more rigorous phasing of our current error sources, ultimately facilitating a substantial expansion of our MBH hunting campaign and the prospects for kinematic searches in larger samples of dwarfs.

Although flat bands are well-known in geometrically frustrated structures like the kagome lattice, they can also emerge dynamically in systems featuring competing interactions or couplings. The kinetic coupling between ultra-cold atoms and optical lattices offers the advantage of accessing both symmetric and asymmetric flat-band scenarios, alongside the ability to smoothly adjust bandwidth-to-bandwidth ratios, interaction strengths, and dimensionalities. This review examines flat-band physics in ultracold atom systems, detailing recent and forthcoming experiments that reveal in interaction-driven unconventional superfluidity, frustration-driven quantum spin liquid-like behavior, and various topological effects, many of which rely on flat bands. deciphering the mutual dynamics within time series. This research presents an innovative approach to forecasting the future synchronization states of two financial time series. Specifically, we employ cross-recurrence plot analysis as a nonlinear technique to quantify multidimensional coupling in the time domain and assess synchronization levels. By utilizing a deep learning framework, we predict synchronization states based on diagonal recurrent rates extracted from recurrence plots generated through recurrence mapping. We apply this forecasting methodology to the time series of Apple and Microsoft. Our findings indicate that the synchronization between these companies follows a binary state: either they are not synchronized or they are fully synchronized. Furthermore, there is a high probability of accurately predicting their future synchronization states. Finally, we evaluate the efficacy of using future cross-recurrence features to forecast synchronization, revealing that utilizing future cross-recurrence rates slightly enhances prediction performance compared to relying on historical data. These results suggest that leveraging future cross-recurrence rates is a viable approach to anticipate the future evolutionary dynamics of two financial systems. Additionally, this study offers a fresh perspective on assessing multidimensional coupling in financial systems. Our work also provides a novel approach for determining whether two time series are synchronized in multi-state scenarios and for predicting their future synchronization states. We believe this research has significant practical implications for traders and portfolio managers. Specifically, our findings suggest that leveraging future cross-recurrence rates can potentially generate excess returns. This is particularly relevant given the intricate, nonlinear relationships between key market drivers and the inherent unpredictability of synchronization patterns. Our outcome measures include the accuracy of synchronization state predictions and the average annual return achieved by a trader utilizing this method. Although building codes and fire standards typically restrict highly flammable exterior materials like certain insulated metal panels, current regulations lack specific provisions regarding their safe exposure duration after smoke damage. This study addresses this gap through an analytical model that evaluates the relationship between visible smoke exposure, wall material properties, and the risk of igniting overlying roof structures. The model accounts for the optical transmission of wall materials, the radiant emission of damaged walls acting as black bodies, and the absorptivity of the roof to radiation. By simulating wild-fire events with varying burn times, the model calculates the thermal equilibrium between the roof and the ambient ambient air to assess wildfire-induced roofing failures. Results indicate that building envelopes with low optical transmission offer better protection against smoke, delaying the threshold beyond which walls become too hot to prevent roof failure. Specifically, every 10% increase in a wall material's optical absorptivity extends the safe burn time by approximately 1 minute, while every 10% increase in optical transmissivity adds about 17 minutes to the safe burn time. Consequently, building designers can utilize this model to select wall materials with higher optical absorptivity (and lower transmissivity) when anticipating the potential loss of visibility due to smoke. Furthermore, this modeling approach can be extended to other scenarios such as fires in commercial spaces or wildfires affecting glass curtain walls. Ultimately, this work offers a method to estimate the safe exposure time following wild-fire damage, thereby informing decisions on whether damaged buildings can be safely occupied following cleaning. We introduce a privacy framework based on Rényi divergence to bound the expected loss of privacy for conditionally dependent data. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of achieving this level of privacy under Gaussian process conditional priors. In simultaneous resource allocation scenarios where multiple agents must allocate resources without full knowledge of others' preferences, learning these preferences requires communication. Under a non-cooperative game framework, we demonstrate that, in the limit of infinite communication, the learned Nash equilibrium converges to the von Neumann max-min value of zero-sum games or to the saddle point of constant-sum matrix games. We also examine an intermediate scenario involving limited communication to evaluate the accuracy of predicted payoffs. This research builds on our previous work [1].

We address the challenge of generating synthetic traffic datasets that mirror the characteristics of real data for training location recommendation systems. This problem is critical because numerous location apps rely on user data, necessitating a robust assessment of potential privacy risks. Specifically, we aim to synthesize trajectories that are conditional on a subset of the original data to guarantee privacy for the remaining locations. To achieve this, we develop a conditional generative model that learns the joint distribution of multiple trajectories, enabling the synthesis of new routes given a shared subset. This approach ensures that synthetic trajectories follow similar patterns while maintaining user privacy. We validate this methodology using both a single trajectory and multiple trajectories from New York City and San Francisco. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves high utility in both inference and synthesis tasks. This work builds on our prior publication [1].

(NLP) applications designed for code-mixed (CM) or multilingual text, driven largely by the widespread use of language mixing in social media within diverse, multilingual regions such as India, Mexico, parts of Europe, and the USA. Although word embeddings are fundamental components of modern NLP systems, handling CM text remains an uncharted area because existing methods fail to address its unique characteristics effectively. This paper introduces position-sensitive embeddings, a technique designed to improve the representation of code-mixed text by modifying standard embeddings to account for the specific language (English or Hindi in this study) at each token position. This straightforward yet powerful approach not only enhances existing embedding algorithms but also lowers the risk of model bias when processing multilingual text. Consequently, the authors hope these embeddings will foster greater community interest and research in complex linguistic scenarios like CM text. Experimental results across various Indian languages demonstrate that the proposed method significantly surpasses state-of-the-art embeddings in most cases. Specifically, for English-Hindi mixtures, the results indicate an approximate 2% to 5% increase in accuracy compared to current leading embeddings. Furthermore, the experimentally observed drop in performance when processing Italian-Hindi mixed text compared to English-Hindi confirms that language specificity is crucial when applying these embeddings to new linguistic pairs. This approach enabled we to identify the most significant "soft" phonon modes and map out the various displacive and charge disordered metastable phases within the parent compound of RbSnF$_3$. Specifically, we determined that all metastable structures, when displaced from the high-symmetry paraelectric phase by approximately 5% of the idealized antiferrodistortive superlattice period, exhibit spontaneous polarization. Our findings indicate that displacive antiferrodistortive metastable phases possess lower total energies than their ferrodistortive counterparts, and both are energetically more favorable than the naturally occurring charge disordered variant. These findings offer fresh insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing the diverse transitions observed in RbSnF$_3$ and hold broad significance for other transition materials. Additionally, they provide a robust numerical framework for theoretically determining the likely metastable structures of such materials under external strains. Both the predicted structures and the computational techniques described can guide experimentalists in creating specifically designed displacive antiferrodistortive and ferrodistortive metastable phases and their respective domain structures. Such engineered materials hold potential for applications in modern nanoscale device technology and materials science. for thruster-assisted bipedal robot walking. Assuming well-tuned supervisory controllers, we concentrate on refining desired joint trajectories to meet specific performance goals. To ensure these constraints are met, we develop an intermediary filter grounded in reference governors. Since modifications and impact events cause deviations from desired periodic orbits, we robustly guarantee hybrid invariance by employing predictive schemes within a brief time window during the gait cycle. We achieve this hybrid invariance by utilizing the distinctive capabilities of our thruster-based model. The primary advantage of this approach is that, after rigorous training, the thruster-assisted gait operates autonomously, requiring minimal human intervention during actual walking. Furthermore, the thruster's capacity to generate substantial impulses enables the robot to successfully execute diverse dynamic walking behaviors, including high-speed progression, lateral locomotion, and thoracic rotation. Simulation and experimental outcomes validate the proposed methodology. Finally, to establish the advantages and potential future applications of thruster-assisted bipedal walking, we compare the proposed methodology with existing control techniques. Specifically, unlike prior approaches, our thruster-assisted bipedal robot walking ensures hybrid invariance while fulfilling performance constraints over predictable gait cycles. This innovative technique establishes a robust foundation for developing supervisory control architectures for bipedal robots, advancing the development of energy-efficient human-like locomotion and contributing to the broader goal of operational autonomy for bipedal robots. The underlying research was published in the book \textit{Advances in Modern Control and Development Methods}, edited by Dr. Saeid Nahavandi and published by Itech publishers in 2020 (ISBN 978-953-51-6659-1), under the chapter title \textbf{\textit{Performance Constraints Satisfaction and Thruster-Assisted Gait Design for Bipedal Robot Walking}}, which can be accessed at \url{https://www.intechopen.com/books/10.5772/intechopen.9789535166584}.
