Additionally, we investigate how to determine the stress tensor when dealing with a broader range of hairy black holes. In these instances, we argue that the Extremality Theorem necessitates that certain extremality conditions be imposed on the full nonlinear metric to compute the stress tensor accurately. We also explore related methodologies for deriving a similar form of stress tensor. Finally, we highlight a parallel between our findings and those regarding charged extremal holes in AdS/JLA, as detailed in arXiv:1704.05826.

Existing approaches utilize various memory mechanisms to store navigation history for this purpose, though they typically depend on a pre-mapped representation of the unknown space, such as occupied area maps or navigation option maps derived from simulation or real-world data. This reliance limits their applicability to real-world scenarios, as accurate pre-mapping is often impractical. To address this, we propose remembering sensory information instead of raw action histories. Specifically, we utilize a co-memory to save both visual observations and laser rangefinder data, enabling the agent to retrieve relevant information about its current location as it progresses toward the goal. Furthermore, we employ a specific architecture designed to encode this co-memory efficiently. This architecture facilitates goal-conditioned planning and the selection of appropriate actions to navigate the environment. Our evaluations, conducted using the TORC simulator, demonstrate that these methods enhance navigation performance. We obtain comparable results to prior state-of-the-art methods that rely on pre-mapping unknown environments, while our approach requires no a priori mapping of the space and exhibits strong potential for deployment in real-world contexts. Additionally, detailed qualitative results are provided to offer insights into how agents effectively utilize the encoded co-memory for navigation. This work reports results from our submission to the 2021 CVPR Challenge on Goal-oriented Navigation using Real-World Images in Indoor Environments. We review several prominent arguments found in the literature that justify the necessity of complex formalism and offer additional insights by introducing alternative perspectives. Our goal is to reinforce the challenging pedagogical task of explaining why Quantum Mechanics requires complex numbers. Specifically, we present and discuss an alternative mathematical formulation of QM built entirely upon real numbers. Next, we review the standard pedagogical explanation found in most QM textbooks regarding the fundamental reason for the involvement of complex numbers; we demonstrate that this approach suffers from significant weaknesses and leaves many students with puzzling questions. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive mathematical construction of our real-number-based quantum formalism. This approach avoids the pitfalls of the conventional explanation by fulfilling a set of criteria and establishing QM over the real numbers through carefully designed transformations within the existing Hilbert space framework over complex numbers. Finally, we provide computational tools available in Python to facilitate an interactive exploration of this real-number-based quantum formalism. This practical component serves as a crucial complement to the theoretical exposition, enabling both students and instructors to build the formalism and grasp the following statement: "the quantum formalism based on real numbers can be no simpler." These resources are intended to support students developing independent research proposals on the foundations of QM, as well as instructors and researchers constructing advanced courses, such as those focused on the mathematical foundations of the theory or quantum information. Additionally, they can assist anyone interested in fundamental questions regarding the possible involvement of complex numbers in quantum formalism by providing a robust, consistent, and relatively simple set of mathematical tools already established in the literature. The computational resources will be accessible via GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Rui-Liu111/QM-real-numbers. This resource comprises computer algebra code implementing the quantum formalism based on real numbers, accessible through a set of probabilistic models available in both Julia and Python, along with a comprehensive user guide explaining the code. This foundation has previously been utilized to elucidate quantum models in scientific literature, including hidden variable theories, superdeterministic theories, superquantum non-signaling theories, and general probabilistic theories. We extend our gratitude to this GitHub platform for facilitating this interactive presentation.

Keywords: Quantum Mechanics, Mathematical Foundations, Quantum Information, Computational Physics, Julia, Python.

of compactly supported homeomorphisms on a Tychonoff space, such as viewing it as a colimit of homeomorphism groups with fixed compact supports or as a subgroup within the homeomorphism group of the space's Stone-\v{C}ech compactification. A space possesses the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property (CSHP) when these two topologies are identical. The authors introduce methods demonstrating that products of specific spaces with CSHP—like the Long Line and the Closed Long Ray—retain the CSHP. Additionally, conditions under which disjoint unions of spaces with CSHP also exhibit this property are examined. The primary criterion established for a Tychonoff space X to have CSHP involves the relationship between compact subsets and closed subsets that are both uniformly approachable by compact subsets. The study further investigates the connection between CSHP and the uniformization property regarding compact subsets. Notably, complete locally compact Hausdorff spaces with no non-trivial convergent sequences are the sole Hausdorff spaces that are compactly supported homeomorphic to their one-point compactifications. Research is also conducted on "weak" versions of CSHP; a space has the Weak Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property (WCSHP) if the compactly supported homeomorphism group coincides with the induced subgroup from the Stone-\v{C}ech compactification's homeomorphism group. While every space with CSHP also has WCSHP, examples exist where WCSHP holds without CSHP. Finally., spaces where the compactly supported homeomorphism group equals the induced subgroup are defined as having the Strong Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property (SCSHP). Every space with CSHP has SCSHP, and examples exist where SCSHP exists without WCSHP. The investigation reveals that the ordinal sum of the Long Line and a point is the unique Tychonoff space that is strong compactly supported homeomorphic to its one-point compactification. Similar patterns are explored for other "small" spaces, such as the Irrational Line. Lastly, the issue of factorizing homeomorphism groups into short exact sequences is briefly mentioned.

This work demonstrates the successful growth of monolayer bismuth on n-doped graphene (n-dG) on SiC substrates at temperatures low enough to avoid bi-layer formation. Due to the substantial lattice mismatch between bismuth and graphene, the domains are extremely small, causing intrinsic low-energy loss signals from the bi-layer to be obscured by those from the single-layer. Additionally, the large mismatch results in a non-hexagonal net of atomic columns visible in scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images, alongside blurring in transmission electron microscopy images caused by a high density of defects within the graphene lattice. Given the strong affinity of bismuth for oxygen, post-deposition air exposure is expected to generate even more numerous defects in the graphene layers. To effectively characterize the monolayer bismuth, we calculated Stokes shift and group delay maps from electron energy loss spectroscopy data, effectively isolating the single-layer signal from the bi-layer signal for the first time. Our findings indicate that the bismuth monolayer is flat, net-hole doped, and exhibits a high mobility estimated between 265 and 609 cm²/Vs. These results establish the feasibility of growing various material monolayers directly on graphene using remote epitaxy, enabling access to a broad spectrum of potential materials for novel applications. Furthermore, the developed growth and characterization techniques hold promise for application beyond the bismuth-graphene system.

We demonstrate that the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) construction serves as a left adjoint to this restriction process. To correctly define this adjoint relationship, it must be understood as a weak natural transformation—a 1-morphism within an appropriate 2-category—instead of merely as a functor mapping between categories. This optimized framework successfully isolated heart sounds in 75% of previously inaudible recordings (those lacking audible heart sounds) and improved the average noise reduction ratio across the dataset from 30.47 dB to 14.65 dB. Ultimately, we demonstrate that extracting heart sound features alongside BWN during acquisition, combined with training a CNN on thermal representations of these noise characteristics, is feasible and effectively leverages non-diagnostic signals to elevate diagnostic performance, particularly in signals obscured by heavy noise. This research was conducted using simulated heart sound data generated by the Japanese Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science, and Technology. Mathematics & Statistics has aimed to cultivate an inclusive and welcoming environment for all students pursuing mathematics. Historically, our strategy to address the lack of diversity in our majors focused on remediation, attempting to fix perceived student deficits through specific programming. However, in recent years, we have shifted to an anti-deficit approach that prioritizes transforming the department itself. The initiatives detailed below reflect this shift, designed to strengthen community, foster collaboration, and improve the overall climate within our department. We invite all math departments to consider these ideas as they plan their own initiatives, encouraged to adapt them to fit their unique contexts. As our motto asserts, "We do math TOGETHER."

The "Math Coffee Hour" was initiated in Fall 2019 to give students a casual space to build a sense of belonging within our department. Every two weeks, undergraduate and graduate students gather over coffee and donuts to connect with one another and our faculty. This informal setting allows our graduate students, who spend most of their time isolated by research, to engage with the broader mathematical community. Furthermore, it enables undergraduates to interact with diverse role models in mathematics, including those from underrepresented groups. Essential to this hour is its low-barrier, anti-deficit nature; it requires minimal preparation and allows participants to focus on personal interests or simply chatting. This has successfully created a platform for students to network within and across our department, with many forming collaborations on research and outreach based on shared passions. Additionally, the informal atmosphere has enabled meaningful conversations between students and faculty regarding our department's climate, directly influencing the decisions made through other initiatives like this one.

In collaboration with our Student Government and other student leaders, we have worked to improve the overall student experience within our department through various outreach and programming efforts. One significant undertaking was a comprehensive and ongoing needs assessment conducted across both undergraduate and graduate student populations in both written and oral formats to better understand our student body and identify the most pressing climate issues to address. Findings from this assessment have been shared with our Faculty Senate and used to guide future initiatives that genuinely reflect student needs and desires. Another key project is the "First-Day of School" program, which has been running for over a decade to help first-year undergraduates transition from high school to college by covering their first week's logistical challenges. Recently, the day has expanded to give undergraduates a broader overview of graduate opportunities within our department, featuring a presentation by a recent PhD recipient and time for asking questions. perceived credibility of an auction format influences bidding strategies and final results. Through a series of laboratory experiments, we assigned a human subject to the role of seller, who retained the auction revenue and, contingent on the experimental treatment, possessed the authority to manipulate the outcome. Our findings indicate that in the non-credible version of the second-price auction, the vast majority of bids fall between the theoretical predictions of the first-price and credible second-price auctions. Although participants in this non-credible setting attempt to infer the seller's actions, their efforts are largely unsuccessful. Furthermore, the seller's ability to distort results is significantly more impactful when buyers believe credibility is absent. We attribute these outcomes to two primary factors: (i) buyers adopt a defensive strategy, bidding higher in a non-credible second-price auction to avoid overpaying, and (i)) sellers are more likely to raise prices under a non-credible framework, knowing that bids will exceed the true value. These data align with a new theoretical bidding rule derived from Bayesian Nash Equilibrium, which posits that in a non-credible second-price auction, bidders should submit offers between the credible second-price reserve price and the value of their prize. Finally, we investigate the enduring nature of these effects across multiple repeated auctions, discovering that while behavioral effects persist, they diminish markedly with increased repetition. Crucially, even after many repetitions, buyers continue to bid significantly higher than in a credible second-price auction, and the effects of seller credibility on raised prices remain strongly present. These results suggest that buyers should exercise caution when utilizing the second-price auction in a non-credible context, as they risk paying substantially more than in a credible scenario. Furthermore, policymakers should be aware that public auctions, even when conducted by a trusted official, may yield higher prices if they are perceived as non-credible. Finally, our result regarding the slowing impact of seller credibility on bidding behavior after numerous repetitions contradicts the rapid learning hypothesis found in private value auctions, instead supporting the gradual learning hypothesis.

Our proposed solution involves a novel class of symmetric teleparallel gravity known as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ mediates gravitational interactions, potentially addressing several unresolved issues. To investigate the universe's early stages, we assume an anisotropic locally rotationally symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I spacetime and derive the corresponding field equations. Our analysis of the energy density, equation of state, and skewness parameter reveals that the models exhibit anisotropic spatial geometry during the early universe, likely driven by an anisotropic fluid. However, as time progresses, inflation and the diminishing anisotropy of the fluid cause the universe to transition toward isotropy. Furthermore, the skewness parameter demonstrates an inverse relationship with energy density; specifically, at low energy densities, the fluid is highly isotropic, whereas at high densities, it becomes significantly isotropic. Based on these findings, the universe's early universe is characterized as undergoing holographic dark energy dominated by an anisotropic fluid with equation of state parameters within the range $-1 < \delta < 1$. Eventually, as the universe expands, it evolves into a dark energy driven by cosmic hologram. Finally, we construct and present the behavior of the bulk equation of state and scale factor density phase-space trajectories, noting that their trajectories closely align with those of the current $\Lambda$CDM model. These results suggest that the early universe may have possessed an anisotropic structure before smoothly transitioning to the present homogeneous and isotropic state. Furthermore, the phase-space diagrams indicate that $f(Q)$ can effectively bridge the early and current eras of the universe within the framework of $\Lambda$CDM. While this study examines only LRS Bianchi-I spatial geometry, future research should explore other geometric configurations to enable more accurate predictions regarding the universe's initial conditions. Additionally, the comparison should extend to include metric theories of gravity to validate the efficacy of our proposed mechanism in explaining the universe's early evolution.

Feeding the world's population over the next few decades will demand approximately 50% additional livestock feed. Accelerating crop variety improvement is therefore crucial to mitigating this demand and avoiding the environmental consequences associated with expanded agricultural land use. Breeders currently depend on phenotypic data to guide breeding decisions, but manually collecting this information is labor-intensive. Computer Vision offers a solution by enabling high-throughput phenotype characterization, which can inform individual plant selection for breeding programs. This project aims to build a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of predicting traits in various grass species important for animal nutrition. The developed model would assist breeders in making more informed decisions, potentially enhancing the efficiency of traditional breeding methods. The study involves training a CNN on images of various grass species to classify them and predict key visual features. These images were collected during the growth season of a greenhouse experiment conducted at the University of Leeds. The proposed modeling approach involves transferring the weights of a pre-trained network to the target one and fine-tuning it with the available data. Specifically, we will utilize the EfficientNet network family for this purpose. Our initial evaluations indicate that the efficientnet-based model achieved over 90% accuracy in species classification and provided useful estimates for several phenotypic traits.

This paper introduces a new algorithm for generating images conditionally on natural language data. Our approach employs a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) where the discriminator is modeled as a Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN). This architecture allows the model to assign varying levels of importance to different words within the input sentence. To evaluate the quality of our method, we compared our results against state-of-the-art approaches using several metrics, including the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and inception score. Our results suggest that our model is potentially superior to current state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we provide a qualitative comparison with existing techniques.

The dynamics of $p$-adic valued dynamical systems are fundamentally influenced by their critical points, whose nature determines the system's overall behavior. This paper introduces a method for computing the index of an isolated zero of a $p$-adic dynamical system defined on $\mathbb{Q}_p^n$. We demonstrate that this index exists, is well-defined, and remains invariant under any equivalent linear change of coordinates; consequently, it serves as a valuable tool for studying $p$-adic dynamical systems. We also provide several illustrative examples of both analytic and non-analytic systems. Furthermore, we generalize the classical definition of the topological degree for real differentiable maps to include discrete $p$-adic valued dynamical systems, offering a novel approach to this longstanding challenge in topological degree theory.

In 2021, Saeed and the author introduced the concept of $r$-divisibility in commutative rings, investigating its properties and providing examples of rings where every element is $r$-divisible. This notion was later named "property $(Q)$" in a 2022 article by Anvar and Saeed, which explored various aspects of rings possessing this property in the context of commutative algebra. The current study builds upon the work of (El-Shafei et al., Bulletin of Pure \& Applied Mathematics, Vol. LXXIX-No.1, 2012, pp. 1-9), where the authors examined $r$-divisibility in associative rings that may lack a multiplicative identity. Building on that foundation, this article investigates the properties of $r$-divisibility in rings potentially without identity. We have characterized rings with this property and determined the maximal possible value for $r$. Additionally, we analyze several associated topological properties of these rings.

While recent advancements have clarified and exemplified topological insulators within conventional condensed matter systems, they present significant challenges regarding diverse physical properties, complex many-body interactions, and non-equilibrium dynamics. Integrating topological insulator concepts with quantum many-body systems and driven processes is crucial for deepening our comprehension of novel physical phenomena and real-world applications, particularly in quantum information. This minireview introduces the current understanding of topological insulators and matter through recent examples in ultracold atomic systems, which serve as clean and tunable quantum gases. Furthermore, this review highlights emerging directions in the field of topological many-body phenomena and topological response functions within ultracold atomic systems, which hold promise for uncovering entirely new topological matters. In this contribution, we introduce a method to generate W states of arbitrary amplitude distributions in cold atomic ensembles. This approach is grounded in the Hamiltonian of two topologically connected cavities containing atoms with controllable two-body couplings. We analyze the entanglement properties of the produced states and demonstrate that these states can be generated in the fundamental mode of the optical cavity. Furthermore, we show that the entanglement of the resulting states remains robust against both photon losses from the cavity and dephasing of the atoms. Finally, we propose a scheme to determine the phases of the W states. In summary, the state generation is driven by a non-topological response of the cavity, yet it is robustly supported by a qualitative change—namely, a topological transition—of a related effective atomic interaction. This apparent contradiction motivates a investigation into the topological properties of the state-generated W states. Based on these findings, we suggest that topological W states can be exploited for quantum information processing and quantum information retrieval. Keywords: Topological response, Quantum states of motion, Quantum states of light, Quantum information processing.

The evolution of quantum states can become chaotic, defined by the exponential divergence of initially close states as governed by the Lyapunov exponent; consequently, measures of quantum state complexity, including quantum entropy evolution, should exhibit similar characteristics. This study examines the entropy of open systems interacting with environments through a master equation, utilizing the Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) form to model evolution in quantum systems like qubits or qubits interacting with thermal baths. Specifically, we analyze entropy complexity within the Nakajima-Zwanzig (NZ) equation for the reduced density operator, incorporating an exponential cutoff in the system-bath coupling to induce chaos. Our results demonstrate that the reduction process itself is chaotic, a finding corroborated by the full system (comprising both system and bath), and highlight the potential for controlling complexity via NZ equation reduction. These insights provide a pathway to manipulate complexity and entanglement between two qubits through the system-bath coupling exponent in an interacting double quantum dot model. Overall, this research offers valuable directions for investigating the chaos and entropy of quantum processes within broader physical contexts, encompassing fields such as quantum thermodynamics, black hole physics, and the study of complexity. Furthermore, these findings have implications for quantum measurement theory, optical detectors, and observational astronomy. In the context of the double quantum dot system, the outcomes can be experimentally verified using standard low-temperature transport techniques. Additionally, since analogous interactions occur between photons and atoms or between atoms and light, the observed effects may also manifest in these platforms. To address this, we introduce differentiable inversion, a framework designed to derive parametric information from image data via reverse inference. Leveraging extensive historical traffic data, this study proposes a new theoretical framework for probabilistic O-D demand and flow distribution. The approach begins by deriving the probability density function (PDF) of travel times between origin-destination (OD) pairs, accounting for stochastic link travel times influenced by fluctuating traffic volumes and capacities. Subsequently, an optimization problem is formulated using these time PDFs as inputs, with a variational principle proposed to determine flow distributions that optimally fulfill the PDF requirements. Furthermore, closed-form expressions are derived for the mean and variance of random travel times between OD pairs, allowing the development of deterministic equivalent problem formulations. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted on a small test network to validate the proposed methodologies. These simulation results demonstrate that the optimization models effectively generate mean and flow distributions matching observed traffic data while strictly adhering to constraints, thereby confirming the proposed probabilistic modeling approach. Our analysis demonstrates the emergence of global phase-locked states within finite lattices and explores their numerical destabilization. As model parameters vary, these states lose stability, giving rise to localized periodic and chaotic oscillations. In cases of weak nonlinear frequency dispersion, the system exhibits metastability similar to that observed in almost-conservative systems. Furthermore, we contrast our findings with the phase-approximation approach, where amplitude dynamics are adiabatically eliminated. We note the existence of hybrid states that are stable under the full Newtonian formulation but unstable within the associated phase system. Additionally, our study examines the implications of random frequencies and phase-locked configurations for wavelet-coherent states in finite-size periodic boxes. In this context, the global phase-locked singlet localizes at the lattice's center of mass, generating periodic trajectories for the center of mass despite the adhesion of all oscillators. Various random wavelet coherent packets can be maintained in a phase-locked state via appropriate tuning of nonlinear frequencies. We extend this analysis to the continuous continuous nonlinear wave equation with coherent wavepackets. These methodologies are relevant for generating random data tests compatible with global consistency conditions for numerical algorithms. They also offer novel perspectives on the localization of energy within lattices, a phenomenon that remains mechanism-agnostic. This framework has broad generality and could be essential for analyzing the relaxation of isolated conservative systems toward coherent structures or solitary waves. Finally, we argue that the phase-approximation approach is essential for identifying the instability mechanisms underlying the aforementioned states. The anisotropy of interactions can be modeled by assigning different random frequencies to oscillators along the three Cartesian directions; this configuration destroys the availability of localized periodic orbits stable under the Newtonian full formulation. However, phase-locked solutions persist within a broader parameter range, exhibiting nonlinear localization governed by random nonlinear frequency dispersion. These solutions remain stable until the Newtonian full formulation becomes unstable, a regime where the phase approximation fails to recover these states. Instead, within the phase system, they destabilize via the formation of rolling waves linking the envelopes of neighboring oscillators. These results highlight the critical role of adiabatic approximations in analyzing coherent structures in nonlinearly interacting fields. Specifically, the absence of adiabatic damping prevents the separation of timescales between slow precession and fast rotation, leading to the merging of fast and slow motions and altering the instability mechanisms compared to the Newtonian full system. However, we demonstrate that intensity-dependent dispersion yields novel features in the stability analysis of these black solitons. Specifically, the spectral stability problem admits only isolated eigenvalues within the unit circle. Furthermore, energetic stability arguments remain valid within Sobolev spaces equipped with exponential weights. Additionally, the black soliton serves as the unique minimizer of energy among states sharing a specific norm, and scattering data approaches that corresponding to a soliton as the initial condition evolves away from the steady state. The isolation of eigenvalues despite the continuous spectrum raises questions regarding the applicability of standard spectral theory techniques. To address this, we adapt existing methods to establish energy stability in Sobolev spaces with exponential weights—a result previously unattainable due to spectral constraints. Notably, the black soliton is not orbitally stable under norm constraints; instead, it exhibits orbitally stable center-manifolds consisting of another family of black solitons rotating at distinct speeds. Unlike the cubic defocusing NLS equation, which possesses an inverse scattering transform, our proof relies fundamentally on estimating H^k norms via the NLS equation itself. Unlike recent approaches examining black solitons with potential wells—which rely on the cubic nonlinearity's invariance against a modified Schrödinger operator—our method directly leverages the intensity-dependent dispersion of the NLS equation. This work constitutes the first study on the orbital stability of black solitons in the intensity-dependent NLS (iNS) equation within Sobolev spaces and the first to derive isolated eigenvalue properties in the iNS equation without a potential well. Furthermore, it relies uniquely on a family of conserved quantities rather than those associated with the linearized operator. These findings represent the first step toward extending inverse spectral methods to the iNS framework. Lastly, this approach may offer a pathway for ultimately proving the orbital stability of the ground state, which remains an open problem. World Wide Web. Consequently, numerous systems are emerging to accommodate the rising demand for creating, sharing, and managing content. However, as the volume of data generated by users expands exponentially, the necessity for efficient storage and robust data models has become paramount. This dissertation addresses these critical storage and modeling challenges within specific user-generated content domains. Specifically, it examines challenges in three systems: Twitter, the Social Graph, and the YouTube ecosystem. The work proposes solutions grounded in new insights into the structures, access patterns, and information paradigms of these platforms, ultimately leading to the development of effective storage strategies. The primary contributions of this thesis are summarized as follows:

1. **Twitter:** The large scale, distributed storage of Twitter data presents significant hurdles. We conducted an empirical investigation into Twitter data structure and access patterns using an extensive archive comprising over one billion tweets. This analysis revealed the "Twitter log file format," an empirical study of in-memory data structures at Twitter, and distinct behaviors observed between active and retired accounts, all of which inform a distributed storage solution designed for both efficiency and scalability.

2. **Social Graph:** As user-generated content grows, so does the demand for social networking services, making social graph data prevalent. This paper introduces a novel graph partitioning algorithm tailored for social networks, delivering substantial performance gains. Additionally, it details an empirical analysis of social network structures, highlights a critical flaw in current partitioning techniques, and introduces a new graph characteristic essential for developing robust partitioning algorithms.

3. **YouTube:** Empirical research was performed to comprehensively characterize the Title, Description, and Comment (TDC) data found on YouTube, a substantial body of unstructured social content. Our findings outline the characteristics of this data across various timeframes, sizes, and scopes, demonstrating that this information holds unique value that distinguishes YouTube from other social media channels, distinguishing textual from non-textual content, and separating active from retired accounts. Leveraging these insights, the study proposes a data model optimized for unstructured social content derived from user-generated sources.

4. **Twitter Analysis Tool:** A highly adaptable, scalable analysis tool was developed leveraging the efficient distributed storage mechanism for Twitter data. This tool enables fast, online analysis with an average runtime of under a minute per query, supporting both real-time and historical data. Its efficacy was validated through multiple use cases, including trending topic detection, hashtag analysis, and follower analysis.

5. **Twitter Marketing Strategy Analysis:** Another empirical study of Twitter data was performed to uncover valuable insights for marketing purposes

This study investigates the impact of cross-polarized, stochastic wind flows on these devices. It demonstrates that even weak, random cross-polarized flows generate random phase perturbations across the entire bandwidth of the metagrating, regardless of the specific flow model or its statistical characteristics. Consequently, these phase fluctuations cause random resonant scattering from the unit cells, leading to the complete destruction of both local and global field control, which depends strictly on Bianisotropic Magnetoelectric (MBE) cross-polarization. Finally, to maintain the desired local field control, the paper concludes that metagratings must be designed to withstand expected flow velocities, a requirement that can be met more easily by utilizing stronger Bianisotropic MBE cross-polarizations, thereby enabling device operation in highly dynamic settings. This work provides essential new insights into the design of active acoustic metagratings intended for airborne use, a domain that remains largely unexplored to date. Given the virus's high transmissibility, WHO recommendations now mandate that all patients, regardless of symptom severity, undergo screening for SARS-CoV-2. Although reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) remains the gold standard diagnostic test, it is often unaccessible in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) due to costs, the need for specialized equipment, and a lack of trained personnel. Consequently, there is a critical need for a rapid, affordable point-of-care test. This review examines the current diagnostic landscape for SARS-CoV-2, evaluating the feasibility, accessibility, and performance metrics of Point-of-Care Testing (POCT) in LMICs. We conclude by discussing the challenges inherent to POCT in these regions and offering recommendations for its effective implementation.

This paper aims to extend that result by restricting the number of permissible summands from a fixed finite set. Specifically, we demonstrate that if A and B are integer subsets of size k such that the difference B-A achieves a minimal sumset of size roughly 2k, then A and B must be highly structured, resembling generalized arithmetic progressions. Our approach builds on the innovative techniques introduced by Ahlswede and Huang, as further developed by the author and Shmerkin. The primary innovation lies in analyzing the case where the sumset size falls short of 2k by an amount (k-1)(|I|+1), where I represents the index set for the summands of A and B. This specific configuration is linked to the concept of I-dilates of A and B. We prove that the existence of such a sumset implies that A and B are actually I-dilates, provided that either set contains more than one element. To the best of our knowledge, this extends the classical Klyachko theorem, which applies when only a single summand is permitted, to scenarios involving a greater number of summands. Ultimately, our findings establish a discrete analogue to a recent theorem established by the author, Demeter, and Shmerkin within the framework of harmonic analysis. These conclusions depend on understanding additive "curves," a topic explored in a preceding paper by the author. Those methods also reveal that the primary result by the author, Oh, and Shakan regarding integer sets of similar size with a sumset of size roughly 3k/2—where each set element has a coefficient of at most 2—can be sharpened to yield a divisor relation between the sets. Similarly, the sumset of two integer sets of size k, with elements having coefficients of at most 2, cannot exceed a size of 4k-5. Furthermore, if a set with a maximum coefficient of 2 lacks "linear" elements (integers divisible by numerous primes greater than 2), its size is bounded by 2k+1, implying that most elements are non-linear. Finally, we demonstrate that any set missing just one element of an arithmetic progression with a maximum coefficient of 2 cannot exceed a size of 3k-3. Inferring the social backdrop of a visual scene requires more than just object recognition; it demands a deeper grasp of the people involved, their attributes, and their interconnections. To address this, an effective computational strategy involves employing a graph-based structure to model individual relationships within a scene and analyzing this graph to deduce the overall social context. in computer vision. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved great success, their reliance on local kernels restricts their ability to model long-range structured relationships. Although fully-connected networks and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are effective for this purpose, they struggle with high-dimensional input data. To address this, various Transformer-based architectures have emerged, leveraging self-attention to successfully capture long-range structured dependencies. This paper introduces a novel attention mechanism rooted in self-forecasting, designed to generate attention maps that anticipate input data at attention heads. This approach effectively models long-range structured dependencies in high-dimensional data, making it highly suitable for computer vision tasks. The proposed method, Forecasting Attention Network (FANet), achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark datasets for semantic segmentation and semantic segmentation with absent objects. Furthermore, it surpasses current state-of-the-art attention mechanisms for novel classes during few-shot learning. These results highlight the method's superior capability in learning long-range structured dependencies, even with very limited training data. The code and model will be made available at \url{https://github.com/fourier-transformer-networks/FANet.git}. These findings are compared against results obtained from kinetic theory using the relaxation time approximation and from causal first-order theories. Our analysis reveals that all divergence-type approaches share comparable structural characteristics regarding dispersion relations, with distinctions arising solely from the specific coefficients of their divergence-type equations of motion. Furthermore, these theories exhibit relaxation frequencies proportional to $k^2$, mirroring the behavior observed in divergence-type causal first-order frameworks. Notably, some divergence-type representations of viscous relativistic fluids demonstrate stability, whereas comparable stability characteristics are also maintained in divergence-type causal first-order theories. Our findings indicate that PBHs are unlikely to be the primary source of this radiation. Specifically, the total energy density of PBH emission across all frequencies amounts to only about $10^{-15}$ of the density of supermassive black holes. While PBHs may contribute a minor excess at a frequency of approximately 100 MHz, this effect is negligible at frequencies near 1 GHz, where (Li & Zhao 2020) claims to have detected an excess. Therefore, (Li & Zhao 2020) do not address the significant radio wave excess expected at 1 GHz. Additionally, we explored the possibility of detecting the Hawking effect on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). Our analysis shows that virtual particle-antiparticle pairs originating from the Hawking process do not appear to explain the non-Gaussianity (bimodality) observed in CMB temperature fluctuations by (Mao 2021). Consequently, any alternative explanation for these observations remains unclear. Finally, we examined the impact of Hawking radiation on black hole evolution and found that, given their low density and small mass range, PBHs do not significantly influence black hole evolution on cosmological scales. This conclusion remains robust even when considering uncertainties related to gravity modification theories or horizon models. While Hawking radiation remains unobserved, our results suggest that PBHs do not threaten information preservation within black holes. Specifically, most information seems to remain safe within massive black holes, implying that the Hawking process does not necessitate the formation of remnants or the violation of unitarity. In this context, Hagedorn strings may contribute to resolving the information loss problem associated with black holes. Furthermore, our results do not support the hypothesis that a low-energy gravitational wave background, generated by Hawking radiation, is the source of the recently detected stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) by LIGO/Virgo. the inaugural comprehensive system designed to execute a multi-opcode, general-purpose sequential processor using Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) for Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC). VSP safeguards both data and the functions applied to that data against adversaries during secure computation offloading scenarios, such as cloud computing. We have developed an optimized FHE library to accelerate individual FHE operations and implemented a tailored processor architecture that minimizes overhead while maximizing security. To demonstrate the platform's capabilities, we compiled a rich set of complex instructions, including those from the RISC-V instruction set architecture (RISCV32IM), enabling the secure offloading of applications to untrusted environments. We also presented a 32-bit instruction processor featuring reduced instruction memory and register files. Furthermore, we implemented two application benchmarks—an image logo detector and a multiinstruction benchmark utilizing a Hardware Description Language designed for secure FHE-based computing. These benchmarks were executed on an Intel i7-8700K processor running Linux, utilizing Seal's FHE library. Experimental results indicate that our proposed architecture significantly reduces both latency and bandwidth for secure offloading to an untrusted cloud. Specifically, the image logo detector exhibited approximately a 10.82% decrease in overall execution time, the image logo detection latency dropped by 61.7%, and the multiinstruction benchmark experienced a approximately 40% reduction in execution time. Compared to existing FHE-based architectures, our design features fewer instructions per operation (IPOs), thereby achieving higher performance. Looking forward, we plan to integrate more intricate benchmarks, such as cryptographic primitives like AES and advanced multi-party computation protocols. Additionally, we aim to develop a fully architectural processor supported by a complete instruction set architecture (ISA). These initiatives will provide a more holistic understanding of FHE-based computation and facilitate extensive applications in secure offloading to untrusted clouds. The complete source code for the VSP32IM repository can be accessed here: https://github.com/Virtual-Secure-Platform/VSP32IM. This paper introduces UPOA, an unsupervised constituent parsing model that derives an Outside Association score exclusively from the self-attention weight matrix of a pretrained language model to serve as a syntactic distance metric for spanning structures. We also present an enhanced variant, UPOA', which utilizes the output vector of the final transformer layer in addition to the score. Question: What core enhancement does UPOA offer for constituent parsing? Answer: The primary contribution of UPOA is its ability to derive an Outside Association score solely from a pretrained language model's self-attention weight matrix, utilizing this representation as a syntactic distance metric for spanning structures. This approach enables highly competitive parsing results without relying on large annotated corpora, provides a strong alternative to leveraging syntactic dependency trees as a graph representation, and significantly boosts parsing performance when used as a proxy for syntactic structure. This paper aims to rigorously establish the RAM model from the ground up by presenting a version that possesses significant algorithmic properties and robust complexity classes, specifically LIN (linear-time computable problems) and CONST-DELAY-lin (enumeration problems solvable with constant delay following linear-time preprocessing). the automorphism group $\text{Aut}(X)$ acts transitively on $X$. We define the transitivity degree of $X$ as the maximal integer $m$ for which the $\text{Aut}(X)$-action on $X$ is $m$-transitive; if the action is $m$-transitive for every $m$, the degree is infinite. In this work, we calculate the transitivity degree for all quasi-affine toric varieties and numerous homogeneous spaces of algebraic groups, while also examining a conjecture and several open questions concerning this invariant.

Civinelli, Kalinin, Kent, and Tiozzo demonstrated that for a semi-simple Lie group $G$ with a unimodular Iwasawa decomposition $G=KAN$, the left action of $G$ on its flag manifold $\mathcal{F}$ is transitive. Building on this, Dalalyan, Kilicerman, and Teo proved that for the associated flag variety $\mathcal{B}$, the action of $G$ via algebraic morphisms is also transitive. They further conjectured that for any complete toric variety $Z$ embedded within $\mathcal{B}$, the $\text{Aut}(Z)$-action on $Z$ is transitive. Ono and Toplal extended this by showing that the action of a subgroup $G'$ of $\text{Aut}(Z)$ containing a maximal torus is transitive. In this paper, we generalize these findings: for any complete toric variety $Z$ with dense torus $T$ and automorphism group $G'$ containing $T$, the $\text{Aut}(G')$-action on $Z$ is transitive. Additionally, we determine the transitivity degree for unipotent toric varieties. We conclude by investigating the transitivity degree of the flag variety $\mathcal{B}$ and posing related questions. Specifically, we investigate whether the action of $\text{Aut}(\mathcal{B})$ on $\mathcal{B}$ is transitive and propose that this action is actually $d$-transitive for all $d \in \mathbb{N}$. If this conjecture holds, it would imply that the transitivity degree of $\mathcal{B}$ is infinite.

Keywords: Algebraic variety, automorphism group, complete toric variety, flag manifold, flag variety, quasi-affine toric variety, transitivity degree

Current approaches typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras to forecast weather, yet these methods incur incremental costs and offer limited scope. To guarantee the uninterrupted operation of all transportation services regardless of conditions, a more robust detection technique capable of operating without sensors or cameras is necessary. This study generates weather-forecasted images by applying Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to weather reports. Specifically, we utilize Time Series to Image Translation GANs to convert weather report data into representative images. To gather the required data, we collected over 50,000 weather reports from the Japan Meteorological Agency. Furthermore, to simulate various scenarios and ascertain the optimal location for report collection, a simulation was employed to evaluate how different quantities of report data influence the quality of generated images. The results indicate that this approach can effectively predict images for conditions unencountered during the training phase, provided a sufficient volume of report data is utilized. Consequently, this technique has the potential to enable transportation services to function consistently despite adverse weather.

Using Discrete Choice Data from 1996 to 2020 regarding various environmental issues, we track interest levels in environmental topics across four demographic segments in Germany: political, economic, social, and cultural spheres. Through Bayesian estimation techniques, we analyze attention shifts toward climate change and estimate a model describing the interaction effects of public discourse on these interests. Attention categories are defined by specific topics within environmental discourse; for instance, "environmental org" refers to their activities, "environmental NGO" refers to their activities plus their efforts to influence others, and "company sphere" refers to environmental efforts within German companies. Similar logic applies to the "environmental industry" and "industry sphere." Besides background-specific attention shifts, we introduce interaction effects where the output attention of one sphere influences the input of another (e.g., environmental industry output influences company sphere input, termed "lock-in" effects), alongside one-sided interactions between the four spheres. Finally, we combine these interaction effects with a diffusion model of opinion change to fully capture public discourse dynamics. Input climate change interest was highest among the cultural sphere, followed by the economic sphere, while it was lowest in political and economic spheres. Similarly, output climate change interest was strongest among economic spheres and weakest in cultural spheres. Beyond these trends, we identify significant differences in how public discourse interacts to influence societal groups, with all interaction effects being statistically significant. Specifically, output climate change interests from the cultural sphere interact with all spheres to influence them, whereas output interests from the economic sphere only influence output interests in the company sphere and output interests are influenced by the industry sphere. Traditional environmental issues influence all spheres, while output climate change interests are influenced by all spheres. The proposed model offers a comprehensive view of climate change discourse impacts and provides a novel approach to studying public discourse effects, potentially extendable to other topics. This work enables a nuanced assessment of public discourse effects, which is crucial for creating effective policies to steer environmental public discourse toward specific goals. Moreover, most existing soft actuators depend on external power or battery sources; a significant subset, particularly those driven by pneumatic actuation, fails to grasp autonomously, limiting their practical utility. This multi-functional gripper demonstrates self-adaptive holding forces, successfully securing items of varying sizes and shapes ranging from 56 to 138 mm in diameter, including bottles and fruits. A 3D-printed prototype gripper was deployed across diverse applications, confirming the method's potential for broad use. Additionally, because the gripper's behavior is entirely data-driven and scalable, the optimization framework can be readily adapted for actuators utilizing other fluid sources, such as liquids. Finally, finite element analysis and experimental results indicate that scaling down the unit's size significantly boosts the specific power and specific force of the gripper, highlighting a key advantage for applications constrained by weight and volume, such as aerial manipulators. However, GD is hindered by several drawbacks, including susceptibility to local minima, slow convergence, and a high risk of stalling at stationary points. Surfaces of typical cost functions often consist of diverse regions with varying geometries and topologies, featuring ST isometric manifolds. The presence of these complex features should theoretically enable certain algorithms to reach the true global minimum more easily. This study investigates how the topological characteristics of the search landscape—specifically ST isometric manifolds—affect various optimization algorithms, especially GD. Additionally, we establish a clear ranking of optimization algorithms based on their performance when utilized in conjunction with the proposed reflow transformation. This research underscores the power of reflow in optimizing complex functions, such as machine learning models, by exploiting the intrinsic topological and geometric features of the search landscape. Ultimately, this work introduces a novel class of Topology-Based Optimizers and lays the foundation for advancing geometric deep learning and higher-order programming paradigms. This workflow comprises three core components: (1) a technique for generating conforming meshes around and within a three-dimensional fracture network, (2) the discretization of governing equations via a second-order scheme, and 3) an optimization of the resulting algebraic system. Specifically, we employ the matrix discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method for spatial discretization, utilizing weak derivatives formulated across the discrete fracture matrix grid. This approach ensures mass conservation, maintains second-order accuracy in allspatial dimensions, and enables the creation of locally refined meshes; however, it generates a large, sparse system of algebraic equations. To address this, we propose an approximate Schur complement-based domain decomposition method enhanced by multilevel numerical methods for both fracture and matrix domains. Numerical results demonstrate mass conservation and convergence rates proportional to the polynomial degree. Furthermore, we validate the method's capability for rapid time step advances, which is essential for transporting radioactive isotopes through both matrix and fracture networks in geological storage scenarios. Testing with the tracer GE-80 (cerium-142) reveals ultra-rapid fracture transport due to its high mobility, whereas a low mobility coefficient causes tracers to take significantly longer to exit the rock volume. Finally, we investigate adaptive local time stepping, showing that it readily accommodates diverse fracture geometries, including irregular and branching structures. This capability allows for substantial time step increases once all tracers have departed the rock. Together, these findings indicate that fracture and matrix properties directly influence model output specific to a given scenario, emphasizing the necessity of efficient numerical methods for exploring a wide range of potential time scales. This is particularly relevant as new storage scenarios increasingly involve deeply buried, highly fractured, and/or fault-rich rock volumes.

Traditionally, this process requires access to both the training data and the teacher's internal parameters. We introduce a novel technique enabling KD without needing the training data or the teacher's parameters. Instead, our method trains the student model using synthetic data generated from a teacher's diffusion model, which reconstructs the original training data by progressively adding random noise. Since the student's objective function is also based on this diffusion process, it effectively learns to match the teacher's underlying objective through the synthetic data. Consequently, even with zero access to the original data or the teacher's parameters, the student still acquires information valuable for its final application. Experiments on image classification show that students trained on these synthetic inputs achieve performance on real data that surpasses existing KD methods relying solely on distribution matching. This approach significantly expands the scope of KD, allowing small models to incorporate various large models as knowledge sources, including those trained on distinct datasets, granting them enhanced capabilities beyond their initial training data. Veech conjectured that specific arithmetic properties of this path length would remain invariant under renormalization. More recently, Dvorak and Nandor demonstrated that for Veech matrices associated with quadratic irrationals, the bond path length is either always a odd number, always an even number, or can take on both odd and even values. Building upon their findings and incorporating the concept of projection paths between atoms within tree structures, this paper extends their results to encompass a broader class of arithmetic irreducible graphs. A key distinction between our approach and the original work by Dvorak and Nandor is the utilization of different graph invariants.

Over the last twenty years, researchers have proposed various generalizations of the bonds path within a tree to understand and explore the topological characteristics of monomial reductions of free associative algebras, which are fundamental objects in mathematical physics. More recently, these bonds paths have found applications in statistical mechanics, particularly regarding the critical behavior of the three-dimensional Ising model. This document introduces a novel generalization of the bonds path, termed the "atom path," which remains equivalent to the original definition for all trees. We then present multiple examples of atomic graphs where the bond path length can assume both odd and even values; notably, the lengths of projection paths within these graphs are invariably odd. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a specific subclass of atomic graphs—multilevel graphs—every projection path is guaranteed to be odd. Our findings indicate that the natural bicolourability of level graphs serves as a crucial arithmetic invariant for multilevel graphs.

The methodology involves utilizing the theory of local F-pairs and the tight closure concept introduced by Brodmann and Sharp. Specifically, a hypersurface singularity is k-rational if and only if its m-th component of the test exponent module vanishes under the condition that the characteristic is greater than k, where m equals k. Our primary finding is the equivalence between local complete intersections possessing k-rational singularities and those with k-Du Bois singularities. Given the reliance of our definitions and theorems—especially concerning F-pairs—upon a finite field of characteristic p, it is essential to briefly explain how to extend these ideas to mixed characteristic. The authors draw inspiration from the approaches of Friedlander and Srinivas, as well as Rego and Zhang. Examples indicate that for a given singularity type, the threshold value of k is inherently determined. Given the moderate intralayer exchange coupling ($J/k_\mathrm{B} = 6.8$ K), applying laboratory-scale magnetic fields generates significant $XY$ anisotropy in spin correlations. This effect establishes a robust BKT regime at temperatures below a transition temperature $T_\mathrm{BKT} \approx 4.5$ K, specifically inside a susceptibility peak characterized by an angular width of only $\Delta H_\mathrm{peak} \sim 0.15$ T. Furthermore, applying a magnetic field induces exponential growth of the interlayer exchange coupling, effectively driving the system toward true global $XY$ symmetry. This expansion enables the experimental observation of the gradual critical temperature transition from the three-dimensional BKT state to an extended $XY$ critical state, all using lab-scale magnetic fields. These theoretical and experimental findings offer a complete understanding of experimental susceptibility angular widths near $H_c$ and provide a methodology for locating and characterizing the global $XY$ critical region in other weakly coupled spin-1/Heisenberg $XY$ systems. Additionally, the experimentally extracted BKT correlation length is shown to align with predictions from recent Monte-Carlo simulations of the global $2D$ Heisenberg $XY$ model and the non-linear $\sigma$-model. This theoretical analysis confirms the actual location of the BKT transition and precisely identifies where the asymptotic BKT scaling regime begins. Finally, we establish a methodology based on an effective interlayer exchange coupling for predicting the global $XY$ critical line in any strong $1D$ Heisenberg $XY$ system and define the universal triple point at $T_\mathrm{c} \approx 0.71J$ and $k_\mathrm{B}T_\mathrm{c}/J^\ast$ varying between $5.6$ and $6$ (with $J^\ast$ denoting the reduced coupling at the triple point). These established methods serve as essential guides for designing future external-field experiments on other strong $1D$ Heisenberg $XY$ systems to fully explore their critical regions.

2020, LAMOST conducted a time-domain spectral survey covering four nights between 14:00 and 22:00 CST each night, utilizing 236,988 single-exposure spectra of stars with apparent V-band magnitudes between 9 and 16. Since these arrays are integral to both specialized and general-purpose chips for data storage and computation, SRAM entropy pools offer a low-cost method for enhancing security through the creation of true random numbers. Nevertheless, existing SRAM TRNG sources are limited to specific architectures or require extensive modification of standard standard-cell arrays to extract entropy, creating a critical need for a straightforward, universal post-processing scheme to exploit entropy in standard arrays. This paper leverages the inherent variations in cell charging and discharging speeds to enhance entropy extraction efficiency. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of supply voltage fluctuations on random number generation and define its coefficient of variation. Using a TRNG implemented in a 65nm standard-cell environment, we confirm the method's universality and achieve an entropy rate of 2.8 kbits/joule. We also verify that this approach meets NIST randomness criteria and is suitable for applications such as cryptography and secure key derivation. Ultimately, this proposed technique significantly improves SRAM TRNG performance, reducing the circuit's area and component count while boosting production yield.

expansion formula for one-dimensional two-state quantum walks, serving as an analog to the expansions for Sturm-Liouville operators developed by Weyl, Stone, Titchmarsh, and Kodaira. Our approach avoids the utilization of adiabatic coin operators. Instead, we apply a non-adiabatic transformation that converts the time evolution into a lower triangular matrix. This yields a lower triangular resolvent, from which the eigenfunction expansion is derived using the standard method of variation of constants. In this context, our primary innovation lies in applying this formula directly to resolve fundamental questions regarding the type, multiplicity, and asymptotic growth rates of eigenvalues. As a primary application, we demonstrate that the multiplicity of eigenvalues within the essential spectrum of this quantum walk equals three. To achieve this, we employ an alternative characterization of essential spectrum that differs from the standard definition employed in the analysis of quantum search algorithms. Furthermore, this formula enables a straightforward derivation of the time complexity for quantum search on an unstructured graph with $N$ nodes, resulting in a $\Theta(\sqrt{N})$ complexity. We also examine applications to weighted quantum search on binary graphs. Additionally, as a secondary application, we establish that every real symmetric tridiagonal matrix possesses $N$ real eigenvalues, utilizing this result to prove a related formula regarding the multiplicity of quantum walk eigenvalues. Finally, we provide an application to the analysis of random quantum search.

We derive a closed-form expression for the transition amplitude of a coin-assisted quantum walk on one-dimensional graphs with arbitrary initial coin bases. This formula facilitates the straightforward derivation of well-established results concerning coin independence in unbiased search on unstructured graphs, the impact of biased coin operators on search type and success probability in graph search, and the time complexity of quantum search on both unstructured and structured graphs. Using this coin-assisted transition amplitude, we determine the exact probability of not finding a target item during $t$ time steps, thereby enabling the calculation of average query complexity for quantum graph search. While scholars have extensively studied the conditions under which diffusion occurs and its violation, there remains uncertainty regarding the magnitude of this effect and how it varies across different complex systems. This work presents a robust theoretical framework capable of quantifying time-dependent transport properties. Utilizing this method, we investigate three particular complex materials: a geological porous matrix, a biological cellular network, and a distributed electronic circuit. Our analyses reveal that these materials exhibit significantly slower transport rates, characterized by mean first passage times that are multiple orders of magnitude longer than predicted by normal diffusion models. We emphasize that applying a diffusion interpretation to these systems is non-trivial, demanding intricate state-space constructs and complex stochastic differential equations. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a unified approach can characterize the dynamics of complex systems, offering profound insights into their behavior. We begin by constructing a cryptocurrency trading network, where nodes represent individual cryptocurrencies and links denote Granger causality derived from their weekly log returns, subsequently analyzing its temporal evolution. Focusing on 2020 and 2021, we investigate the logarithmic USD prices of these currencies, highlighting two key events: the initial Bitcoin Halving in May 2020 and the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused significant global price volatility. Our analysis employs the weighted shortest path as a metric for metric entropy production, enabling a comparison of information exchange characteristics between market currencies. We observed a marked increase in metric entropy production leading up to the Halving event and during periods of high volatility caused by the pandemic, suggesting accelerated information flow. Contrary to prior research, our findings indicate that Bitcoin does not function as a central hub for information flow. Furthermore, we identified an inverse relationship between the network's small-world properties and metric entropy production, where higher entropy correlates with less pronounced small-world characteristics. These results offer a novel perspective on the metric evolution of cryptocurrency networks, ultimately contributing to a deeper comprehension of their underlying dynamics.

This study investigates the role of zero-point motion (or quantum nuclear dynamics) in modeling small sulfuric acid-water clusters using path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) at the density functional theory (DFT) level. Generally, zero-point motion slightly distorts the mean structure of chemical clusters by locally enhancing chemical bonding within the solvent and at the cluster-solvent interface. This problem can be tackled using various autoregressive (AR) techniques; however, while numerous methods exist for selecting the AR order, most are tailored for linear AR models, limiting their applicability to broader scenarios. Building on the research of Kirkup and Sullivant, we demonstrate that these marginal independence models can be transformed into toric varieties through a linear coordinate change. Tensors possess numerous significant applications, particularly in statistical analysis. This paper proposes and investigates two distinct statistical models based on tensors: the "marginal model" and the "diagonal model." The marginal model assumes that a tensor's elements can be decomposed into multiplicative components derived from vectors associated with each index. Similarly, the diagonal model posits that tensors can be represented as sums of diagonal vectors for each index. We outline various interpretations of these models and demonstrate that both can be formulated as toric varieties. Specifically, we present two distinct parametrizations for the marginal model and introduce a corresponding model for the diagonal case. In both scenarios, we derive constraints on the vectors that characterize the model and illustrate how these models address specific problems within statistical physics and combinatorics. For the marginal model, we focus on independent set polytopes and bipartite graph coloring problems, whereas the diagonal model applies to Z_q-coloring problems. Additionally, providing an algorithm to compute maximal-rank tensors, we establish the complexity of this problem in terms of NP-harshad.

Many statistical models can be defined by assuming that data points originate from a low-dimensional linear subspace. While minimizing the Euclidean distance between data and this subspace is generally well-behaved, it remains an open question whether minimum-distance estimation remains consistent and efficient when subspace identification is ambiguous. This paper demonstrates that answer is negative for a specific class of models known as toric ideal models. We illustrate this failure using the simplest case: estimating parameters for a random graph.

We construct a dynamic framework for distributing such opportunities within a society characterized by mobility bottlenecks, where optimal allocation involves balancing the immediate benefits to the current generation against the potential to uplift future generations' socioeconomic composition. Our analysis demonstrates that optimal allocations emerge from continuous optimization problems spanning multiple generations, revealing that these solutions often prioritize individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds over slightly more successful high-status peers—a form of affirmative action that arises organically from welfare optimization. This perspective of broad affirmative action as a mechanism for enhancing long-term socioeconomic diversity, rather than solely improving individual outcomes, represents a novel contribution to the literature. Furthermore, we examine how solution stability is impacted by variations in the density of socioeconomic statuses and planning horizons defined by the number of generations considered. These insights offer potential applications for policymakers aiming to maximize long-term socioeconomic diversity through more strategic access to educational opportunities. Extensions of this model to multi-dimensional capability spaces constitute ongoing research. Overall, our framework of affirmative action planning provides policy-level guidance, illustrating affirmative action as one component within a generational planning framework designed to maximize long-term welfare. This sheds new light on the function of affirmative action within optimized multi-dimensional systems, allowing us to investigate affirmative action through multiple new lenses. Finally, we derive these continuous-time solutions and discuss discrete refinements applicable to real-world scenarios. Our model represents a distinct contribution by linking affirmative action policies to affirmative outcomes across generations.

Within non-relativistic quantum mechanics, standard angular momentum properties explain the $(-1)^{2s}$ sign factor acquired upon swapping particle coordinates, directly linking spin to exchange statistics without extra conditions. We demonstrate that the relativistic Klein-Gordon equation, which describes two massless particles in 3D space, inherently encodes this parity symmetry and correctly yields the $(-1)^{2s}$ factor for spin $s$ within the standard angular momentum framework, thereby guaranteeing proper exchange statistics. For scalar particles where $s=0$, setting $s=1$ would incorrectly produce a positive sign factor and fail to provide the required antisymmetric wavefunction for identical particles. Additionally, for massless relativistic particles, the helicity remains invariant under Lorentz transformations, implying that all spinor wavefunctions retain a definite parity, mirroring the behavior in the standard angular momentum scheme. However, scalar wavefunction properties arise in specific contexts; thus, the connection between spin and statistics is not universally explicit in the standard quantum mechanics of massive particles with fixed spin. Furthermore, the relationship between relativistic covariance, quantum superposition, and quantum statistics remains unclear. Finally, we show that the massless relativistic Dirac equation for spin-1/2 particles in 3D space possesses only helicity-conserving solutions, indicating that Dirac particles do not possess a superposition of spin states with distinct parity signs as do scalar particles. This highlights a distinct disparity between spin-1/2 Dirac particles and spin-0 bosons. These findings clarify the otherwise obscure connection between relativistic covariance and quantum statistics for spin-1/2 Dirac particles. To achieve the required wavefunction antisymmetry for identical spin-1/2 Fermi-Dirac particles, one must combine helicity states with an appropriate energy factor of $i$. This specific factor of $i$ emerges naturally from the Dirac equation's properties, ensuring that the total phase factor for swapped coordinates is precisely $-1$ to satisfy relativistic covariance requirements for these particles.

We introduce a hybrid measurement attack utilizing solely linear optics, homodyne detection, and single-photon detection, targeting the prevalent vacuum-plus-weak-decoy-state QKD protocol under conditions of partial source phase randomization. This attack successfully induces key leakage without being repelled by phase randomization, exploiting the coherent state component of the source to masquerade as the transmitted key. Our proposed attack executes successfully with any partial phase randomization and yields superior key leakage compared to prior attacks, surpassing both the continuous-variable attack and the nonlinear measurement attack from Entanglement Attack. Consequently, this research highlights the persistent susceptibility of current QKD protocols to quantum attacks and underscores the urgent necessity for more secure and practical QKD systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the attack remains effective even when the source deviates slightly from an ideal coherent state plus vacuum state due to fractional phase randomization; surprisingly, this slight imperfection accelerates the onset of key leakage. These findings emphasize that ensuring rigorous phase randomization is critical for the practical security of QKD systems employing the vacuum-plus-weak-decoy-state protocol. Additionally, these results illuminate the potential of quantum hacking as a potent instrument for assessing the security of quantum cryptographic protocols. More broadly, they suggest that post-processing techniques in quantum information science, such as vacuum state preparation and weak measurement, possess substantial utility in executing attacks against quantum communication protocols. This finding signifies a novel discovery in quantum hacking, expanding the current understanding of quantum security. These insights may inspire the development of more robust and practical QKD protocols that offer secure communications regardless of detection or source implementation specifics. This study utilizes the vacuum-plus-weak-decoy-state protocol, which is prevalent in both academic research and commercial products. We will detail these proposals and the requisite parameters for implementing such safeguards in a forthcoming work. Moreover, we will demonstrate that this attack remains effective even with substantial phase randomization and low source vacuum components. Thus, quantum hacking remains a significant threat to quantum security, and these findings may aid researchers in exploring further solutions to secure QKD systems. This study examines how the source and scale of the pretraining corpus influence in-context learning within HyperCLOVA, a Korean-focused GPT-3 architecture. Our comprehensive investigation yields four key findings: (1) in-context learning performance is strongly influenced by the domain source of the corpus, whereas corpus size alone does not dictate the emergence of such abilities; (2) a model trained on a mixture of multiple corpora can develop in-context learning skills even if each individual corpus fails to produce them independently; (3) pretraining with data related to a specific downstream task can enhance learning outcomes when combined with few-shot examples, yet adding such task-specific data to an existing corpus does not guarantee performance improvements; and (4) there is no consistent correlation between downstream benchmark scores and in-context learning abilities across various shot settings. These results offer a detailed analysis of how training corpus composition affects in-context learning, offering valuable insights for future large-scale language model research and development. This cold gas is believed to originate from ICM cooling and is frequently observed in advanced cooling flow clusters as a dense, star-forming disk. In clusters that have undergone cluster-wide heating events, such as those driven by AGN feedback, this cold gas component is significantly suppressed. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that the "leaky accretion disk" scenario represents an age-dependent evolutionary stage in massive galaxy clusters, during which significant cluster-wide heating events slightly inhibit the accumulation of total cluster core cold gas mass. This paper aims to discover and model perceptual acoustic units that encompass both steady-state and transient regions of speech.
