Since nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures correspond bijectively to real Killing spinors, the deformation framework can be expressed using spinors and Dirac operators. We demonstrate that the space of infinitesimal instanton deformations is isomorphic to the kernel of an elliptic operator. Leveraging this approach, we establish the rigidity of abelian instantons. This provides a complete classification of instantons on these spaces, yielding, for instance, 12 distinct self-dual connections on $G_2/\varpi_{1,2}$. Furthermore, we offer a geometric interpretation for the rigidity proofs. Regarding the deformation theory of coassociative 3-folds, we note that the identity component of the group of diffeomorphisms acting by pullback acts transitively on the set of such forms within a fixed de Rham cohomology class. Consequently, the deformation space of coassociative 3-folds is determined by the moduli space of closed 3-forms $\phi$ where $d^\ast(\ast \phi^3)=0$, modulo diffeomorphisms. Thus, the analysis presented here fully resolves the long-standing question concerning the deformation space of these objects. Our methodology also recovers and refines the results previously established for the standard coassociative 3-folds $\mathbb{R}^7$ and $\mathbb{O}$. Lastly, we utilize this approach to derive the rigidity of self-dual connections on the other three nearly parallel 3-forms. Since the resulting self-dual connections reside on non-simple Lie groups, the adjoint reduction is generally ineffective in proving rigidity; however, this issue does not arise in the context of nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. This work introduces a novel approach to detecting ETPA in gases by analyzing the absorption of two simultaneous laser pulses within an entangled pair as a function of their time delay. The study utilizes signal pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, where the pump laser is pumped by a mode-locked Ti:sapphire laser at 800 nm with a repetition rate of 80 MHz and a pulse duration of 100 fs. Experiments were carried out using an N$_2$ gas jet as the non-linear medium. Results indicate that ETPA occurs when the time delay between the signal and pump pulses falls within the dephasing time of the molecular transition, specifically in the green region at 523 nm. Furthermore, the relationship between non-linear absorption and time delay is modeled using a dual-photon lineshape. Beyond characterizing ETPA dynamics in gases, the absorption data were employed to determine the half width at half maximum of the N$_2$ molecular X$^3\Sigma_g^-$ electronic transition, yielding a result of 3.5 ns. Finally, the experimental data are compared against calculations derived from the three-photon absorption (TPA) cross-section at the same wavelength in N$_2$, which was previously measured using 64 ns pulses with a pulse energy of 0.6 $\mu$J. This study demonstrates that ETPA can be effectively characterized by measuring absorption versus time delay using short (sub-ps) pump and probe pulses with femtosecond jitter. Additionally, the research highlights that ETPA remains significant even when the average two-photon flux is several orders of magnitude lower than TPA. These findings suggest that ETPA plays a crucial role in explaining the low-light absorption observed across various materials. Furthermore, the ability to modulate ETPA through time delay control between the pump and signal pulses opens new avenues for investigating the non-linear optical properties of gases.

This paper investigates an idealized ground-sound model grounded in elastodynamic halfspace theory to determine when such sound is perceptually significant versus when it is obscured by the object's modal tones or transient acceleration noise. Our analytical approach yields a smooth, closed-form formula for ground surface acceleration, which can be applied via the Rayleigh integral or as an "acoustic shader" within finite-difference time-domain wave simulations. We conclude that when modal sounds are inaudible, ground sound becomes audible only near the impact point; otherwise, it remains imperceptible because the ground-accelerated air is masked by the object's tones. This methodology can be extended to complex multibody systems, such as robotic dogs, where specific conditions make ground sound audible. Ultimately, we aim to encourage further research on ground sound, especially within robotic impact sound generation, by demonstrating that it is typically imperceptible except in scenarios involving very soft materials or robotic objects possessing extremely low natural frequencies. \textit{Toward realistic multi-tone synthesis}, we build upon the analysis to create a numerically efficient method for generating realistic modal waveforms. This approach is divided into two categories: the "always-type" and the "sometimes-type" proofs, both of which have been extensively studied. To date, nearly all existing "always-type" proofs of Bell nonlocality have been derived from perfect correlations inherent in stabilizer states. Consequently, it is a common assumption that only perfect correlations can facilitate such "always-type" proofs. In this work, we introduce a novel "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof of Bell nonlocality based on non-perfect correlations, thereby dispelling this long-standing misconception. Our findings offer fresh perspectives on the investigation of Bell nonlocality and may hold significant potential for applications in various quantum information technologies. Additionally we have provided a video which provides a more accessible explanation of our results. Bell's theorem, a cornerstone of quantum foundations, has been the subject of numerous studies, with the all-versus-nothing proof representing one of its most direct formulations. These proofs generally fall into two categories: always-type and sometimes-type. While the sometimes-type approach relies on highly perfect correlations with minor tolerances, the always-type proofs we present can accommodate perfect correlations among non-adjacent parties as well as those with non-zero probabilities of error. By leveraging noisy perfect correlations, we have recently achieved information causality violations and strengthened the lower bounds of information distance to demonstrate nonlocality. This study not only clarifies the always-type all-versus-nothing proof but also offers new insights into quantum nonlocality and its relevance to quantum information technologies. Furthermore, our findings may aid in the design of high-performance quantum networks. Additionally, we have included a video that offers a more accessible explanation of our findings. Our results may also inspire further "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs of Bell nonlocality using other noisy perfect correlations. In many of these contexts, the underlying systems are dynamic, and due to their inherent complexity, constructing mathematical models suitable for clustering is often unfeasible. This paper introduces a novel methodology for clustering dynamic systems directly from time-series data, inherently capturing the system's dynamical behavior. However, the technique's sensitivity is influenced by the specific choice of Koopman observables; therefore, developing an optimal observability graph that facilitates both clustering and interpretability is suggested as a priority for future research. We demonstrate that this problem is unsolvable without a prior assumption that points are localized within disjoint compact clusters, as such an assumption is necessary to define what constitutes a single node. Generally, we assert that no algorithm can solve this counting task without incurring either excessive false positives or false negatives. However, if a cluster satisfies two specific conditions—(C1) that any two disjoint sub-clouds are distinguishable, and (C2) that each cluster can be covered by a specific collection of sets—we can develop an efficient, randomized algorithm with high probability. The algorithm's success relies on two parameters: $\ell$, representing the number of random observation vectors (each with real entries), and $k$, the count of vectors required to certify a count-up to $\ell$. We establish that $\ell$ and $k$ are governed by the geometric characteristics of the clusters. We explicitly detail the conditions ensuring that no false positives or false negatives occur, along with the computational complexity of our algorithm. To illustrate that these geometric criteria are broadly applicable and that our algorithm is practically efficient, we provide examples of infinite cluster families where $\ell$ and $k$ are constant; this includes convex regions, cross-shaped regions, and regular polygons with a sufficient number of vertices. Furthermore, we prove that a necessary condition for the counting complexity is the coverability of clusters by finitely many sets, and we offer explicit examples of cluster families where both $\ell$ and $k$ are unbounded. Finally, we present a variant of the algorithm that, while potentially less efficient, guarantees that a count-up to $\ell$ is never compromised by noise. We propose a novel approach rooted in the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition. Unlike conventional methods that treat the Hamiltonian constraint as a second-order elliptic equation for a specified mean curvature $K$, our method solves an algebraic equation for $K$ given a chosen conformal factor. A group $G$ is defined as having a Schreier growth gap $f(n)$ if the volume growth $\mathrm{vol}_{G, X}(n)$ of every faithful $G$-set $X$ is bounded below by $f(n)$. This study investigates such gaps within the context of finitely generated solvable groups. We demonstrate that any metabelian group $G$ which is either finitely presented or torsion-free, and is not virtually abelian, possesses a Schreier growth gap of $n^2$. Specific examples include the wreath product $C_p \wr \mathbb{Z}^d$, which exhibits a gap of $n^d$, and $\mathbb{Z} \wr \mathbb{Z}^d$, which has a gap of $n^{d+1}$; these lower bounds are shown to be optimal. In a CO longitude-velocity map at a Galactic latitude of 0 degrees, the Far Arm appears as a continuous structure stretching from the Galactic center (l=0) to the anti-center (l=180), paralleling the Near Arm. Quality diversity (XD) represents a cutting-edge area within evolutionary algorithms that seeks to discover solutions balancing diverse objectives. However, XD remains inaccessible to many researchers due to its Java-based implementation and reliance on pheno.genetic algorithms, which hinder ease of use and applicability to diverse problem types. 3qd, a new Python-basedXD framework built on neuroevolution, utilizes a feed-forward artificial neural network for direct digital hardware deployment without manual parameter adaptation. We conducted an extensive empirical analysis comparing performance against state-of-the-art methods on benchmark problems like Rastrigin. Additionally, we explored how hyper-parameters influence solution diversity and fitness, offering insights into selecting the most hyper-effective configurations for various challenges. This work signifies the first comprehensive comparison of XD solutions using a novel, widely accessible, and highly customizable implementation. Key findings include: 3qd generating significantly higher fitness than XD-GAs, achieving comparable quality to TAE, with hyper-parameter settings that ensure solution diversity remains robust even at peak fitness; the approach is easily accessible via GitHub, enabling rapid adaptation to novel challenges, and is particularly effective for discovering highly fit, hardware-deployable solutions without manual parameter tuning.

We introduce Stacked Quality Diversity (SQD), a novel framework that integrates the discoverability of the Pareto front with the generation of hyper-diverse solutions. By training a surrogate model on previously evaluated solutions to predict unexplored regions of the phenotypic landscape, SQD identifies high-fitness, hyper-diverse candidates that maintain uniqueness relative to existing solutions. This leverages a form of indirect fitness feedback. Experimental results on continuous black-box functions demonstrate that SQD surpasses leading-quality diversity baselines in both solution fitness and diversity, even when evaluated traits vary in relevance to fitness, and does so with fewer evaluations. Furthermore, transfer learning applications highlight SQD's robustness and discoverability compared to current leading methods. Open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/UW-Neuroevolution/SQD.

Consequently, developing rapid and adaptable decoding algorithms capable of handling faulty syndrome measurements is essential. This study demonstrates that decoding can be reframed as a dynamic graph coloring challenge. Through this novelty, we generalize existing algorithms to accommodate faulty syndrome measurements by introducing a novel random graph coloring problem driven by dynamic vertex and edge insertion. We recast this issue using online graph coloring theory and derive upper bounds for both the number of colors needed and the algorithm's time complexity in terms of vertex and edge operations. Specifically, for triangular lattices, the algorithm requires $O(N \log^{2} N)$ operations per step, where $N$ represents the total interactions (sum of qubit and syndrome-measurement errors). For square lattices, the requirement drops to $O(N \log N)$. These bounds are substantially lower than those of traditional sliding-window decoders. Additionally, through numerical simulations, we show that our dynamic graph coloring approach surpasses current triangle and square lattice decoders, particularly under high syndrome fault rates. The algorithm's efficiency is further defined by its logarithmic complexity relative to the total cumulative faulty syndrome measurements. Furthermore, this dynamic graph coloring framework applies extensively to leading surface code variants, including surface codes with defect anyons. Overall, dynamic graph coloring emerges as a promising quick fix for advanced decoding algorithms capable of managing faulty syndrome measurements. This study evaluates the potential of the upcoming DUNE experiment to detect sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Since the design of the Near Detector remains undetermined, we calculate the anticipated number of sterile neutrino decays within that volume. Our most optimistic projections suggest that the resulting constraints on mixing could be comparable to previous estimates for the LBNE. Because the time step necessary to resolve collision dynamics is significantly smaller than that required for fluid flow, the computational expense of using the traditional soft-sphere model—which explicitly calculates all collision interactions—becomes prohibitive. While existing reduced models, such as the superposition model (SM) and collision-time model (CTM), eliminate most computational costs associated with the full soft-sphere approach by considering only near-contact interactions, they introduce artificial collisions and fail to preserve key kinetic properties of the dispersion equation, respectively. To address these efficiency and accuracy challenges, we propose the multiple-time-step approximation (MTA) for particle collisions, a method that utilizes two distinct time steps: one matching the fluid simulation duration and a smaller sub-step specifically for resolving contact events. The standard MTA follows the multiple-time-step approach found in finite-difference methods, where the short collision sub-step is applied to the most recently formed contacts while longer time steps are used for earlier ones. To validate the effectiveness of this multiple-time-step framework, an improved version incorporating the SM is developed, termed the improved multiple-time-step approximation (IMTS). Both the MTA and IMTS were implemented in a particle-resolved direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) code to investigate isotropic gas flows containing spherical particles of equal size under moderate Knudsen numbers. Simulation results indicate that the IMTS is highly efficient, offering remarkable savings in computational cost while fully retaining the kinetic characteristics of the MTA. The advent of Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) offers a pathway to achieve this, as data stored in NVM-based main memory persists during system crashes due to its inherent non-volatility. However, the presence of volatile caches necessitates logging and explicitly flushing cache contents into NVM to guarantee consistency and correctness prior to a crash, a process that often incurs significant runtime overhead. This paper presents an algorithm-centric approach to establishing crash consistency for HPC applications within NVM environments. By slightly modifying application data structures to incorporate metadata, the method ensures that both modified and non-modified structures—whether central or distributed—are consistently crashed, requiring only a single hardware fence to atomically commit all transactions to persistent storage. Benchmark results demonstrate that the resulting overhead is minimal and does not degrade application performance. This work introduces a novel technique for introducing crash consistency to HPC applications using NVM, with experimental evaluations showing that the introduced overhead results in less than a 3% performance penalty compared to non-persistent applications. These findings suggest that NVM can serve as a viable solution for mitigating checkpointing overhead in High-Performance Scientific Computing (HPCSC). Furthermore, the method is adaptable to Central Processor-based, Many-Core, and Distributed High-Performance Scientific Computing Systems. An open-source implementation of this approach is available at https://github.com/IITB-EMCP/emcp_cnmv. This research extends our prior publication titled "Towards Crash Consistent High-Performance Scientific Computing Applications using Non Volatile Memory" [1].

By simulating and analyzing one million realizations for various initial conditions—covering both equal and unequal mass configurations and random position and velocity setups—we evaluate position entropies, collision frequencies, final outcomes, energy escaptions, and capture events. These findings are then matched against analytical models including straight-line trajectories, parabolic orbits, and the summation of two-Body Interaction Summation (2BS) approximations. The statistical distributions show good agreement when using the 2BS approximation for entropies, collision rates, and final results. Comparisons with state-of-the-art theoretical models reveal that p$p$-like references have only a minor impact on these measurements. Significant deviations are observed in low to intermediate $p_{\rm T}$ bins, whereas good agreement exists for low $p_{\rm T}$ bins in both rapidity forward directions. The results also indicate that both states experience similar suppression mechanisms. Finally, states produced in the forward direction relative to the Pb nucleus in dPb collisions exhibit strong suppression that rises with increasing collision system size. This suggests that both states interact with the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in a similar manner during the initial stages of collision system expansion. Additionally, the magnitude of the nuclear effect varies depending on whether the produced state originates from the hard scattering process or from recombination of charm and light quarks within the QGP. These findings align well with theoretical predictions and previous results from LHCb at 5.02 TeV. Additionally, a PDF analysis combining both ATLAS and LHCb data produced predictions consistent with these findings. This paper will present these results in detail, including a comparison with LHCb data from lower energy collisions.

To facilitate this embedding, we employ a streamlined version of the continuous logic hyperdoctrine, where the category of equivalence relations is equivalent to that of complete metric spaces and uniformly continuous maps. Following an examination of natural continuous logic theories and their associated syntactic hyperdoctrine, we demonstrate that every object in the resulting 2-category of hypercategories constitutes a topological category equivalent to a category of continuous abstract algebraic categories. We subsequently present examples of continuous abstract cohomology theories, including one encompassing OBRA's E-theory for C*-algebras, as well as continuous abstract cohomology theories based on continuous first-order logic in the style of Makkai and Reimann. Finally, we illustrate how these abstract frameworks apply to continuous group theory, providing an example of a continuous abstract cohomology theory where the resulting continuous 2-functor aligns with the functor that maps Murray-von Neumann equivalence classes of single generators to C*-algebras. This equivalence was previously established by Brown, Greenberg, and the authors. Software systems evolve continuously to accommodate user demands and operational shifts, often resulting in binary bloat that hinders timely identification of functional variations. To mitigate this, this paper introduces a novel algorithm for normalizing software binaries. Designed to efficiently compare large binaries, the method decomposes them into mathematical vector space representations. This transformation enables various operations within the function space, including the measurement of functional similarity and the clustering of functions. The technique has been successfully applied to monitor binary evolution across multiple versions of Linux distributions.

Software systems constantly undergo modification to accommodate new user requirements and environmental shifts; however, these changes can inadvertently introduce temporal functional variations. Binary normalization serves to decompose a software binary into a compact summary, facilitating quick comparison with subsequent versions to measure version similarity and differentiate functional shifts. This research presents a algorithm for normalizing large binaries into a dense vector summary that compresses the original code while maintaining version similarity. This process allows for the efficient comparison of large binaries to measure similarity or cluster functions across a dataset, thereby enabling the identification of temporal functional variations through cluster comparison. The approach has been effectively applied to analyze large software binaries, such as those from the Linux distribution, across multiple versions.

Executing database queries is often hindered by vast, distributed datasets. While traditional methods rely on indexing and query planners to locate relevant data, a alternative strategy involves learning the dataset's structure using neural network ensembles to locate relevant regions directly. This study proposes a method for querying distributed datasets using such ensembles. We developed a neural network architecture trained on distributed data to rapidly identify relevant regions for queries, plan their execution, and locate the software component responsible for storing the required information. This architecture was integrated into a distributed file system where each node hosts a neural network trained on its local data. Experimental results indicate that this approach can significantly reduce query execution times on both small and large distributed datasets.

In high-intensity laser plasma experiments, X-ray diffraction serves as a probe for the collective behavior of quark matter at these intermediate densities. To support future measurements, we developed a Monte Carlo x-ray scattering (MCXS) program capable of calculating the differential scattering cross-section across the complete accessible momentum transfer range. This tool x-rays finite nuclei modeled as liquid drops, incorporating surface roughness and skin thickness as variables, while fixing the internal density profile. Our findings indicate that two-phase coexistence does not significantly influence the scattering pattern at low momentum transfers (low $q$). Furthermore, we have computed the inverse small-angle correlation length as a function of momentum transfer $q$ to assess short- or long-range correlations. Our results demonstrate that the assumed internal density profile of nuclear matter has minimal impact on the calculated correlation length. Finally, we derived the radial matter density distribution from the computed form factor to compare with experimental data, which we expect to report shortly. This density profile derivation method is also applicable to determining the density distribution of any finite nucleus given an internal matter profile. The derived densities align with the droplet model's assumptions regarding the nuclear matter density inside the nucleus. This computational code is essential for interpreting future lab-based small-angle X-ray scattering experiments, particularly for probing the phase structure of dense hadronic matter in the intermediately dense quark phase. This capability is anticipated to be realized in the upcoming GLUEX experiment at Jefferson Lab, which will utilize heavy-ion collisions at intensities 10 orders of magnitude greater than currently achievable in nucleus-nucleus scattering experiments. Our results confirm that the derived matter density inside finite nuclei serves as an effective order parameter for the phase structure in the intermediate dense region. This insight is crucial for interpreting experimental data to investigate the phase structure of dense matter and supports the prediction of a hadronic phase structure similar to liquid water across a wide parameter space. The developed code is publicly available for community use to enable the planning and interpretation of upcoming diffraction experiments. Additionally, these tools can aid in analyzing laboratoryXs and provide a foundation for future research into the phase structure of dense matter at moderate densities.

This study examines a phenomenon termed "reverse coalescence," where isolated liquid droplets merge during the complex dynamical evolution of a gas-liquid system characterized by high input pressure. Utilizing atomic force microscopy (AFM), we captured images of the gas-liquid interface, revealing that this reverse coalescence is driven by the multi-dimensional chaotic mixing within the system. Furthermore, we calculated the Lyapunov exponent (LE) across various experimental conditions to assess system stability; a larger LE value signifies enhanced chaotic mixing. By systematically varying the input pressure gradient between the gas and liquid phases, we identified specific LE thresholds that enable gas-liquid chaotic mixing, allowing for the reverse coalescence of small liquid droplets into a broader network. These findings demonstrate that reverse coalescence arises from the synergy of chaotic mixing and self-similar multi-scale structures in the phase-distributed gas-liquid network, a outcome supported by phase-field simulation results. Consequently, this mechanism holds significant potential for advancing various gas-liquid processing technologies.

matter and life. Recent debates in virology have questioned whether viruses are considered living or non-living based on their ability to replicate only by hijacking host cellular machinery. However, when indigenous microbial cells are infected by bacteriophages, these viruses not just repurpose but also reprogram their host systems. This reprogramming extends beyond the host microbiome to include complex multicellular organisms like humans, animals, and plants. This perspective article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of bacteriophage-host interactions, focusing on the genetic and molecular mechanisms of viral entry, signaling disruptions, host system reprogramming, and the elimination of infected cells. Additionally, it examines the evolution of specific virulence traits linked to pathogenicity and the impact of viral infections on host evolution. The document concludes by outlining future research directions and potential applications of this knowledge. Key areas for further study include using phage-host reprogramming to eliminate cancer and other diseases, developing phage therapies, utilizing phage-mediated immunomodulation to treat various conditions, creating advanced bioreactors through controlled microbial cell-reprogramming by phages, and applying phage therapies for tumor imaging. Ultimately, understanding the mechanisms of phage-induced microbial cell-reprogramming holds immense promise for creating new therapeutic, diagnostic, and biotechnological solutions supported by phage therapy. Furthermore, insights into the mechanism of phage system reprogramming illuminate the previously obscure process of horizontal gene transfer, a primary driver of microbial evolution, offering a new dimension to evolutionary thinking. This is particularly true for human health, given that phage-host interactions represent both lethal and beneficial outcomes of viral infections. Consequently, microbial host-cell reprogramming by phages is identified as a fundamental force shaping Omicron evolution and the co-evolution of hosts with microbial communities. Therefore, phage-host reprogramming of microbial cells is recognized as both a threat and a solution for emerging infectious diseases like COVID-19 and for the sustainable management of human health. This force also underpins the evolution of complex adaptive systems and the detection and eradication of tumors through phage therapy. Ultimately, the mechanism of phage-induced microbial host system reprogramming is acknowledged as a key factor determining microbial virulence and the source of both microbial adaptive evolution and intelligent design. This understanding significantly enhances insights into life's mystery and offers new perspectives on evolutionary thoughts within the broader context of the co-evolution of living and non-living systems. Furthermore, the mechanism of microbial host system reprogramming by phages provides insights into the evolution of infectious diseases like COVID-1

While Hubble-type HII region chains in these systems have been utilized to elucidate HII region locations and the primary gas accretion mechanism behind spiral arm formation, Hubble-type chains have not yet been identified in E-type arped disks. This study employs a novel technique to determine the centers and axes of Hubble-type HII region chains across various galactic scales, applied here to an E-type arped disk, NGC 4093. We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Additionally, we analyze harmonic functions on complete gradient Ricci solitons with nonnegative sectional curvature and provide a comprehensive classification of linear harmonic functions on 3-dimensional complete gradient Ricci solitons with positive sectional curvature. Finally, we explore related differential geometric issues concerning gradient Ricci solitons possessing constant harmonic functions. In this context, we derive new estimates for the potential function and gradient of potential functions on complete non-compact gradient Ricci solitons with positive sectional curvature, utilizing estimates for these functions to obtain estimates for holomorphic functions with positive f-harmonic Laplacian eigenvalues. Our findings indicate that any bounded holomorphic function is constant on complete gradient Ricci solitons with positive sectional curvature and arbitrary Ricci curvature bounds; consequently, any harmonic function with polynomial growth is trivial on such solitons within dimension 3. These results generalize existing outcomes for harmonic functions on complete smooth metric measure spaces with positive curvature. Furthermore, we provide a classification of linear harmonic functions on 3-dimensional complete gradient Ricci solitons with positive sectional curvature. Building on these outcomes, we derive estimates for linear harmonic functions on 3-dimensional complete gradient Ricci solitons with nonnegative sectional curvature and bounded Ricci curvature. This bounding applies to bounded harmonic functions exhibiting bounded gradients and specific growth conditions on certain geometric quantities. We establish a Reynolds formula for weighted complete gradient Ricci solitons with bounded Ricci curvature to prove a Liouville theorem for bounded harmonic functions with Casimir zero, thereby extending previous results. We also investigate non-constant bounded harmonic functions with bounded gradients on 3-dimensional complete gradient Ricci solitons with positive sectional curvature, deriving estimates for the potential function's gradient in the process. These derivations lead to estimates for the first eigenfunction of the Laplacian with the first positive eigenvalue. Applying these results, we demonstrate that the first positive eigenvalue of the Laplacian is simple on 3-dimensional complete gradient Ricci solitons with positive sectional curvature and bounded Ricci curvature. This implies that the corresponding eigenfunctions are trivial on such solitons. Our work generalizes existing findings for eigenfunctions with the first positive eigenvalue on complete smooth metric measure spaces with bounded Ricci curvature and positive sectional curvature. This geometric arrangement facilitates chiral phonons, characterized by atoms circulating around their equilibrium points. While this concept initially appears inapplicable to metals and doped semiconductors—where macroscopic polarization lacks a clear definition—we demonstrate that, within clean conductors, moving beyond the adiabatic approximation yields well-defined nonadiabatic Born effective charges. These quantities are frequency-dependent, scaling with $Z^2/m$ (where $Z$ is the atomic number and $m$ is the electron mass), indicating that nonadiabatic effects enhance the response of semimetallic valence electrons to nuclear displacement. Consequently, nonadiabaticity amplifies intrinsic phonon Rayleigh scattering signals near TO-LO splits in polar metals. Furthermore, we provide theoretical support for recent experimental observations of significant nonadiabatic contributions to phonon lifetimes in Na and Ta, representing fundamental departures from the adiabatic approximation previously assumed in such studies. Additional electronic contributions follow similar principles, offering broader theoretical insights for investigating nonadiabatic phenomena. Additional insights regarding complex materials may address chemical doping disorder, lattice distortions, electronic nonlinearity, and electron-phonon coupling. Finally, these theoretical findings likely serve as essential foundations for interpreting emerging data from ultrafast nonadiabatic pump-probe experiments on metallic sublattices. Aligning with Betchov's insightful predictions from over six decades ago, this critical scale corresponds to the Kolmogorov length, despite being orders of magnitude larger than the mean free path. Consequently, the deterministic incompressible Navier-Stokes equation fails to accurately describe the dissipation range in molecular fluids; instead, the Landau and Lifshitz fluctuating hydrodynamics equation is required. Specifically, our analysis suggests that the exponentially decaying energy spectrum and far-dissipation range intermittency predicted by Kraichnan for deterministic systems are generally superseded by Gaussian thermal equipartition at scales slightly below the Kolmogorov length. Finally, we provide a theoretical explanation for why general shell models—featuring either Gaussian or non-Gaussian forcing—are applicable to turbulent flows, arguing that they function as effective coarse-grained stochastic representations of the underlying molecular stochastic fluid. Design discussions are recognizable by specific design-related keywords and design-driven content that relies on minimal domain context. This study designates a set of terms as salient when their presence strongly indicates a discussion's relevance to design. We present a design-based labeling system derived from design theory, applied to a collection of 1,955 labeled threads from GitHub. Our design-based label system demonstrates superior performance compared to content-based features like topic and design salience on their own. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the model's predicted labels alongside a thorough examination of the model and features regarding their strengths and limitations. This research contributes new considerations for maintaining system architecture and for developers as a guide to improving design discussions within the codebase. Machine learning models trained design-aware code are significantly influenced by how design annotations are collected. However, existing approaches suffer from low inter-annotator agreement due to ambiguous guidelines, resulting in inconsistent and unrepresentative labels. Moreover, current methods focus primarily on syntax and semantics, often overlooking social and psychological aspects critical to software design. To resolve these issues, we introduce "Design Sense," a novel framework that defines ten attributes of design sense encompassing technical, social, and psychological dimensions. We release a design-sense-labeled dataset comprising 27,939 public GitHub pull request threads to support future ML research in this field. Additionally, we provide detailed analyses of the attributes to offer insights for both ML model designers and practitioners, ultimately aiming to enhance the effectiveness of ML models in identifying important design issues. The dataset is available for download from https://github.com/zeromaxwei/Dataset_2_Sense. Source code can be found at https://github.com/zwknight/Annotation_System_ML.

This study investigates two instances of no-cost structural decomposition within nonconvex optimization task sequences: low-rank matrix factors and a hidden orthogonal matrix. These examples align with recent advances in no-cost structural decomposition, including Fast-ADC for low-rank problems and Pro-ADC for orthogonality-promoting problems. By unifying these cases under the general framework of prox-outer iteration, we extend both Fast-ADC and Pro-ADC to support arbitrary task ordering, a capability potentially valuable for enhancing structure exploitation, as observed in the more sophisticated ADC training of large language models. Additionally, we generalize Fast-ADC to accommodate arbitrary task weights and investigate numerical stability, with empirical results accessible in our experimental repository. This research establishes a novel structural decomposition paradigm, defined here as structural outer acceleration (SOA), which encompasses Fast-ADC, Pro-ADC, and various other significant tasks. Furthermore, this work represents the first systematic examination of Fast-ADC's numerical stability regarding task weighting and adaptive weight decay across diverse effective rank structures, while also introducing a new adaptive weight decay mechanism to enhance performance on canonical datasets like MNIST. Overall, SOA stands as a unified structural paradigm for efficient learning across a vast array of datasets, models, and modular architectures. We emphasize that this paper's contribution lies in being the first systematic structural outer decomposition analysis for both Fast-ADC and Pro-ADC; subsequent work has yielded empirical improvements or theoretical guarantees for specific subcases of SOA. Our goal is to catalyze further research into no-cost structural exploitation within OC-DAC to build toward a comprehensive theoretical understanding of this phenomenon. Finally, we acknowledge that SOA is inherently loss-based, a limitation that we address as a potential future research avenue. In this work, we offer a unified theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of addressing these challenges. We establish core definitions, contrast architectural differences, examine performance and combinability, and discuss potential future applications. Furthermore, we highlight how these models can serve as a foundational framework for rational drug design. The provided references encompass 115 papers from diverse fields, including medicine, pharmacology, and computer science, while excluding two books and reviews. This framework encompasses three primary categories of relational machine learning models designed to manage large, sparse data, leveraging relational structure for combinatorial reasoning. Specifically, we focus on graph neural networks, attention mechanism-based models, and knowledge graph neural networks. We define each category by its optimal use case, underlying assumptions, and structural characteristics. Furthermore, we analyze key differences between these categories and within them, offering recommendations for selecting the most appropriate model for a specific task. Selections are guided by factors such as domain knowledge availability, attribute richness, and network comparability. Additionally, we review the influence of established design principles on performance, including transductive learning, unsupervised pretraining, and generative modeling. We also address the potential for networks to serve as drug combinatorial generators, illustrating how they can guide combinatorial decisions through inverse modeling to achieve desired health outcomes. Finally, we outline several open research questions, such as handling private data, reducing environmental impact, and enhancing interpretability for therapeutic use. While reinforcement learning has traditionally been the go-to method, recent advancements in learning imitation algorithms from data are gaining traction. These neural approaches offer improved generalization when expertise varies across tasks and generalize well to unencountered scenarios. However, despite their success in academic settings, these methods struggle to deploy effectively in real-world applications where expert data is imperfect, limited, and uncovered. Furthermore, expert behaviors are often unknown to both the agent and data collectors, hindering generalization to new tasks. Our objective is to develop an agent capable of imitating diverse expert behaviors by observing and reasoning over them without explicit expertise guidance. We introduce an algorithm that learns to simulate expert behaviors in latent spaces using latent expertise guidance, facilitating imitation of unknown expertise, and can reason about it for tasks beyond the expert's experience. Evaluations across a 2D grid world, multi-agent environments, a virtual driving simulator, and a robotic corridor benchmark show that our method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in accuracy for imitation and expertise guidance, offers superior generalization to new tasks, and generalizes to real-world settings. This enables autonomous agents to solve new problems by observing and inferring expert behaviors from various sources, such as humans, teammates, and itself. This study investigates these alternatives through the lens of star cluster evolution, specifically examining how the clustering environment influences individual stars. Using a formalism originally developed by Larson (1969, 1971, 1967, 1972, 1971), we developed a cluster evolution model that accommodates both clump and power law initial mass functions, calculating the dynamical history of every star, its current mass, and its accreted mass fraction. Our simulations demonstrate that two-core fragmentation consistently generates lognormal mass functions, although these functions gradually shift toward the cluster's overarching mass distribution over time. Ultimately, if mass accretion ceases abruptly, stars revert to their initial distribution; however, accretion evolving slowly maintains the lognormal profile, albeit broader than the initial state. Consequently, the clustering environment of a cluster's progenitor cloud dictates the final mass distribution of low- and intermediate-mass main sequence stars. This occurs because accretion predominantly augments the masses of already formed stars rather than creating new stars, causing most low- and intermediate-mass stars today to possess the same mass distribution as the protostars from which they evolved. Furthermore, our clusters exhibit mass segregation for intermediate masses once cumulative formation times exceed $10^7$ years, implying that modern clusters typically display mass segregation by masses exceeding two solar masses, provided stars in this range still form within today's dense clusters. Finally, our models indicate that the fraction of a star's current mass that was accreted during its evolution may be higher in smaller, older, and lower-density clusters than previously thought, as the majority of a star's mass was likely accreted from its circumstellar disk during the late stages of cluster evolution. This supports the contemporary view of star formation as a continuous evolutionary process. This formulation uniquely predicts the cluster evolution mass function of low- and intermediate-mass main sequence stars. Furthermore, this approach avoids the numerical and physical complications, such as excessive gas fractions and the "twin problem," that have plagued other cluster evolution models. Similarly, it sheds new light on whether a star's current mass was indeed accreted during cluster evolution. Various clusters may exhibit different levels of mass accretion, yet our clusters likely retained more mass on stars than earlier models, with most of this accreted mass having occurred late

The approach first constructs an HMM from the training data and subsequently identifies anomalies by assessing the likelihood of each test sample using the learned model's observation probabilities. Unlike conventional HDA methods that depend on scoring functions like log-likelihoods, the proposed approach employs a two-threshold scoring mechanism. This mechanism defines anomalous regions within the score space by integrating likelihoods from both the HMM and a standard uniform distribution. Further refinement of the model can be achieved through Baum-Welch algorithm-based learning. The efficacy of this proposed method is validated through anomaly generation experiments utilizing the synthetic dataset D7 from the existing collection of 24 time series. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms four existing HDA techniques, with performance gains of over 20% and 40% respectively when applying log-thresholds and non-logarithmic (ln-free) thresholds. Notably, the ln-free thresholding yields superior results compared to logarithmic thresholds. Furthermore, the proposed method requires significantly less computational time than the four compared techniques, particularly during the test phase. Finally, this guide likelihood analysis framework is highly robust and highly transferable across different time series data. This study investigates whether substructures in both scattered light (gas) and millimeter continuum (dust) provide initial constraints on the physical properties of these gas features. Utilizing synthetic data generated from a radiation-hydrodynamics simulation of a weakly turbulent disk containing a 0.09 solar mass planet, we performed emission line reconstruction at 5 microns (via Next Generation Extremely Large Telescope coronography) and millimeter continuum reconstruction (via ALMA). We applied various data processing and fitting techniques to extract initial estimates of gas substructure properties (density and/or flow) and millimeter continuum substructures (spacing, contrast, and width). Subsequent component analysis and Bayesian fitting yielded initial assessments of the uncertainties associated with these derived parameters. Our findings indicate that a significant portion of the variability in scattered and millimeter light arises from multiple overlapping substructures influencing one another. Furthermore, variations in scattering efficiency produce distortions in the spatial extent and spacing of these features compared to dust structures. Without accounting for these efficiency variations, the inferred gas substructure characteristics are distorted, specifically showing an excess width and reduced contrast relative to the actual simulated values. Post-processing techniques were required to isolate and resolve these scattering effects. Consequently, current observations do not support the interpretation of gas substructures as pure gas clumps in pressure-dinned, hot gas; instead, they suggest an average increase in local surface density and/or local cooling rates. Given the complexity introduced by scattering, determining the specific local changes in density and flow required to match observations is beyond the scope of this paper. The proposed methods for extracting and fitting initial constraints on substructure properties can be applied to real data for individual cases, utilizing a prior informed by the statistical properties of the simulated disk to derive more precise constraints. These techniques are adaptable for reconstructing three-dimensional structures from the rich data that will be produced by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array and ALMA. Ultimately, as explanations for substructures evolve, they will assist in refining our understanding of the complex interaction between these disk substructures.

However, as time resolution, input channels, and event volumes increase, the resulting data volume often overwhelms conventional processing methods. To address this, we created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), a robust, versatile, and user-friendly software solution designed for the efficient analysis and visualization of time-tagged data. Unlike traditional start-stop measurements, our tool enables flexible correlation extraction from time-tagged datasets of arbitrary complexity. By integrating state diagrams with straightforward code snippets, ETA maintains high computational efficiency while supporting sophisticated analytical workflows. We illustrate this capability by directly comparing various pulse-overlap extraction state diagrams implemented via backend code snippets, thereby eliminating the need to convert time-tagged data into other formats such as binned histograms or free-range histograms. Furthermore, ETA offers multiple pre-defined and customizable correlation metrics, including joint and conditional probabilities of varying orders. To ensure transparency and avoid vendor lock-in, the software utilizes open and well-documented scripting languages without relying on proprietary black boxes. Written in Python and Java, ETA remains true to the UNIX/POSIX philosophy, ensuring true compatibility with standard data-handling and processing environments while integrating seamlessly with widely-used analysis tools such as MATLAB and ROOT. Additionally, the software features a comprehensive graphical user interface that provides detailed statistical metrics and intuitive visual representations of all discussed calculations. This includes joint and conditional probabilities for up to third-order correlations, delta-correlations, various overlap types, mean delay with confidence intervals, rate estimation, and hit rates. These outcomes are accessible through diverse graphical formats including histograms, scatter plots, correlation circles, and loop diagrams, facilitating immediate data assessment and interpretation. Ultimately, ETA serves as a reliable foundation for advanced time-correlation analysis and visualization, operating as a standalone application or a complementary tool within broader analytical suites to handle time-tagged data of any complexity. Both the source code and a graphical demo version are available for free and without restriction at https://www.uni-mainz.de/fzk/soft/eta/. This study extends the findings of Cannarsa and Capuani to the specific context of mean field games of controls. In this framework, a continuum of players influences the trajectory of a consensus variable, which represents the average of all individual strategies; notably, no player can affect the consensus variable independently. Each player aims to minimize a cost function that includes a terminal component with a strong lean toward $L^1$-type regularity. To address the challenges posed by the combination of control variables and the consensus constraint, we substitute the original cost with an unconstrained "relaxed" cost. We demonstrate that a mild solution exists for the first-order mean field game of relaxed controls, and we prove that any sequence of approximate solutions possesses a convergent subsequence, with the limit serving as a solution to the first-order mean field game of measures. Finally, we illustrate how to derive a solution to the original mean field game of controls from the solution of the consensus-constrained problem by applying the "no loop theorem" of Soner and Ewald to the gradient of the value function's viscosity solution of the transport equation. In our experiments, the raft—a collection of particles—is uniaxially stretched by the widening air-liquid interface beneath it. The resulting failure patterns evolve continuously with the stretching speed. Hopf differential decomposes into a real function and a meromorphic quadratic differential. This differential is holomorphic across certain leaves of the associated minimal surface defined by the meromorphic factor and possesses poles with strictly alternating residues along every closed loop within these leaves. These isothermic surfaces emerge as critical points of the area functional under constraints imposed by the real part of the meromorphic quadratic differential and additional poles of the Hopf differential. We demonstrate that the resulting minimal surfaces adhere to Euler-Lagrange equations that mirror those of minimal surfaces in complex space $\mathbb{C}^2$. Furthermore, the corresponding Gauss-Codazzi equations are equivalent to the integrability conditions of a specific zero mean curvature family of surfaces within $\mathbb{C}^2$. These surfaces can be constructed via the Wu-Hopf section theorem or derived from factorization properties of certain oriented orthonormal frame bundles. Additionally, we explore how such surfaces can be viewed as solutions to specific first-order systems of partial differential equations and present several examples. Finally, we analyze how these constraints influence the index and nullity of the Laplacian. These findings may offer valuable insights for understanding the topology and analytic properties of surfaces with zero mean curvature. To investigate the driving mechanisms behind these specific edge-on SFR enhancements, we conducted a multi-channel investigation comprising near-infrared imaging, optical spectroscopy, and radio continuum observations. not only as the world's highest-energy accelerator for protons and heavy ions but also for photon-photon and photon-hadron ($\gamma$p and $\gamma$Pb) interactions. This capability arises because the accelerated protons and ions generate electromagnetic fields that act as sources of photons, enabling these photons to interact with one another or with hadrons. Ultra-Peripheral Collisions (UPCs) occur when incoming ions pass at impact parameters exceeding the sum of their radii, avoiding the strong nuclear force, and are driven by the exchange of virtual photons between the nuclei. Since the number of emitted photons scales with the square of the nuclear charge and their energies rise sharply with beam energy, the LHC's high beam energies make it the most powerful photon source ever constructed. Specifically, the production of heavy vector mesons via photoproduction is favored due to their strong coupling to photons. This paper presents recent findings on forward J/$\psi$ production in Pb–Pb UPCs at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV using the ALICE detector. The data confirm that the equivalent point nucleus model accurately describes these measurements when higher-order effects, such as photon-boson fusion and two-photon exchanges, are incorporated. Additionally, comparing these results to proton-proton and ppbar–J/$\psi$ data offers insight into quantum chromodynamic (QCD) effects within heavy-ion environments. Furthermore, the measured rapidity distribution aligns with predictions based on the parton distribution functions available at such high energies. Finally, a future increase in beam energy to 8 TeV is expected to enhance the production cross section by a factor of four and may provide additional insights into QCD effects. This talk will also explore potential implications for research during the High-Luminosity LHC era.

hyperbolic 3-manifolds possess Euler classes with a norm no greater than one. Over the last twenty years, efforts have been made to construct examples for each possible value. While circular foliations account for all cases where the Euler class norm equals one, proving the existence of taut foliations for the remaining cases has relied on extensive computer verification. This paper presents a novel approach to construct taut foliations, thereby providing a streamlined proof for each case of Thurston's classification. Our methodology leverages the duality between affine manifolds and variation geodesics within the space of geodesics. As an auxiliary result, we offer a new characterization of variation geodesics grounded in convexity principles. To explore these findings, we develop a symplectic manifold named the linear path space and demonstrate that its symplectic form can be defined via Skolder's metric. Finally, we illustrate how to reconstruct a finite volume hyperbolic 3-manifold with a positive first Betti number from an affine manifold through the addition of a singularity, a process that also yields a taut foliation. This specific case study examines the relationship between singularity types in flat manifolds and the dynamics of associated holomorphic flows. Overall, this work provides a fresh perspective on constructing taut foliations. To support this, we include a background section detailing essential definitions and theorems regarding affine manifolds, variation geodesics, and link invariants required to establish our main result. Additionally, we present several conjectures and directions for future research.

solar wind is examined using data from the Fast Plasma Investigation (FPI) and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe (SDP) instruments aboard the Magnetospheric MultiScale (MMS) mission. FPI data enable investigation down to the sub-ion scale region ($f_{sc}\gtrsim 1$ Hz) before instrumental noise dominates, while SDP data are utilized to accurately determine the plasma wavelength associated with plasma waves detected by FPI. This methodology was applied to an multi-component study focusing on plasma waves with periods greater than 0.1 seconds. A primary finding is that all wavelength estimates derived from SDP data demonstrate a clear power law dependency on frequency up to $f_{sc}\sim$ few Hz. Furthermore, within the range of $f_{sc}\gtrsim$ few Hz, all measured plasma wavelengths are comparable to the local ion gyroradius ($\rho_i$). A minor deviation from power law behavior observed around $f_{sc}\sim$ few Hz aligns with a previously noted change in spectral slope occurring at $f_{sc}\sim$ few Hz. Given that all reported plasma wavelengths indicate a transition to sub-ion scales near $f_{sc}\sim$ few Hz, where all processes become kinetic, these scales are frequently described as undergoing an anisotropic transition toward the background magnetic field. However, the measurement of plasma waves with finite wavelength $\delta$ propagating at a speed $U_r$ relative to the plasma frame reveals that the transition to sub-ion scales and the subsequent change in anisotropy depend not only on the wave frequency but also on the product $\delta f_{sc}U_r$ being less than or exceeding the ion cyclotron frequency ($\Omega_i$). Additionally, the study confirms that the plasma is approximately incompressible for all measured waves and within the $f_{sc}$ band analyzed here. Consequently, a transition to Bernstein-perpendicular waves is disallowed for all waves except those with the largest wavelengths. Finally, within the analyzed $f_{sc}$ band, the evidence suggests that all plasma waves with $\delta f_{sc}U_r<\Omega_i$ are likely foreground Alfvén waves. Therefore, the observed transition to sub-ion scales and anisotropy for these specific waves is attributed to phase mixing and energy cascade processes. When turbulent viscosity is negligible, this equation simplifies to the classical second-order Roberts equation. We demonstrate that our derived turbulent viscosity eddy coefficients align with the two-equation Turbulent Kinetic Energy and Dissipation Rate of Energy two-equation (TKE-DPE) turbulence model developed by Launder and Martin. Furthermore, considering specific scenarios for stratification and mean shear, we identify conditions under which the new TG equation admits exponentially growing solutions at large amplitudes—the criterion for the onset of Rayleigh-Taylor instability. Specifically, when linear shear instability (Kelvin-Helmholtz instability) is absent and turbulence is weak, the model captures the emergence of Rayleigh-Taylor instability as originally described by Landau. Additionally, the model allows for the calculation of the critical Richardson number corresponding to this instability. This work was previously published in Phys. Rev. E, 107, 014110 (2023). The proposed method, known as the "tuning method," operates by adjusting the order of the polynomial basis to locate areas with abnormal variance. To implement this, the fabric image is first converted into its Fourier transform and reshaped into a virtual image representing the fabric's cross-section via a line scan. This virtual image is then smoothed horizontally to remove noise without compromising the detection of pattern defects. Following transformation back to the frequency domain, a low-rank approximation isolates the defect component within the single scan image. To pinpoint the exact location and extent of the anomaly, the variance between the residual image (comprising only the defect) and the original scan is calculated across the scan index. To enhance accuracy, the polynomial basis is engineered to exclude frequencies associated with the regular pattern, ensuring that variance spikes indicate defects rather than the expected fabric design. Additionally, to mitigate potential false positives, the method is applied to a filtered version of the scan image that excludes regions likely to cause misinterpretation. Finally, to accelerate subsequent analysis, only the identified suspect regions are retained for processing. To validate the method, its ability to recover added white noise is measured using the signal-to-reconstruction ratio, alongside an assessment of computational cost. Unlike most other detection techniques, the tuning method relies on two primary parameters: the defect frequency and the polynomial basis size. Unlike prior research, this approach does not require multiple captured images or extensive pre-processing to execute the tuning method itself, although pre-processing is recommended to eliminate false positives and enhance overall efficiency. The resulting algorithm effectively removes the regular pattern while precisely and efficiently recovering the image. Furthermore, the tunable basis allows the algorithm to adapt to varying noise levels and specific pattern characteristics across different fabrics with minimal re-parameterization. We demonstrate that a single line scan can detect both localized defects, such as stains, and repeated defects, such as missing threads. These findings suggest that the tuning method is a strong candidate for replacing current detection systems in specific patterned fabric sectors. However, to fully endorse the method across the broader textile industry, future work must expand the method's applicability to a wider variety of fabrics, as it currently effectively removes the regular patterns found on colored and floral fabrics. Our future research will focus on evaluating whether specific parameters or modifications to the tuning method can identify defects in other types of patterned fabrics to satisfy industry needs regarding this new detection algorithm. The ultimate goal of this research is to drive electronic motion in matter using controlled high-energy electric field waveforms and to initiate investigations into intracyclic phenomena. These outcomes represent essential experimental milestones in the emerging field of coherent strong-field control. Ultimately, the integration of high-harmonic generation and high-energy photon science holds immense promise for unlocking new frontiers in light-matter interactions and for deepening our fundamental understanding of light fields, fields, and matter.

We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. When a manufacturer encounters a product failure, the customer typically contacts them to arrange a repair. However, if multiple instances of the same product are involved, the manufacturer may choose to replace all affected units with new ones rather than repairing the failed ones. This study examines the dynamic behavior of two makers engaged in both forward and backward competitive relationships. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the probability of making a new sale follows an exponential distribution, and the time required to fix faulty products also follows an exponential distribution.

The proposed model quantifies the profitability of forward and backward competitive strategies, thereby assisting manufacturers in decision-making regarding the adoption of these strategies. By enabling manufacturers to anticipate expected payoffs, the model supports the formulation of constant failure and repair rates that align with specific strategies. This capability facilitates optimal planning of production and after-sales service activities. Additionally, the findings allow manufacturers to assess potential earnings compared to those of their competitors. To validate the model, numerical illustrations are provided using two practical applications.

Unlike traditional Trojan attacks that embed small, insignificant patterns onto clean host images, our approach treats triggers as complete images representing semantically relevant object classes. Because the backdoored classifier learns the abstract semantics of these trigger images instead of specific pixel patterns, it can be activated by visually distinct yet semantically similar inputs. to modal logic found in existing literature by employing the language of topological categories over Set. Drawing parallels with categorical logic, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the relationship between the syntactic structure of (and various extensions of) the modal language and the semantic structures of topological categories within this framework. Consequently, this approach enables a conceptual grasp of the abstract architecture of modal logic. Furthermore, within this framework, the transfer of modal structures to other categories becomes as straightforward as defining a functor from the category of sets to the category of topological spaces. Finally, we illustrate the utility of this framework by demonstrating the connection between Kripke semantics and modal algebras.

Additionally, using topological categories over Set as a semantic foundation, we investigate modal extensions through the lens of functors mapping the category of sets to the category of topological categories over Set. We examine the interaction between these modal extensions and topological functors, demonstrating that modal extensions correspond to specific properties of these functors. Leaning on this analysis, we derive a category of topological categories over Set, encompassing all relevant semantic structures for modal logic, and establish an equivalence between this category and the category of algebras over the language of the modal logic under consideration. This equivalence facilitates a comprehensive analysis of the connection between (various extensions of) modal logic and (properties of) both topological categories over Set and algebras of sets with operations, thereby generalizing both Kripke's representation theorem and Esakia's theorem to this broader context.

Finally, we explore the connection between modal logic and other categorical structures present in topological categories over Set, such as frames and probabilistic categories over Set. This leads to the investigation of specific properties of morphisms in these categories, with a focus on properties inherent to functors between them. This approach allows us to analyze the links between different semantic frameworks for modal logic via (properties of a functor from the category of frames to the category of probabilistic categories over Set, which is equivalent to) (properties of morphisms in the category of topological categories over Set, which is equivalent to) (properties of algebras corresponding to the modal language in question). Thus, this research establishes a novel approach to studying the relationships between modal logic and these various semantic frameworks. (Some of these findings were presented at the Logic, Topology and Set Theory Research Seminar (LTSRS 6) at Kyung Hee University in Seoul, South Korea, in November 2019.)

Specifically, NNS are gaining significant traction in fluid dynamics for simulating solution fields and learning optimized control strategies. However, a critical concern remains regarding the learning capabilities of deep learning models applied to highly nonlinear systems, particularly concerning optimization and optimization learning tasks. A key factor influencing these learning capacities is the architectural design of the NN. While prior research has extensively explored optimizing NNs for solution optimization, no prior learning model has addressed optimization through learning of optimization processes. This study introduces "optimization learning of neural networks" to derive solution-revealing insights. This approach employs a hierarchical configuration of NNs: the lower level focuses on optimization learning, while the upper level handles solution optimization. By addressing this learning process at the lower level through solutions generated from the higher level, we achieve learning and optimization simultaneously. The proposed method is demonstrated using a neural network framework based on the extremum principle of variational problems, applied to a coupled forward and adjoint variable problem within the extremum principle. Although various modeling techniques and software tools are available, selecting the most appropriate occupancy model for a specific study remains challenging due to diverse data characteristics, model structures, and software limitations. To address this need, we introduce "ecoCee," a flexible R package featuring multiple built-in occupancy models, Watanabe's approximate Bayesian information criterion (WBIC) for comparing models, and visualization tools. The package supports data analysis, model comparison, and result interpretation, making it an essential resource for ecologists conducting occupancy analysis. As an integrated environment for occupancy modeling, ecoCee offers easier access to models compared to other available software. To ensure usability, the package includes help files and a case study featuring real data. Our analysis used hermit crab data from the coastal rocky shores of Wakasa-bay, Fukui Prefecture, Japan, collected in November and December 2019. We tested several hermit crab species using data from 32 transects and 20-meter quadrants while accounting for cluster randomization transects, individual-sized covariates, and clustering. First, we applied ecoCee to estimate species-specific hermit crab occupancy based on transect-level data. Second, we estimated species-specific occupancy at the transect level by integrating transect-level hermit crab counts and occupancy estimates, employing the inverse Dirichlet process mixing model. Finally, we mapped the occupancy patterns of the two most common hermit crab species across the study area. This analysis not only confirms ecoCee's ability to handle cluster randomized transects, clustering, and individual-sized covariates but also reveals new insights into hermit crab community structure in the region. The ecoCee package and its associated analysis are freely accessible to researchers at https://gpkoda.github.io/ecoCee/.

This architecture integrates a standard variational autoencoder with a physics-based Gaussian process (GP) that maps the latent code to the physical state space. By learning the joint distribution of the latent space, the model achieves two outcomes: it constructs a complete likelihood over the full state space and simultaneously executes dimensionality reduction. Consequently, the model can fill in missing data points and reconstruct the full state from low-dimensional summaries derived via projection. When sampled latent codes are passed through the GP, they yield samples of the full physical state, including uncertainty, enabling exact sampling of the physical domain. Additionally, our continuous GP provides an analytical expression for the change-point detection problem, eliminating the need for post-hoc sampling of the latent space or Full Exhaustive Search. By leveraging the complete likelihood and sampling capabilities of the model, we formally evaluate performance using standard metrics across both synthetic datasets (covering various dimensions, aspects, and gradients) and a real 3D turbulent flow system. The results demonstrate that our PAE surpasses existing baselines in both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Results indicated that when particles are large and/or highly concentrated, entrainment rates within the particle-laden plume decrease compared to a pure fluid plume with identical initial conditions. Furthermore, these findings indicate that particle addition can potentially alter predictions regarding the development of sediment deposits over time. We introduce an enhanced architecture featuring dedicated layer-based node sets for each modalities, shared hidden units, and contrastive divergence (CD) updates. The architecture demonstrates effective learning from a dataset of 300,000 technical document pages, producing realistic image pages and limited text samples. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between reconstruction quality and free energy parameters, observing that higher average negative log pressure ("temperature") correlates with more realistic outputs, whereas lower values indicate better reconstruction accuracy. Finally, the CD update rule is analyzed in the context of multimodal learning, revealing that simultaneous updates for multiple modalities do not guarantee correct gradient estimation for the energy distribution; therefore, alternating updates are suggested as a practical solution for deep energy-based joint models.

Document image generation serves as a valuable technology for document layout analysis, enabling the synthesis of realistic training data and serving as a preliminary visualization step. While several approaches exist for generating static images using Variational AutoEncoders (VAEs) or auto-encoders with convolutional generators, very few methods currently address the simultaneous joint generation of documents and their corresponding text. This paper proposes a solution by integrating existing unimodal VAE techniques into a joint framework based on deep joint models represented by Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs). While DBMs have previously been used to model multivariate discrete distributions, this work extends the concept to handle multiple input types, including digitized document pages. Unlike prior applications in physics that relied on Monte Carlo sampling, our focus is on approximate inference suitable for large-scale data. We evaluate learning outcomes on two technical document datasets of varying resolutions. Experiments show successful learning from a Spanish electrical installation guide containing 30,000 pages, resulting in realistic page reconstructions, generated electrical circuit text, and estimated joint distributions. Additionally, we demonstrate joint learning from a Russian technical book with over 10,000 pages, though with lesser success. Finally, the paper discusses the application of approximate inference techniques, such as message passing and mean field approximations, to deep energy-based joint models. Key challenges remain in effectively capturing dependencies between visual and textual modes and managing the vast joint state space. Future work will explore ways to improve the framework's scalability regarding both data volume and model depth.

Furthermore, individuals undergo mutations at Poisson events driven by independent rates $\{\lambda_n\}_{n\geq1}$, creating distinct population branches. These branches accumulate an infinite number of annotations, forming a branch process $\{Z_t^{(n)}: t\geq 0, n\geq 1\}$, which records the sizes of the population subset carrying each specific annotation. This process evolves into an infinite sequence of Yule processes. This paper extends the recently introduced and novel concept of Young diagrams, originally defined by Dyson and later generalized by Baryshnikov and Penney, to this general branching framework. These diagram processes evolve via both branching and shifting. We detail the asymptotic behavior of these processes as time $t$ approaches infinity. Notably, if the lifetime distribution has a finite right endpoint and is not atomically distributed there, the asymptotic proportions of the diagram process (conditioned on its width) conform to the Gibrat-Yule measure on Young diagrams defined by Mays and Moggah Goshy. However, if the distribution features a positive atomic component at the right endpoint, a singular measure emerges in the mesoscopic scale asymptotics of the diagram processes. Additionally, we briefly explore further properties of this diagram process when lifetimes are distributed uniformly on $[0,t]$. Specifically, we demonstrate that the area under the diagram process satisfies a central limit theorem with variance of order $t^4$. Finally, we provide an alternative expression for this variance that connects it to the fourth central moment of a certain polynomial sequence.

To accomplish this, we propose integrating an attentive activation function, specifically the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU), into an end-to-end spoofing countermeasure framework built on a deep neural network with an auxiliary branch.
