Notably, our approach achieves a equal error rate of 10.9% against TTS speech and 3.9% against stolen voice, thereby setting new records for spoofing detection performance. To facilitate broader security community evaluation of such systems, our framework has been deployed within OpenOracle, a cloud-based, real-time, hosted system targeting French language inputs. We have also made the system's source code available. Our findings suggest that the proposed framework successfully detects subtle features in French speech artifacts, highlighting the potential for detecting similar subtle features in other languages as well. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed system effectively distinguishes between synthetic and genuine speech artifacts within French input. To our knowledge, this represents the first end-to-end deep learning-based spoofing countermeasure system developed for French speech. Finally, we show that our framework maintains robust detection capabilities even under noisy conditions, successfully identifying artifacts in French speech within both clean and noisy environments. Our results indicate that the proposed framework yields superior detection rates compared to alternatives using AReLU or standard ReLU activation functions. While Hausdorff famously demonstrated that such a partition exists for $\aleph_1$, we show that the spectrum of possible cardinalities for Borel partitions of $\mathbb{R}$ can be quite arbitrary. This distributional characteristic suggests that CTAs may exit the market at the first signs of adverse price impact. Finally, although futures trading remains price-sensitive, the findings imply that spot traders, such as hedge funds, could potentially absorb some of the liquidity supply-demand imbalances caused by CTAs. This process enables subsequent protocols, such as IP protocol analysis, to more accurately parse protocol messages and effectively identify cyber threats. However, existing detection methods often struggle with both zero-day and known attacks. To address this, the study proposes Bayesian Network (BN)-based protocol detection that integrates process knowledge and structural knowledge. Process knowledge encompasses the rules governing message exchange during protocol interactions, while structural knowledge refers to the network architecture featuring directed edges between nodes representing protocol entities like sources, destinations, and ports. Structural knowledge is derived through data-driven techniques, whereas process knowledge is established via expert domain knowledge. This BN model serves as a robust inference engine capable of detecting protocol violations by comparing actual network interactions with pre-defined process knowledge. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, given that the Bayesian model is probabilistic, it can successfully detect protocol violations involving zero-day attacks. To enhance performance, the authors also introduce an improved structure learning algorithm that leverages structural knowledge to further refine the BN model. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that this approach achieves convergence more rapidly than standard learning algorithms and raises the protocol detection accuracy to 99.8%. The efficacy of the proposed process knowledge and structural knowledge significantly contributes to this high detection accuracy. Using back-gated p-MOSFETs with Al2O3 gate dielectrics and amorphous p-type silicon channels (approximately 4 nm thick), we first identified optimal characteristics for mosSAW devices. Additionally, the MOSFET threshold voltage exhibited shifts consistent with changes in the effective gate field. These findings suggest that mosSAWs hold potential for use as integrated active or passive gate materials in ultra-thin MOSFETs, as well as for integrating sensing and logic functions on silicon substrates. Furthermore, mosSAWs could enable higher packing densities for silicon-based integrated circuits compared to conventional top-down integrated gate schemes. Finally, these results support the viability of strain-assisted effective electric field modulation for integrated active material applications. This approach complements recent developments in strain-assisted effective stress field modulation for integrated sensing applications [Phys. Rev. Appl. 9, 044024 (2018)]. The current work establishes a foundation for strain-assisted effective gate field modulation in integrated active materials. These findings offer new avenues for silicon integrated circuit design and demonstrate that local deformation-induced dynamic modulation is feasible for mosSAWs. Our results suggest that mosSAWs can operate as complete gate materials to toggle channel conduction, potentially enabling diverse applications in silicon integrated circuits, including strain-assisted switching and modulation. Specifically, the employed mosSAW could toggle the MOSFET channel between depletion and nondepletion states, functioning similarly to a back gate; this principle may facilitate novel silicon integrated materials capable of detecting and responding to both strain and electric fields. Moreover, strain-assisted effective gate field modulation serves as an essential mechanism for achieving higher performance in mosSAW sensors and switches. Nevertheless, federated environments often encounter novel classes characterized by entirely unseen data distributions from every user, user participation is stochastic, and communication bandwidth is constrained. To address these specific challenges, we introduce a meta-learning approach designed to minimize the user participation budget required to achieve user data distributions that are novel across the board. Our solution employs an information-theoretic analysis of this constraint to develop an effective training strategy. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves superior user data novelty and reduces the participation budget by at least 40% compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we establish that the budget reductions achieved are statistically significant at the p < 0.05 level. Additionally, our approach yields more balanced performance across new classes and neighbors within the novelty space compared to standard techniques. Finally, extensive experiments confirm the method's effectiveness against completely new classes that were not present in any user's local dataset.

In many federated learning scenarios, such as mobile and edge contexts, it is beneficial for the global model to adapt to local user data, necessitating continuous retraining with new arrivals. However, this requirement conflicts with two key constraints in federated settings: limited communication bandwidth and privacy concerns. In this work, we propose meta-federated learning to simultaneously address bandwidth limitations and enable adaptation to local data without excessive communication. This approach trains a meta-model on a limited subset of new users to generate initial parameters for subsequent learning sessions. We analyze the impact of meta-federated learning on system performance and evaluate the advantages of combining it with quantization to further compress transmission information. Extensive experiments across multiple deep neural network architectures and real-world datasets validate the method's effectiveness. Our results indicate that meta-federated learning can reduce communication costs by up to 90% in early training sessions (initially empty datasets) with as little as 5% participation, achieving performance within 2% of standard federated learning baselines when using only 20% participation. We also explore strategies to gradually increase participation over time and report experimental findings supporting the proposed approach. The code is accessible at https://github.com/TalShw/ML.

human ability to generalize systematically, a developmental process typically marked by a rapid surge in proficiency known as an inflection point. This study sought to replicate such a trajectory by training a reinforcement learning agent on the give-$N$ task, which involves selecting $N$ items from a binary vector $\mathbf{x}$ to maximize reward, $R(\mathbf{x}, N) = N \log_2(1 + 1/p)$, based on the probability $p$ of $1$s in $\mathbf{x}$. Our results demonstrate that Q-learning agents quickly reach performance plateaus, whereas off-policy behavior cloning agents gradually inflection points aligned with these plateaus when trained sequentially on distributions with varying $p$ values. These findings indicate that both off-policy behavior cloning and incremental training are essential for developing systematic counting capabilities in infants and adults, offering insight into how humans grasp the structure of natural numbers through continuous engagement with statistical sequences of variable item counts. Furthermore, these mechanisms highlight a form of latent structure within a task, revealing that training agents on the give-$N$ task off-policy using behavior cloning allows them to infer the stochastic structure of the counting task without explicit instruction. This supports the view that both behavior cloning and incremental training underlie the gradual acquisition of systematic knowledge in human children, reinforcing the importance of unstructured experience in cognitive development. Additionally, the ability of behavior cloning agents to uncover structural knowledge remains a promising benchmark for evaluating next-generation neural network architectures. Overall, our results emphasize the significance of both unsupervised learning and incremental training in the evolution of systematic counting skills. These mechanisms not only offer a novel explanation for the development of systematic counting but also demonstrate that behavioral cloning and incremental training can be effectively implemented through attention over input positional embeddings and a growth mechanism for network width, respectively. Finally, we show that linear value function approximation can also induce inflection points in behavior cloning agents when trained sequentially on give-$N$ tasks with varying $p$ values, suggesting that both linear and off-policy behavior cloning approaches yield comparable results. This work thus provides strong evidence that both incremental behavior cloning and linear value function approximation can uncover the stochastic structure of give-$N$ tasks, providing a generative story for the gradual acquisition of systematic counting in human children through continuous exposure to binary binary semantic sequences of variable item cardinality. Chazelle introduced a probabilistic set membership structure requiring $O(\log n)$ time, while Bloom filter variations exist that achieve $O(1)$ query time but at the cost of increased space. This paper presents a new data structure termed the Probabilistic Cuckoo Filter, which combines the constant-time queries of Chazelle's design with the space efficiency of standard Cuckoo filters. Although we provide an asymptotic analysis of false positive rates in the online setting—filling a gap left by Chazelle's work, which was originally analyzed offline—we prioritize a comprehensive experimental evaluation. Our results demonstrate that the Probabilistic Cuckoo Filter outperforms both traditional Cuckoo and Bloom filter variants in terms of space efficiency. Additionally, we propose two enhanced versions of the structure that further reduce false positive probabilities and overhead. The first variant employs two distinct Probabilistic Cuckoo Filter instances, while the second utilizes two arrays with different bit counts. Both improvements rely on the same fundamental Probabilistic Cuckoo Filter logic but utilize separate arrays to handle distinct bit allocations. Our empirical comparison confirms that this proposed structure outperforms standard Cuckoo filters, particularly in terms of space efficiency. ### Introduction

This paper presents the top-ranking solution for the NeurIPS 2021 AWS DeepRacer Challenge, which tasked participants with autonomously navigating a drift racing course using reinforcement learning. Participants were required to train their models within a provided simulator, evaluate them via an oracle system, and finalize their submission using the evaluation framework. Our approach secured the highest scores under the official evaluation criteria. While our solution does not claim to represent a new learning algorithm, it introduces an innovative methodology for constructing the state space and action representation. These design choices were made to directly maximize the reward obtained from the simulator's evaluation code. We hope this solution will serve as a valuable benchmark for future racing competitions and similar tasks that incorporate explicit evaluation codes. The official scoring system comprises three parts: course completion time, average drift angle, and average full throttle time. By analyzing this criteria, we developed a strategy to create the most effective solution. The implementation was developed in Python 3.7 and Keras 2.2.4, optimized for performance without compromising clarity. To ensure the solution reflects the competition's evaluation code more accurately, we modified the original Python code to better align with it. While our solution was the leading entry in the official contest evaluation, we acknowledge that it may not represent the superior solution when compared against alternative methods of calculating quality.

In response to the scarcity of image-to-video deepfake datasets, we introduce Face2Video, a comprehensive resource featuring real-world video streams with identity-matched reference images. Addressing another gap, we have released FakeVideo, a large-scale video dataset designed for cross-media forgery detection. The dataset offers three primary contributions: (i) a new baseline demonstrating that existing video forgery methods yield poor results on it; (ii) an in-depth analysis of synthetic artifacts in MMS and MMM videos that aids in developing more robust detectors; (iii) an exploration of cross-media techniques for forgery detection, revealing cross-correlation among cross-media classifiers. Employing density functional theory (DFT) enhanced with the GW approximation and noncollinear spin calculations, we investigate the electronic and magnetic properties of EuS/InAs bilayers, focusing on a (100) interface oriented along the [110] direction. Our results identify p-type doping in InAs adjacent to the EuS layer, where the proximity effect induces a magnetic transition at 2.6 K, consistent with experimental findings. Furthermore, we observe the formation of magnetic polarons that disrupt the topological surface state near the interface. The influence of the exchange field on InAs is most significant at a EuS thickness of 5 unit cells, achieving an exchange splitting exceeding 0.1 eV. Finally, we provide detailed insights for topological applications regarding the magnetic doping level, the specific magnetic structure, and the orientation of the exchange field relative to the interface.

Solving CMDPs to establish effective operational policies faces two primary hurdles: the immense size of the state and action spaces, and the difficulty in calculating the transition kernel. This paper introduces a sampling-based primal-dual algorithm designed to tackle CMDPs. The method alternates between regularized policy iteration to refine policies and subgradient ascent to uphold constraints. Under mild regularity assumptions, the algorithm achieves a convergence rate of $O(\log(T)/\sqrt{T})$ over $T$ iterations. Furthermore, for CMDPs with weakly coupled structures, the approach leverages embedded decomposition to significantly lower problem dimensionality. Applied to two key scenarios with such structures—multi-product inventory management and multi-class queue scheduling—the algorithm demonstrates that its generated controls surpass existing state-of-the-art heuristics. Notably, the method proves effective even when the underlying dynamical model is misspecified. Beyond practical utility in unknown environments, the algorithm offers theoretical insights for solving CMDPs. Specifically, it proves that the strong duality gap for CMDPs can be tightly bounded in terms of the Riemannian volume of the control space and the Lipschitz constant of the cost and transition functions, a bound that is essentially tight. Leveraging this finding, the work derives operator and primal-dual convergence rates for solving CMDPs. Crucially, unlike most theoretical bounds dependent on environment size, the Riemannian volume of the value function provides a measure of complexity that remains invariant to the dimensions of the state and action spaces. This facilitates the development of scalable CMDP solving algorithms with strong theoretical guarantees, even in high-dimensional settings. The findings are illustrated through the multi-class $G/\Phi/M/c$/S queue, a generative flow-based generative model, multi-class $M/M/\infty$ inventory, and multi-class $M/M/1$ routing.

$p \geq 5$ can be expressed as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$, where $k$ is defined as the $\textbf{generator}$ of $p$. Twin primes are uniquely characterized by sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. Consequently, it is logical to investigate twin primes by analyzing their generators. This paper introduces a novel approach to proving the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ using a sieve method designed to identify all twin primes within a specific range $[5r, 5r^2]$, employing a function $F(n, p)$ linked to integer sequences that contain no $p$th powers for primes $p \leq \sqrt{r}$. The author demonstrates that the third derivative of this function yields a result of either $0$ or $5$ at any positive integer $r$. To extend this methodology toward the $\textbf{Twin Prime Theorem}$, an infinite range for $r$ must be established. Furthermore, the study examines the statistical traits of generators for twin primes to support this objective. Significant outcomes include determining whether every twin prime has a $\textbf{successor}$ and analyzing the \textbf{properties} of these generators, with the ultimate goal being the verification of the Twin Prime Conjecture. Furthermore, this reasoning can be readily extended to prudent twin primes $(5r \pm 1, 5r \pm 3)$. The conclusion posits that the \textbf{Twin Prime Theorem} holds true, thereby establishing the validity of the Twin Prime Conjecture.

This paper introduces a closed-loop path planning and obstacle avoidance framework designed for mobile mapping missions using uncalibrated sensors. The system relies on primary feature tracking and mapping, which are integrated with map decompositions and obstacle detection to support dynamic indoor navigation. Specifically, dynamic obstacle trajectories are estimated via affine invariant tracking of primary features, while detailed local geometry is captured through secondary feature tracking and mapping. These components enhance volume estimation and collision detection via obstacle modeling and the secondary mapping update. This paper investigates the quotients formed by two such palindromic numbers, addressing fundamental questions regarding the sets of integers and rational numbers that result. For instance, we demonstrate that it is algorithmically decidable whether a given integer N can be expressed as a ratio A/B where both A and B are palindromic. Furthermore, for integers that admit such a representation, we establish an upper bound on the magnitude of the numerator within the minimal representation. We also examine the rational numbers that possess a minimal minimal representation—where the numerator is the smallest possible for that specific ratio—and provide lower and upper bounds for them. Notably, the lower bound is an irrational number with a remarkably elegant closed-form expression, which we refer to as the silver-matrix golden-beer constant, due to its significant relationship with the originally defined silver-beer constant and the golden ratio. Additionally, our analysis reveals that this constant constitutes the unique irrational number that cannot be represented as a minimal ratio of two palindromic numbers. Finally, this study was motivated by an unexpected identity linking the constant to the Carmichael function. Along the way, we derive various lower and upper bounds for P(n), the largest palindromic number that is not a perfect square, as well as the count of palindromic perfect squares that do not exceed 2^n. Our findings indicate that these results reach their optimum when the exponent of the upper bound is approximately n^2 / \phi^5, supporting the conjecture that the bounds are minimal at this value of the exponent. While image reconstruction for idealized monoenergetic X-ray sources remains a well-established solved problem, the impact of realistic polyenergetic spectra on image quality has recently garnered significant attention. Previous studies have developed iterative algorithms that incorporate physical properties of interactions, such as energy attenuation and beam hardening, alongside images derived from actual measurements. However, the extent to which measurement errors influence these iterative approaches, particularly regarding artifact generation, remains poorly understood. Our prior work derived an algorithm for iterative polyenergetic reconstruction that accounts for physical interaction properties based on projections from noisy measurements. This study investigates the artifact-producing capabilities of such iterative algorithms by employing mathematical modeling of spectral physical interaction properties and iterative reconstruction based on noisy projections. Through both simulations and real-world CT scans using phantoms, we observe that while noniterative reconstructions yield relatively accurate images with low noise, introducing noise compensation into the iterative framework can generate substantial artifacts in both phantom data and actual patient scans. These findings suggest a need for novel regularization techniques capable of handling realistic spectra and noisy measurements without introducing similar artifacts. Furthermore, we propose innovative regularization strategies designed to address these specific challenges.

CT is widely employed across medical and engineering disciplines to image the interiors of various subjects. Consequently, investigating the internal compositions of unknown objects presents a compelling inverse problem that has driven the development of sophisticated reconstruction algorithms. Historically, reconstruction methods for polyenergetic (realistic) spectra accounting for physical interaction properties have differed significantly from those using idealized monoenergetic sources. Measurement noise is another critical variable; numerous algorithms prioritizing low-noise images for monoenergetic imaging have been created to reconstruct noisy projections. Nevertheless, numerous existing algorithms prioritize low bias over low noise, potentially compromising image quality when measurements are noisy. This study derives an algorithm for iterative CT spectrum finding with physical interaction properties using noisy projections. Our findings indicate that the algorithm's performance is not merely an iteration of the noise-reduction method applied to the initial spectrum estimate; specifically, we provide examples where the algorithm fails to converge to the correct spectrum. We believe this research offers valuable insights into the creation of effective iterative polyenergetic reconstruction algorithms and validates the necessity of novel techniques to utilize spectral finding with noisy measurements for CT image reconstruction. However, modern implementations in languages such as Python, Ruby, and PHP have significantly optimized OOP efficiency, allowing it to match or surpass procedural methods in both performance and readability. Additionally, recent advancements in compiler technology have substantially accelerated OOP execution.

To validate these claims, we conducted execution time tests (with garbage collection disabled) across various programming paradigms to scrutinize their operational characteristics.

The study utilized object-oriented and functional programming techniques in C#, Java, and Python to handle data and perform time-series comparisons of specific attributes.

Execution times were measured in milliseconds using C#'s DateTime.Now, constrained to a 1,000,000 millisecond limit. The experiments involved inputting specific values into the programs, running them to generate output, and terminating the session after a single run. To mitigate random fluctuations in execution duration, each test was repeated ten times. Furthermore, the input values were also subjected to repeated comparisons under identical conditions.

Data from the computational tests were analyzed using Microsoft Excel to calculate the mean, variance, and standard deviation for each result set.

It is important to note that the input values were intentionally selected to induce comparison inconsistencies. Specifically, for attribute A, values ranging from 1 to 1000 were used to trigger divergent operator behaviors; the operator should return TRUE for A <= 500 and FALSE otherwise. Similarly, for attributes B and C, values from 1 to 1000 were utilized, though the specific thresholds for achieving TRUE or FALSE results were designed to vary. All other input parameters were frequently executed during the experiment.

While the object-oriented and functional approaches were implemented to introduce intentional inconsistencies in comparison operations, a significant number of execution attempts resulted in both methods failing to return values or causing termination. To address this, the study incorporated specific checks to ensure valid comparisons and prevent anomalies. To avoid executing comparisons in a vacuum, a loop was implemented to execute the comparison ten times per attempt. Consequently, each comparison operation was executed at least 100 times to ensure sufficient data collection.

Findings indicate that while procedural and object-oriented methods generally require similar execution times, functional programming requires longer durations. However, the object-oriented and functional approaches specifically employed in this research did not consistently produce different execution times, particularly when both compared and uncompared attributes were utilized.

It reviews the governing equations for straw deformation and presents measurements of the Poisson's ratio for the NA62 spectrometer straw, which are critical for determining stability conditions. Additionally, the study estimates the minimum pre-tension required for these tubes. These findings are essential for the design and construction of the NA62 experiment at CERN. Key design parameters, specifically the Poisson's ratio and pre-tension of the straw, must be precisely defined to ensure optimal detection efficiency, operational reliability, and high intrinsic resolution. Furthermore, the minimum pre-tension for NA62 straws is approximately 3–4 N, a figure significantly lower than values reported in existing literature. This method was validated through simulations that modeled the relationship between internal pressure changes and radial straw deformation. The experimental setup employed a vacuum extraction system to alter the internal pressure of the straws, while their radial deformation was monitored using an optical microscope. Finally, the paper compares the experimental data with predictions derived from the theoretical deformation model. This research was conducted within the context of the NA62 experiment at CERN.

While the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) framework offers a general approach to handling such shifts, formulating it effectively remains a challenging task. Specifically, defining a plausible region for the target distribution without encompassing the worst-case scenario leads to sub-optimal solutions, resulting in excessive conservatism. Drawing inspiration from the success of deep generative models in approximating high-dimensional distributions, we introduce direct robust learning (DRL), which employs an inner-loop min-max training procedure to learn a solution robust against distributional shifts within a specified neighbor region. Unlike DRO methods that rely on finite samples from a worst-case distribution, DRL iteratively estimates this region by generating samples via the outer product of the source domain's deep generative representation with a perturbation function discovered in the inner loop. Extensive empirical evaluations across multiple support set perturbation domains demonstrate that DRL achieves superior performance compared to both traditional conservative DRO techniques and selected state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning baselines. The source code for DRL can be accessed at https://github.com/m-y-ang/drl/tree/main. The associated paper is available at https://m-y-ang.github.io/drl/.

Although the impurity's oscillatory motion back-reacts on the condensate by exciting internal phonon modes, it leaves the roton minimum and the periodicity of the matter wave lattice unchanged. The eventual decay of these oscillations is primarily driven by wavepacket dispersion, which we show can be significantly mitigated by modeling the impurity as a bright soliton. Furthermore, when both spin and phonon mode degrees of freedom are considered, the decay mechanisms follow the same order: wavepacket (impurity) > phonon > spin. Finally, we validate our findings regarding impurity behavior—with the exception of roton-mediated decay—which is largely independent of the spin-orbit coupling strength due to its influence on the phonon spectrum rather than the ground state. This confirms the robustness of spin, phonon, and roton modes as candidates for describing the interaction-induced decay of excitations in this system. Our findings offer novel insights into the dynamical coupling between a moving impurity and the elementary excitations of a spin-orbit coupled Bose polycrystal. These insights not only enhance understanding in superfluid systems exhibiting spin, phonon, and roton richness but also serve as a spin-bose-phonon-resonant Bose polycrystal model for investigating the fundamental interaction between a moving impurity and a periodic lattice. This establishes a fundamental connection between spin-orit-coupled Bose polycrystals and solid-state physics. Given a sequence of $n$ points $(s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n)$ arriving sequentially on a $d$-dimensional grid, the objective of a spanner algorithm is to maintain a graph on these points that approximates shortest paths for the original metric. Specifically, a $(1 + \varepsilon)$-spanner for the current set $S_i = \{s_1, \ldots,s_i\}$ must satisfy two conditions: (1) the length of every edge is at most $(1 + \varepsilon)$ times the Euclidean distance between its endpoints, and (2) for any two points $u,v \in S_i$, the distance between them in the graph does not exceed $(1 + \varepsilon)$ times their Euclidean distance.

For an offline version of this problem on $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, King, King, Klein, and King (2019) established a lower bound of $\Omega(\log^{d-1} n)$ for the spanner size and a matching upper bound of $O\left(\log^{d-1} n \cdot \frac{n}{(\log n)^{2d}}\right)$. They further demonstrated that for dimension $d=2$, the exact spanner size is $2n - 2k - 1$, where $k$ represents the number of nested empty convex quadrilaterals.

In this work, we address the online extension of these problems. For a line graph ($d=1$), we achieve a bound of $3n - 2k - 1$, improving upon the prior result of $(4n - 2k - 3)$. For plane point sets ($d=2$), we construct a $(3 + \varepsilon)$-spanner of size at most $10.365(\sqrt{n})$. This improves upon King, King, Klein, and King (2019), who provided a $(5+\varepsilon)$-spanner of size $O(\sqrt{n})$. Additionally, we propose conjectures and open problems regarding online spanner sizes for dimensions $d=2$ and $d=3$. Ultimately, we present an upper bound of $O(\log^{d-1} n)$ for the online Euclidean spanner problem

Although recent studies have successfully used machine learning to fingerprint these devices, they often assume that necessary features are readily available or inexpensive to extract, ignoring the associated costs. This work adopts a more realistic perspective by acknowledging that feature extraction incurs varying costs. Furthermore, we move beyond treating misclassification loss as a simple binary value, instead proposing a framework where losses vary based on performance. More significantly, we introduce the concept of "risk" in IoT device classification, defined as the product of misclassification loss and the probability of it occurring. With feature selection in high-dimensional IoT datasets often relying on human expertise, we aim to develop an automated selection method that minimizes both misclassification risk and feature selection cost. We formulate this as a joint optimization problem involving a risk function, an uncertainty function representing selection cost, and a regularizer for regularized risk minimization. Finally, we present experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed approach.

The paper also explores Offloading Deep Neural Networks (DDNN) for mobile IoT devices. Since mobile nodes typically suffer from limited computing power, they must execute multiple layers of deep models while respecting power and computation constraints. Existing research typically addresses either power/computation limits alone or optimization under perfect channel conditions. In this study, we propose a new joint optimization problem that considers power, computation, and fuzzy stochastic channel constraints. To solve this, we develop a joint optimization framework utilizing DDNN with power, computation, and fuzzy stochastic offloading. We design a novel network with power and computation constraints, introducing an offloading decision function that accounts for uncertain channel conditions to enable an node to offload either the entire NN, a partial portion, or nothing at all. This creates a joint optimization problem with power, computation, and fuzzy stochastic constraints, which is difficult to resolve due to its non-convexity, stochastic nature, and fuzzy variables. This problem is equivalent to a joint optimization of learning rate and weight initialization with fuzzy and stochastic constraints across multiple mobile nodes executing NNs under limited power and computation resources. To address this, we apply an alternating minimization method to optimize these parameters successively. We demonstrate that this proposed framework achieves substantial reductions in NN energy consumption, computation times, and latency compared to other existing methods.

In summary, this letter presents a new joint optimization framework for deep neural network training on mobile IoT devices with power, computation, and fuzzy stochastic constraints. This paper investigates the algebraic and relational characteristics of G\"odel modal logics defined by finite universal relational semantic structures. We establish equivalence conditions for their corresponding algebraic semantics: G\"odel modal algebras, specifically focusing on finite direct products of simple G\"odel modal algebras. Additionally, we examine the complexity levels of the first-order theory associated with these universal semantic structures. Central to our analysis is the concept of a path-connected G\"odel pseudo-characteristic function. Utilizing this tool, we establish necessary and sufficient criteria for the strong completeness of G\"odel modal algebras relative to a class of universal semantic structures, as well as decidability results for their first-order theories. Each molecule was constructed from six tangent spheres aligned linearly, with diameters decreasing in a linear fashion; consequently, the geometry was defined uniquely by a single parameter, $d$, representing the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameter. The system's phases were examined across varying values of $d$ and packing density ($\eta$). Since interactions were exclusively excluded-volume in nature, the resulting phases were determined entirely by configurational entropy. At densities below 0.5, the systems exhibited an isotropic liquid alongside conventional nematic and smectic A liquid crystalline phases. However, for $\eta > 0.5$, in addition to the standard nonconvex entropy, a new phase emerged: an entropy convex phase that is nevertheless more stable than the nonconvex alternative. This convex phase is characterized by molecules adopting an "open book" configuration, where molecules with smaller end-spheres stack based on their larger ends. Furthermore, simulations indicated that monoclinic crystals are more stable than orthorhombic crystals, and chiral wedge-shaped particles displayed less symmetric preferred orientations within their nematic and smectic A phases compared to nonchiral wedges. These findings provide novel numerical insights into the entropy-driven formation of the entropy convex phase. Additionally, we derived approximate analytical expressions for the entropy of both convex and nonconvex phases using hard-wedge shape and statistical mechanics formalism, showing reasonable agreement with simulation results. These entropy expressions may prove valuable for modeling experiments on rod-like particles that exhibit an entropy convex phase. Finally, optimal alignment thresholds were established using the wedge's symmetry plane as a reference. This approach offers a versatile framework for classifying various liquid crystalline structures, including conventional, chiral, charge-separating, energy-separating, polyion, semiflexible, colloidal, electrostatically repulsive/attractive, and magnetic liquid crystals, by illuminating their underlying phase behaviors through simplified wedge-like models. Consequently, this optimal alignment definition enables unified statistical analyses across diverse liquid crystalline systems. As a preliminary step toward experimental applicability, we selected appropriate experimental liquids and applied this framework, yielding valuable insights into optimal alignment threshold values for future experiments utilizing wedge-shaped particles. Finally, the wedge-shaped model may serve as a benchmark for developing experimental techniques to characterize entropy convex phases in rod-like liquid crystals. Consequently, this study introduces a novel approach for characterizing the entropy convex phase and the entropy-driven phase transitions

In these scenarios, the counts of initial and final microstates differ, preventing connection via unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This issue frequently arises when phase space volume changes and has not previously been addressed using Hamiltonian methods. We establish that our framework effectively handles such nonequilibrium processes with varying microstate counts. To validate this approach, we examine a simple model consisting of two distinguishable particles confined within a time-dependent box similar to the Einstein box, ignoring gravitational interactions between the particles. First, we analyze a reversible expansion where the initial state contains one particle while the final state contains two, via a Hamiltonian trajectory. Subsequently, we explore the reverse reversible process—reintroducing a particle into the system—and subsequently present analyses of both systems as concrete examples of irreversible expansion and contraction. Irreversibility is defined here by the inability to return to the initial state using a unique Hamiltonian trajectory. In these irreversible cases, both system evolution and measurement outcome distributions indicate that microstate counts increase during expansion and decrease during contraction. Importantly, our thermodynamic description remains consistent in both reversible and irreversible scenarios. Furthermore, the system's ability to perform work during expansion is enhanced compared to cases where microstate counts remain constant, aligning with intuitive expectations. Finally, consistent with the framework's definition of dissipated heat, we demonstrate that dissipated heat is positive for irreversible expansion and negative for reversible expansion. These findings support the broader validity of microstate thermodynamics in systems where the microstate count evolves over time. Additionally, our work provides a thermodynamic interpretation for quantum tunneling between two regions of distinct particle numbers within a single well, characterized by system sizes of one and two particles, respectively. This is achieved by calculating the probability current at the well's boundary using the phase component of the single-particle wave function. Ultimately, both the thermodynamic analysis and numerical calculations reveal that for both expansion and contraction, heat flows from the system to the bath during reversible processes, whereas the direction of heat flow is reversed in irreversible scenarios. These outcomes further confirm that the system does work on the bath in reversible cases, while the bath performs work on the system in irreversible cases. These findings offer novel insights into particle tunneling phenomena within the thermodynamic framework. Moreover, this study represents one of the initial investigations into contraction processes utilizing Hamiltonian dynamics. By providing Hamiltonian expressions for thermodynamic quantities, our work facilitates the further examination of more intricate many-body systems that involve contraction. We conceptualize Bayesian neural networks as models designed to handle noisy data, featuring a hierarchical structure where hyperparameters are optimized to reflect uncertainty regarding training set parameters. This study demonstrates that human recognition of objects and actions relies on efficiently merging spatial and motion cues, particularly in scenarios where neither cue suffices independently. We achieved this insight by isolating minimal dynamic conditions required for recognition and examining how participants utilized spatial and temporal information under a multidimensional forced-choice paradigm. The results indicate that when object recognition fails due to spatial ambiguity but becomes possible through motion, viewers preferentially extract preferential discriminative motion cues rather than any motion at all. These findings provide robust evidence for a specific mechanism of spatiotemporal integration: a dynamic multidimensional decision rule wherein an object's representation remains undecidable until activated by action-related information. This approach offers a general framework for comprehending the integration of spatial and temporal dimensions in biological vision. Furthermore, these data serve as a rigorous benchmark for evaluating computational models of object recognition and informing the design of artificial systems capable of robustly exploiting both spatial and temporal information. Finally, this research has implications for discovering new principles of perception that can inspire enhanced machine vision and more effective human-computer interactions. However, this work does not specify the temporal or spatial resolution of individual neural encodings; for instance, it does not address whether temporal integration occurs via a sliding window or via a global representation of all events within a time frame. Future computational efforts should focus on elucidating these fundamental aspects of spatiotemporal integration. Moreover, rendering such abstract decisions tangible for robotic systems to emulate will be essential for advancing the next generation of visual technologies. By making this choice tangible, robotics could potentially achieve a level of machine vision that surpasses many current state-of-the-art computational methods. This phenomenon, termed pseudo-symmetry breaking, can facilitate the formation of complex dark matter structures. This paper examines a concrete instance utilizing the $2-3_{RS}$ model featuring pseudo-symmetry breaking. Within this framework, we investigate the suppression of direct detection signals for cosmologically significant WIMP masses, specifically around the TeV scale. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of the co-annihilation region with the Lightest Supersymmetric Particle (LSP) on the parameter space viable for future direct detection experiments. Notably, the $S_5$ model predicts a nuclear scattering cross-section of approximately $10^{-42}$ cm$^2$, which is well below current experimental limits and within reach of next-generation studies. If identified, such a signal would signify that the underlying theoretical framework is a beyond Standard Model extension incorporating horizontal symmetries. Additionally, we observe that the current LUX experiment excludes most of the favored parameter space regarding the Higgs boson coupling; however, this is understandable given the severe constraints imposed by the $2-3_{RS}$ model's specific predictions on Higgs couplings to Standard Model particles. Finally, we demonstrate how the LSP co-annihilation region influences the astrophysical and theoretical preferred parameter space. Our findings indicate that LSP co-annihilation effects shift the preferred cross-section toward lower values, aligning with the lower bound established by XENON1T. Standard WIMP scenarios typically predict scattering cross-sections between $10^{-43}$ and $10^{-42}$ cm$^2$ for TeV-scale WIMPs, whereas in the $2-3_{RS}$ model, these values drop to or below $10^{-42}$ cm$^2$. Since disruptions in this transport mechanism are linked to numerous neurodegenerative diseases, understanding how neurons regulate transport to deliver materials to specific sites is vital. In this study, we introduce a new optimization model to identify key transport events that ensure the timely delivery of materials to neurons' branched regions. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its unsupervised nature, which eliminates the need for feedback and makes it ideal for autonomous learning contexts. This paper investigates the design of molecular systems capable of exhibiting such proto-intelligent behaviors and introduces the first chemical reaction network (CRN) capable of demonstrating autonomous Hebbian learning across any number of input channels. Introduction Understanding intelligent life as a complex adaptive system residing within an open thermodynamic framework provides the most effective terminology for conceiving molecular-scale intelligent devices. While numerous design principles exist for creating simple reactive reactive devices from thermodynamically feasible reaction networks [1], developing responsive systems that can learn from their environmental dynamics remains an unresolved challenge [2]. Although various design principles have been suggested for reversible logical gates within open thermodynamic systems [3], utilizing these physical components to implement sophisticated information-processing algorithms like neural networks for environmental sensing remains unexplored. This work proposes a Feinberg-design chemical reaction network capable of implementing an average-rate neural network, enabling autonomous learning via Hebbian plasticity of its "synaptic" bonds.

Background Neuronal Hebbian Learning In classical neural network models of cognitive processes, neurons are biological entities within the central nervous system whose activities are regulated by intrinsic ion currents and external synaptic inputs. Synapses are specialized junctions between neurons that asymmetrically facilitate signal transmission in one direction, modifying the probability that an action potential in a source neuron triggers a corresponding spike in the target neuron. Neuronal learning refers to innate or experience-driven modifications to a neuron's internal parameters that alter its response dynamics to external inputs. This study focuses exclusively on Hebbian learning, where synaptic connections strengthen solely when both pre- and postsynaptic neurons are simultaneously activated by specific inputs. Although various learning algorithms have been proposed, the rule described herein represents one of the earliest and most straightforward implementations of Hebbian learning. Its simplicity makes it a strong candidate for realization through microchemical systems.

Modern machine learning tools empower anyone to build and execute models that uncover hidden data patterns for scientific use. However, evaluating every possible model against widely used datasets is often cost-prohibitive regarding cloud resources. Consequently, current benchmarking methods rely on representative subsets to estimate performance without full execution. As datasets grow larger, so does the number of models to evaluate, restricting the scope of existing approaches to only a few selected candidates. This study proposes an alternative roadmap for scientific benchmarking that avoids full dataset execution while still assessing all models in the set. Achieved through the generalization of learnings, this method executes models on a few datasets to generalize their behavior across others, thereby estimating performance on the target data. We validate this approach by comparing predictions against actual full-execution results on a diverse dataset of interest. Finally, we discuss the potential of this methodology to accelerate computational AI research in modern computational science.

I. INTRODUCTION

Both artificial intelligence and modern scientific inquiry benefit equally from "large" domain-specific data. This dataset size enables researchers to evaluate many different computational models developed with advanced AI tools. Yet, modern AI techniques allow for the rapid design and development of a vast number of these models, creating a challenge in identifying which yield new scientific insights, insights that standard benchmarking practices often miss. First, "large" data implies a significant number of datasets of sufficient quality to support reliable analysis. Second, the emphasis is on scientific discovery, going beyond mere model ranking, especially in high-stakes scenarios. In this context, researchers compare candidate models to established baselines to determine if superior performance is possible. While it is straightforward to rank models against one another on a single dataset, it is not always clear how these rankings hold up when scaled to multiple datasets of relevant size. Third, the computational cost of execution becomes prohibitive, prohibiting the full run-up evaluation of many candidate models on a sufficient number of datasets of adequate size to distinguish meaningful performance differences. Given these constraints, a scientist might be unable to execute even a fraction of their models on a representative set of datasets to test hypotheses about computational AI learnings.

To overcome these challenges, we introduce a generalizationized benchmarking approach for large-scale AI of science. This method, grounded in computational learnability, estimates the performance of many candidate models on a target dataset of sufficient size by observing their behavior across a small number of datasets of comparable size and content. mechanisms like command-line parameters, allowing users to adjust settings to satisfy diverse functional and non-functional needs, including security, memory footprint, and execution speed. However, certain options are often never utilized by a specific system instance, keeping their values constant regardless of the use case, while others are frequently overridden, resulting in effective, constant default values. These stable or frequently overridden options can be candidate "lock-down" settings, as locking them down can simplify the system and streamline maintenance and security efforts. We present LiSe, a novel approach that identifies efficient lock-down options by analyzing historical setting values to support incremental system simplification. LiSe utilizes Decision Tree learning to detect option dependencies and reverse engineering techniques to generate an efficient state machine that captures valid setting configurations. LiSe is capable of handling complex option dependencies and can verify new options against an established model to suggest additional constraints, thereby ensuring consistent simplification across various software versions. We evaluated LiSe on 300 settings from various open-source systems; the results demonstrate that 25% of all options are lock-down candidates, with averages of 40% for functional options and 15% for non-functional ones like settings and security options. Furthermore, only 9% of rare functional options and 0.5% of non-functional options should theoretically be allowed to run in any configuration, highlighting that lock-down capabilities are more prevalent than rareness indicates. The LiSe tool and all analyzed systems are publicly available. The full evaluation details and findings are documented in the associated technical report. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/IITB-SECL/iitb-seclasel. Simplifying software systems is a continuous effort; future iterations of this tool will feature a GUI and support batch processing to facilitate the simplification of entire software families across multiple versions. Additionally, we are considering extending LiSe to handle version-specific dependencies and generating simple patches to ensure consistent simplification. The options discovered by LiSe will also be integrated into the release process to maintain the simplified versions. Our code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/IITB-SECL/iitb-seclasel, and the respective technical report is hosted at https://github.com/IITB-SECL/iitb-secl-report.

Higgs boson, particle physics has entered a thrilling new phase. A key inquiry remains whether the Standard Model accurately describes nature's scalar sector or if it is merely a component of a broader framework containing additional particles. A primary method for investigating this involves exploring extended scalar sector models at upcoming collider facilities. This discussion examines such models within the context of the high-luminosity LHC, potential proton-proton colliders with center-of-mass energies of 27 and 100 TeV, and future lepton colliders operating at various energy levels. Regarding scalar extended models, significant emphasis is placed on the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model, five-Higgs-Doublet Model, Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, and Majorana Neutrino Mass Models. An overarching theme is that the prospects for these searches will likely be dictated more by current experimental constraints than by the prospects for new physics discovery. This represents a rare instance where "no discovery" could constitute the most significant finding. Consequently, we provide a comprehensive review of existing and projected sensitivity for upcoming collider experiments. Our analysis demonstrates that the potential to uncover new physics in scalar sectors will maintain a positive outlook for the foreseeable future, even as we enter an era of even higher energy colliders. Furthermore, we illustrate that the discovery of the rare muon decay $\mu^{+}\mu^{-}e^{+}e^{-}$ would offer substantial new insights into the scalar sector, even though the resulting limit on the relevant coupling would be dictated by present-day constraints; the anticipated sensitivity of future experiments is then outlined. Ultimately, we argue that the extraordinary prospects of new physics in the scalar sector across the next four decades will likely be governed more by the depth of our current understanding than by the energy of future colliders. As an example, the detection of the lepton-flavor-violating decay $\mu^{+} \rightarrow e^{+} e^{-} e^{-}$ at the Intense Muon Beamline at FRIB could yield novel insights into the scalar sector. Even though the resulting limit on $C_{\mu e}$ will remain constrained by existing experiments, the anticipated sensitivity of future collider experiments is detailed. In conclusion, the scalar sector holds vast potential for novel discoveries at forthcoming colliders, and we emphasize that the "null result" could very well be an exceptional finding.

This approach involves substituting the standard metallic lead with a resistive lead (large $R$ in k$\Omega$) during tunneling spectroscopy. However, current learning-based approaches often strive to identify a single mapping, effectively ignoring the range of stylistic variations. This paper introduces a novel framework that employs a deep neural network to map an input image to a subset of the stylistic spectrum defined by two example images: one from the input and one desired output. Our method utilizes multiple paired training sets to gen-erate a network that produces images falling between the ranges generated by individual learned networks corresponding to each training set. We demonstrate that this method can synthesize images that not only resemble the reference but also lie between the two sets of multi-scale representations. Specifically, we deployed a super-large-scale particle image velocimetry (SLPIV) system that employs natural snow particles as tracers to measure velocity fields and detect vortex structures within a 22 m × 39 m area centered 18 m above ground level. Simultaneously, particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) was used to monitor individual snow particles across a 1.5 m × 3.9 m subsection of the SLPIV field, allowing for the analysis of energy spectra, dominant modes, and vortex characteristics alongside individual particle motions. The research examines how snow settling interacts with ambient turbulence as the particle concentration thickens the boundary layer and destabilizes the atmosphere. Results demonstrate that even at high snow loading conditions, the boundary layer maintains inherent turbulence features, including growing turbulent eddies responsible for enhanced snow deposition (snow pumping), which remain dominant over eddies generated by the falling particles themselves. Direct observations of snow eddy dynamics reveal that larger eddies (exceeding 1 m) extend from the top of the test zone to the ground, whereas smaller eddies nestle edgewise against the ground. Additionally, Rouse number calculations based on field data indicate a transition to a hyper-stable atmospheric condition at the tower's top during heavy snowfall, resulting in eddies thinner than the theoretical thick snow Rouse billows, thereby enabling significant snow pumping. These comprehensive field-based direct observations of snow and eddy dynamics offer valuable insights for improving snow transport modeling in geological and engineering applications. The SLPIV system's ability to measure velocity fields and vortex structures despite the complex, stochastic, and high-concentration nature of snow settling represents a unique advantage over other snow measurement techniques. This system can detect eddies growing from the top down to the ground, even in high-wind scenarios, representing a novel contribution to snow science. The SLPIV method is adaptable for various snow transport situations, such as analyzing snow deposition structures in valleys or the interior of snow caves. Fundamentally, it posits that the brain functions as an approximate Bayesian inference engine, constructing an internal generative model to guide agents toward minimizing surprise. While this theory has yielded promising insights into various cognitive and motor functions, its standard mathematical forms have limited its application to agents capable of self-reproduction. High-throughput scientific information streams produce continuous streams of multidimensional information involving several variables. Introducing analysis systems close to samples yields vast amounts of information about various characteristics of scientific objects, resulting in intricate, high-dimensional information streams that are difficult to handle.

Effective consideration of these streams demands highly parallel processing. Furthermore, analyzing vast, intricate scientific information streams in real time requires rapid, parallel analysis capabilities. Analyzing these streams quickly in real time enables scientists to make well-informed decisions regarding research directions. For instance, during a high-throughput experiment involving many samples, the integration of analysis systems allows researchers to identify samples with unusual features or specific attributes early in the process. This early detection of unique or distinct sample behaviors facilitates targeted research on these specific samples, thereby minimizing time and resources spent on samples unlikely to advance the research objective. Understanding the benefits and challenges of incorporating rapid, in situ scientific data collection and analysis helps develop more efficient scientific data collection and analysis strategies. This paper examines these capabilities and provides examples of decision-making processes that leverage real-time analysis to guide samples and scientific objectives.

Three examples of scientific research domains are discussed here: high-resolution X-ray scattering, optical imaging, and electron microscopy. Numerous other disciplines face similar challenges when confronting vast, intricate high-throughput scientific information streams, including materials science, chemical synthesis, quality control, and high-throughput screenings. Scientific instruments used in these studies are increasingly sophisticated and numerous, capable of generating high volumes of data rapidly. Similarly, advanced and scalable environmental conditions systems, such as material chambers and synthesis labs, accelerate the frequency of scientific measurements.

High-Resolution Small-Angle X-Ray Scattering (HR-SAXS) serves as a specific example of a scientific research domain characterized by vast, intricate high-throughput information streams, applicable to other domains like materials science, chemical synthesis, and high-throughput screenings. In this technique, a focused X-ray beam with a wavelength between 0.5 and 3 Å strikes a sample, generating a high-intensity beam with extremely high energy, measured in a high-vacuum chamber. The resulting patterns are typically acquired using one or more dimensional detectors with very high pixel counts, ranging from 1 to 10 million.

We analyze the self-similar solutions in detail, focusing particularly on the evolution of the curvature at the axis of symmetry as the shock advances inward. Under the assumption of axial symmetry, we investigate how the curvature behaves; if azimuthal symmetry is further assumed, the focus shifts to the curvature at the surface of a rotating liquid column of constant density that generates the shock upon collapse. The Fitzgerald singularity, previously predicted for Fitzgerald-type problems where external curvature evolves without control, is demonstrated to emerge in this Guderley scenario. Kuznetsov [Soviet Physics - Doklady, 38 (1993), S. 277-278], which established that Fitzgerald singularities develop in all Guderley-type problems involving more than one self-similar variable. For the azimuthal symmetry case, we also explore the scenario where the initial angular velocity profile is linearly increasing with the radius, revealing a striking similarity to the Fitzgerald singularity scenario. Additionally, we address the associated inverse problem and demonstrate how to uniquely determine the initial data for a specified self-similar solution. Finally, we provide computational evidence indicating that the Fitzgerald singularity remains non-weak under these conditions. These findings hold significant relevance for investigating the dynamic collapse of liquid interfaces.

This position paper explores the synergies between requirements engineering (RE) and Explainable AI (XAI). We identify key challenges within XAI and propose a framework alongside research directions to demonstrate how RE practices can address these issues. Furthermore, we posit that integrating XAI with RE will significantly contribute to the mature development of transparent and trustworthy AI systems. Specifically, we outline how a "butterfly model" of RE can aid in creating a more systematic, structured approach to XAI. Finally, we suggest that adopting a "cooperative intelligence" model can deeply merge RE and XAI, enabling AI systems to not only enhance their own understanding but also to elevate the intelligence of the humans working with them. This paper serves to highlight the value of applying RE in this context and invites the RE community to examine the identified challenges through their own practical lens. Ultimately, our goal is to accelerate the adoption of XAI by providing a comprehensive framework and generating a bank of ideas for both XAI practitioners and RE experts. is essential for customizing patient care and surveillance strategies, ultimately aiming to prevent or early detect invasive carcinoma. This characterization depends on analyzing tissue samples histologically to assess malignancy and the degree of dysplasia. Although deep neural networks demonstrate remarkable accuracy in recognizing tissue patterns, interpreting their high-level abstract features remains difficult for pathologists. Consequently, integrating expert insights into deep learning models enhances their transparency and reliability. To explore this synergy, we present slide-level annotations derived from conveneional histopathology reports regarding colorectal polyp characterization and carcinomatous progression, alongside the seamless integration of these expert opinions into deep learning architectures for inference and training. We assess how the explicit incorporation of expert knowledge boosts deep learning model transparency and performance. Our findings indicate that expert annotations serve as valuable supplementary data for both trained models and pathologists interpreting expert-level features within complex medical cases. Specifically, incorporating semantic data into deep learning models for colorectal polyp classification boosts classification accuracy by up to 10% without increasing the model's parameter count. To achieve this, we employ late fusion for feature-level fusion and show that simple architectures can achieve superior results compared to complex convolutional neural networks (CNNs) when equipped with semantic information. Furthermore, we investigate early fusion as a feature-level alternative to strengthen expert-CNN collaboration, demonstrating that this approach also greatly benefits classification performance while maintaining lower model complexity than pure CNNs. We make these proposed techniques for semantic-supervised deep learning models accessible to the community through our code repository. Together, our results offer a comprehensive guide for effectively leveraging semantic information in deep learning models for colorectal polyp classification. The source code and associated data are accessible at https://github.com/BiomedicalImageAnalysisImageRepository/SECRePO. All evaluation datasets and results utilized in this study are sourced from CamoR and CamCol. Expert annotations offer a robust and comprehensive method for supervising deep learning models, enabling clear interpretation of classification decisions and enhancing overall classification accuracy for historically difficult cases. These findings offer significant potential to assist pathologists through decision-making support and the explanation of CNN inferences. The integrated approach of combining deep learning with expert knowledge represents a promising new era for AI-assisted histopathology analysis.

The leakage metric is defined as the ratio between an adversary's successful guessing probability after and before observing the codeword, raised to the power of $1/n$, as $n$ approaches infinity for an $n$-length sequence. This specific instance of minimal leakage, known as maximal $f$-differential privacy, has been studied in database recording and image processing. Assuming the confusion graph is represented as a collection of cliques, we address the associated linear programming problem to determine the leakage bound that achieves maximal $f$-differential privacy for any given source distribution and coding scheme. Additionally, the reverse problem is examined, which involves identifying the optimal confusion graph with a specified number of edges to maximize the leakage bound for a given source distribution and target leakage level. Furthermore, we resolve the problem of minimizing the leakage bound for a given confusion graph by selecting an appropriate coding scheme. These findings establish an analogue of the data processing inequality for maximal $f$-differential privacy in zero-error source coding. Notably, in every examined scenario, the leakage bounds derived are at most $\max \{ s_c-1 \}$, where $s_c$ represents the maximum size of a clique in the confusion graph.

This paper introduces MrSARP, a novel hierarchical deep-generative framework designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery that jointly synthesizes target data at multiple resolutions. During training, MrSARP is jointly optimized to recognize target features across these varying scales. This resolution-variance synthesis enables the model to generate target information adaptable to different SAR radar apertures. By combining super-resolution synthesis with reduced synthetic error rates across resolution scales, MrSARP demonstrates significant potential for prioritizing target data based on the specific observational conditions of the system being designed. Ultimately, MrSARP offers value to SAR image designers by synthesizing target observations across different, realistic system parameters.

By applying the Gauss-Green theorem to find the area of an elliptical sector between two points and then adjusting with the area of a triangle, the segment area is derived. For two ellipses, the total overlap is obtained by summing the areas of relevant sectors and polygons. While the derivation of closed-form expressions for overlapping ellipses is well-established, determining the overlapping area among three ellipses remains challenging, especially when they intersect at more than four points or when no analytical solution exists due to non-standard ellipse parameters or orientations. We demonstrate that this variable satisfies a first-order PDE known as the Hamilton-Jacobi-Ishimura equation (HJI). Furthermore, we prove that the high-degeneracy issue identified for the Q-function is avoided with $

Consequently, this study promotes the application of established techniques from the continuous PDE community to RL. Specifically, numerous highly effective algorithms for solving HJI—previously unexplored in RL—can now be directly imported into the field. Finally, we examine the first-order optimality of standard policy gradient against the HJI, revealing a connection to optimality conditions previously unknown to RL researchers. 2 b exhibits periodic and stochastic transits that are best attributed to an escaping debris cloud, though the mechanism generating this cloud remains unidentified. Determining the grain size and sublimation rate of the debris offers crucial insights into the disintegration environment. Using the Large Binocular Telescope, we conducted simultaneous photometry in the g band (0.48 microns) and KS band (2.16 microns) to constrain particle properties. Modeling the photometric data reveals that g-band observations cannot restrict particle size, given the uncertain cloud geometry; however, combined with stochastic photometry, it suggests no significant KS-band emission, resulting in particle radii exceeding 0.1 microns. Simultaneous g and KS band photometry accurately constrains particle radius to approximately 0.2 microns, which aligns more closely with photometric models of disintegrating ultra-short-period exoplanets. Whether used individually or together, g band and stochasic observations provide superior constraints on particle size compared to sole KS band use, effectively limiting the estimated sublimation rate. We conclude that large, disintegrating atoms or molecules are unlikely, and if stochastic debris play a role in these disintegrating worlds, simultaneous g and KS band observations are essential for constraining particle size and refining estimates of the sublimation rate. This methodology is applicable to other disintegrating and disquieted exoplanets. Such observations were only feasible because g band photometry captured new small disintegration events and stochastic variations at short time scales, highlighting the K2 wide-field, high cadence, and lack of high-frequency cadence gaps as pivotal attributes of its space-based observations. Additionally, our joint statistical analysis of the four disintegrating exoplanets, produced during this study, yields new planetary radii constraints and allows us to formally confirm that GJ 9522 b is not disintegrating.

The library maintains source code compatibility with Python's Pandas and Scikit-Learn packages and provides source code that is fully tested and documented. This documentation is accessible via GitHub Pages and mirrors the structure of the library's NuGet package. Daany is developed using Agile practices within an Open Source environment, and users are encouraged to contribute through issues, pull requests, and collaborations. The project is released under the MIT License and is freely available for use on Windows, Linux, and Mac.
